Title: A rational design strategy and validation for protease-resistant fusion-inhibitor antiviral peptides
Authors: Yang, K.; Wang, C.; Topi, F.; Muratcioglu, S.; Kant, R.; Strandin, T.; Bong, Y. T.; Kareinen, L.; Mäki, S.; Saber, S. H.; Binder, T.; Sironen, T.; Subramanian, S.; White, K. I.; Pfuetzner, R.; Esquivies, L.; Vapalahti, O.; Joensuu, M.; Kuriyan, J.; Hepojoki, J.; Balistreri, G.; Brunger, A. T.
Abstract: Peptide-based fusion inhibitors are promising pharmaceuticals in the fight against enveloped viruses relying on membrane fusion for host infection. However, peptide therapeutic applications have long been hindered by their poor stability in vivo. Here, we discovered that peptide inhibitors with the wildtype sequence of the heptad repeat 2 (HR2) domain of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein are efficiently cleaved by Transmembrane Protease, Serine 2 (TMPRSS2), a key protease involved in the SARS-CoV-2 virus-cell fusion pathway. We then identified the corresponding cleavage sites and designed three protease-resistant peptides using ranking based on deep mutational scanning and natural occurrence. The three candidates all exhibit inhibitory activity in a cell-cell fusion assay. A high-resolution cryo-EM structure of the top candidate, HR2-NHN, bound to its HR1 target reveals the molecular basis for its potent activity. The top candidate of the cell-based screening assay showed significantly improved efficacy relative to the wildtype peptide when administered at different times before infection in both an authentic virus-cell infection assay and a mouse assay. More broadly, our results suggest that the design strategies for protease-resistant peptides could be applied to a broad spectrum of other enveloped viruses and pave the way for the development of safe, prophylactic antivirals that can be administered before exposure.

Title: Regulatory plasticity of the rdar biofilm morphotype in clinical uropathogenic Escherichia coli and its modulation by ciprofloxacin
Authors: Mushtaq, F.; Ali, I.; Sarfaraz, H.; Younas, R.; Bala, A.; Uhlin, B. E.; Romling, U.; Ahmad, I.
Abstract: Background: Red, dry and rough (rdar) biofilm formation in Escherichia coli is characterized by the coordinated production of extracellular cellulose and amyloid curli fimbriae. Although rdar biofilm formation has been extensively characterized in laboratory strains, its clinical relevance and implications for antimicrobial treatment remain poorly understood. Methods: We screened 146 consecutive E. coli isolates from patients with urinary tract infections in Lahore, Pakistan (2017-2019) for Congo red morphotypes at 28 degrees C and 37 degrees C. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by disc diffusion and compared between morphotypes using the Fisher exact test. Fourteen isolates were whole-genome sequenced, the csgD-csgBA intergenic region was aligned, and csgD expression was quantified by qRT-PCR. The effect of 10 micrograms/mL ciprofloxacin on rdar morphotype expression, matrix ultrastructure and biofilm formation was examined in ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates (MIC at least 128 micrograms/mL). Results: Rdar-like colony morphotypes were expressed by 36.3% (53/146) of isolates at 28 degrees C and 29.5% (43/146) at 37 degrees C. Nucleotide polymorphisms in the csgD-csgBA intergenic region clustered within annotated OmpR, IHF and CsgD binding regions and were associated with, but did not individually predict, the mode of rdar morphotype expression. Isolates carrying the rdar morphotype were distributed across diverse E. coli phylogroups and sequence types. Resistance to aztreonam, cefuroxime and cephradine was more frequent among smooth and white isolates, whereas resistance to nitrofurantoin was more frequent among isolates rdar-positive at 28 degrees C (45.2% versus 20.2%, p = 0.0097); fluoroquinolone resistance did not differ between morphotypes. Subinhibitory ciprofloxacin (10 micrograms/mL) suppressed rdar biofilm formation, disrupted extracellular matrix architecture and abolished surface colonization on glass, in ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates. Conclusions: Our findings establish the rdar morphotype as a clinically relevant biofilm phenotype in uropathogenic E. coli and show that subinhibitory ciprofloxacin suppresses rdar biofilm formation in ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates. These results underscore the importance of considering antibiotic-mediated modulation of biofilm behavior when interpreting treatment responses and designing strategies to combat persistent urinary tract infections.

Title: Naked antisense oligonucleotides access the cytosol during early endocytic trafficking
Authors: Sitarska, E.; Saminathan, A.; Scanavachi, G.; Somerville, E.; Stock, P.; Shen, P.; Kahne, D.; Courtney, M. F.; Reid, D. A.; Danielsen, M. B.; Davidsen, F. K. N.; Jensen, K. J.; Bennett, F. C.; Kirchhausen, T.
Abstract: Phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) enter cells, but their site of productive escape remains uncertain. We combined live-cell imaging and ratiometric pH measurements to follow a Malat1-targeting ASO internalized without a delivery vehicle. In U2OS cells, less than 4% of internalized ASO reached the nucleus under conditions that reduced Malat1 RNA by >90%. Most ASO accumulated in late endosomes, endolysosomes and lysosomes as foci and broadly distributed luminal signal. These compartments underwent neutralization without detectable membrane rupture or galectin-3 recruitment. ASO foci showed constrained motion, consistent with association with endolysosomal constituents. L-leucyl-L-leucine methyl ester-induced membrane damage or Calcium dependent lysosome exocytosis released dextran while retaining luminal ASO. Loss of the stress-granule scaffolding proteins G3BP1/2 modestly enhanced ASO activity without detectable endolysosomal damage. Tantalosin, a small molecule that perturbs endosomal recycling, redistributed the ESCRT-III protein IST1 to endosomes. It enhanced early escape of SYTOX Green and ASOs, detected by nuclear accumulation, and increased Malat1 knockdown, with cell-type-dependent responses. Tantalosin did not detectably increase nuclear ASO accumulation after sequestration in late compartments. These findings place productive ASO escape early in endocytic trafficking, most likely in early or recycling endosomes, before sequestration in largely nonproductive late compartments.

Title: SMARTFlexDB: a paired apo-holo RNA structure database and analysis platform for RNA conformational flexibility and small-molecule recognition
Authors: Jiang, S.; Wei, J.; Taghavi, A.; Seabra, G.; Childs-Disney, J. L.; Li, C.; Disney, M. D.; Li, Y.
Abstract: RNA structures can undergo substantial conformational changes upon small-molecule binding, yet existing structural resources provide only static RNA-ligand snapshots without connecting ligand-bound (holo) RNA structures to corresponding ligand-free (apo) conformations. SMARTFlexDB is a curated database and analysis platform that uses paired apo-holo RNA structures to characterize conformational differences and RNA-small molecule recognition. Candidate pairs were identified from the Protein Data Bank by matching RNA chains with at least 90% sequence identity and coverage, and fully conserved binding pocket nucleotides. The current release contains 434 binding pockets from 266 holo structures, linked to 186 apo structures to yield 1187 pocket-level apo-holo pairs organized into 734 database entries, spanning 150 small molecules and 23 RNA functional classes. Each entry integrates RNA sequence and secondary-structure annotations, apo and holo three-dimensional structures, RNA-ligand atomic interactions, and quantitative descriptors of global and local conformational changes. An interactive web interface enables users to explore sequence alignments and structural overlays, compare secondary structures and RNA motifs, and upload paired apo-holo structures for customized analysis. By linking ligand-bound and ligand-free RNA structures, SMARTFlexDB provides a robust foundation for investigating RNA structural flexibility and supporting RNA-targeted small-molecule drug discovery. The database and analysis platform are available at https://aidd.rc.ufl.edu/app/smartflexdb/.

Title: Identification of cis-Acting Elements that Regulate Influenza A Virus Segment 7 Differential mRNA Splicing
Authors: Zhou, S.; Pinto, R. M.; Chook, H. W.; Lee, H. M.; Gaunt, E. R.; Digard, P.
Abstract: Influenza A virus segment 7 encodes the M1 matrix protein and M2 ion channel from an unspliced primary transcript (mRNA1) and spliced mRNA2, respectively. Both proteins are essential for efficient virus replication, but the intrinsic sequences that determine segment 7 splicing balance are not fully defined. Here, we systematically investigated how conserved cis-acting splicing elements regulate segment splicing. We found that while the splice acceptor sequence is optimal, both potential upstream polypyrimidine tracts regulate splicing, with the 5' region acting positively and the 3' region negatively to maintain M1 expression. Nucleotide A713 is the most likely mRNA2 branch point, but potentially with redundancy from other local adenosines. Mutagenesis of the mRNA2 splice donor sequence showed that it is nearly optimal but that nucleotides 51 and 55 modestly downregulate splicing efficiency. Most introduced mutations that change splicing balance are nonsynonymous in M1. Nevertheless, polypyrimidine tract and branch point mutations that significantly perturbed M1:M2 balance resulted in viable viruses. In contrast, the splice donor sequence was largely intolerant of mutation. We conclude that M1:M2 balance is maintained via suboptimal splice donor and polypyrimidine tract splicing signals, with the latter allowing more evolutionary flexibility to vary the ratio and/or M1 sequence

Title: timePlex: Increasing mass spectrometry throughput using time-encoded sample multiplexing
Authors: Derks, J.; McDonnell, K.; Specht, H.; Geiszler, D. J.; Agius, M. P.; Xie, X.; Sandow, J. J.; Chen, L.; Warinner, L. K.; Wamsley, N.; Sipe, S. N.; Stewart, P.; Yeh, M.; Slavov, N.
Abstract: Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) can enable precise and accurate quantification of analytes at high-sensitivity, but the rate at which samples can be analyzed remains limited. Throughput can be increased by data-independent-acquisition (DIA) using short separation times and by multiplexing samples in the mass domain with plexDIA; yet multiplexing along one dimension scales throughput only linearly with plex. To enable combinatorial scaling of proteomics throughput, we developed a complementary DIA strategy that multiplexes samples in the time domain, termed `timePlex'. timePlex staggers and overlaps the separation periods of individual samples. This strategy is orthogonal to isotopic multiplexing, which enables combinatorial multiplexing in mass and time domains, and thus multiplicatively increased throughput. We demonstrate this with a 27-plex (3-timePlex and 9-plexDIA) exceeding 1,200 samples (4M protein datapoints) per day. These results establish timePlex as a framework for multiplexing both label-free and labeled samples that supports sensitive and accurate protein quantification and combinatorial scaling.

Title: Bayesian model-based method for clustering gene expression time series with multiple replicates
Authors: Nushi, E.; Douillard, F. P.; Selby, K.; Lindström, M.; Honkela, A.
Abstract: Background: In this study, we introduce a Bayesian model-based method for clustering transcriptomics time series data with multiple replicates. This technique is based on sampling Gaussian processes (GPs) within an infinite mixture model from a Dirichlet process (DP). Our method uses multiple GP models to accommodate for multiple differently behaving experimental replicates within each cluster. We call it multiple models Dirichlet process Gaussian process (MMDPGP) mixture model. We compare our method with state-of-the-art model-based clustering approaches for handling gene expression time series with multiple replicates. Results: To demonstrate the accuracy of our method we use it to cluster synthetically generated data sets. The clusters produced by our method on the synthetic data had a significantly higher purity score compared to the state-of-the- art approaches. We also present a case study where all methods are applied for clustering RNA-Seq time series of Clostridium botulinum with three different experimental replicates. The results obtained from the gene enrichment analysis showed that the number of significantly enriched sets of genes is larger in the clusters produced by MMDPGP. Conclusions: By modelling each replicate with a separate GP, our method can use the natural variability between experimental replicates to learn more about the underlying biology.

Title: Dynamic adhesion device of phage OE33PA drives Gram-positive host recognition
Authors: Schmitt, L.; Chaib, A.; Ptchelkine, D.; Kandiah, E.; Le Marrec, C.; Cambillau, C.; Goulet, A.
Abstract: Bacteriophages (phages) infecting Gram-positive bacteria must bind to host receptors across thick cell walls to initiate infection, yet the underlying structural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Oenococcus oeni siphophage OE33PA, providing the first high-resolution view of a phage infecting this wine-industry bacterium. While the overall virion architecture is conserved, the adhesion device displays distinctive features. Its receptor-binding proteins adopt multiple orientations, revealing an intrinsically dynamic assembly. In situ cryo-electron tomography captures distinct conformations upon host attachment, providing rare structural insight into interactions with Gram-positive hosts. Functional assays further show that a mobile carbohydrate-binding module in the distal tail protein mediates host cell binding. Additionnally, the tape measure protein adopts a hexameric organization, updating the prevailing trimeric model in siphophages. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic adhesion device in a phage infecting Gram-positive bacteria and highlight the structural and functional diversity of phages.

Title: K2P Channels Regulate Presynaptic Organisation through a Membrane Potential-Independent Mechanism
Authors: Meng, J.; Ramakrishnan, N.; Li, Y.; Boulin, T.; Gao, S.; Zhen, M.; Beets, I.; Schafer, W. R.
Abstract: Neuronal ion channels have well-established effects on synaptic plasticity, in many cases by influencing pathways that depend on membrane excitability. Here we find that a C. elegans two-pore domain potassium (K2P) channel, TWK-40, regulates presynaptic organisation through a membrane potential-independent mechanism. Instead, this mechanism depends on TWK-40's effects on intracellular potassium levels. Loss-of-function mutations in twk-40 lead to excessive presynaptic protein accumulation, while gain-of-function mutations lead to depleted presynaptic components and cause synaptic transmission deficits. These changes in presynaptic protein abundance are phenocopied by transporter mutations predicted to alter intracellular potassium homeostasis in the same direction as TWK-40 mutations, but not by sodium channel mutations that mimic its effects on membrane excitability. This indicates that cytoplasmic potassium promotes presynaptic assembly. This process depends on pyruvate kinase PYK-1, a potassium-sensitive enzyme, and three transcription factors. These findings establish a new pathway linking neuronal potassium homeostasis to the control of presynaptic organisation and synaptic function.

Title: Human ribosomes interactions reveal the binding landscape of neomycin
Authors: Wu, M.; Zhu, L.; Wu, K.; Jia, C.; Zhang, X.; Zhao, Z.; Liu, H.; Yi, C.; Sun, S.; Liu, K.; Zhang, Z.; Guo, L.; Hou, X.; Li, W.
Abstract: Aminoglycosides such as neomycin are clinically limited by toxicity, commonly attributed to the inhibition of mitoribosomes. Here, we investigate this model by integrating Cryo-EM and functional assays to assess neomycin's binding landscape and functional consequences for human ribosomes. Cryo-EM reveals extensive multi-site binding of neomycin on both human mitochondrial and cytosolic ribosomes in vitro, including conserved regions of the decoding center. In contrast, ribosomes isolated from neomycin-treated cells show markedly different patterns, with no detectable neomycin density on the mitoribosomes and reduced occupancy at a subset of cytosolic ribosome sites. Functional assays indicate that neomycin remained active in cells, inducing widespread stop-codon readthrough while having minimal effects on global mitochondrial and cytosolic protein synthesis. Together, these findings highlight a disconnect between the structural binding landscape and ribosome-associated neomycin recovered following cellular exposure, while linking neomycin exposure to altered translational fidelity with minimal effects on global protein synthesis.

Title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef.
Authors: Ardanaz Ullate, A.; Agazzi, M.; Lo Iacono, C.; del Campo, J.
Abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province: Madrepora oculata, Desmophyllum pertusum, Leiopathes glaberrima, and Acanthogorgia hirsuta. We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians M. oculata and D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.

Title: The genetic architecture of human DNA methylome variation
Authors: Liu, T.; Macias-Velasco, J. F.; Zhuo, X.; Lin, J.; Porubsky, D.; Zhang, W.; Li, D.; Tomlinson, C.; Belter, E. A.; Dong, Z.; Dong, S.; Human Pangenome Reference Consortium,  ; Eichler, E.; Wang, T.
Abstract: Population DNA methylome analyses remain largely confined to reference-defined genomic space despite extensive human genetic diversity. A central challenge is therefore to define comparable methylation phenotypes across diverse genomes and map the genetic architecture of methylome variation. Here, using 460 haplotypes from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2, we develop two complementary pangenome-based frameworks: one compares methylation within homologous regions while retaining haplotype-specific structural configuration and CpG content; the other represents CpG island (CGI) variation at homologous loci as sequence-resolved alleles. We identified 47,039 CGI alleles, including 8,040 absent from CHM13; 62% were attributable to structural variants and 31% to small variants. Through local genealogies, we reconstructed CGI gain, loss and turnover, revealing how present-day methylation differences align with CGI evolutionary trajectories. We found that genome-wide, methylation variability was buffered against genetic diversity across more than 90% of the genome, with exceptions at extreme nucleotide diversity and locally around structural variants. Our methylation framework enabled population-scale allele-aware methylation quantitative trait locus (mQTL) mapping into non-reference and structurally complex sequence, where mQTL-associated intervals were enriched. mQTLs linked methylation to transcriptomic phenotypes, population differentiation and complex traits, supporting 8% of population differentially methylated regions and colocalizing with more than half of genome-wide association study loci. Together, our study redefines human methylome analysis and our findings reveal a genome-wide architecture of genetic-epigenetic coupling, reshaping how methylation variation is interpreted across human development and disease.

Title: Structure of influenza D virus NS1 reveals a novel Zn-binding site and ssRNA-binding activity
Authors: Ye, K.; Guan, M.; Kim, A. S.; Miller, M. D.; Ma, R.; Hamor, C. W.; Wang, A.; Yuan, Z.; Le, B. T.; Briggs, J. M.; Wan, X.-f.; Tao, Y. J.
Abstract: Influenza D virus (IDV) is an emerging pathogen associated with bovine respiratory disease and has potential for zoonotic transmission. Although nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) is a major virulence factor in influenza A and B viruses, the structure and function of IDV NS1 remain poorly defined. Here, we determined crystal structures of the IDV NS1 N-terminal RNA-binding domain (NTD) and C-terminal effector domain (CTD). The NTD retains the conserved homodimeric six-helix fold, whereas the CTD adopts a distinct architecture containing a novel Zn2+-binding site. IDV NS1 CTD preferentially binds single-stranded RNA, and mutagenesis identified lysine and arginine residues critical for this activity. Single-residue substitutions disrupting either the Zn2+-binding site or RNA-binding interface prevented recovery of infectious recombinant IDV. These findings reveal distinct structural and functional features of IDV NS1 and establish the importance of CTD integrity for viral replication. Conservation of key CTD residues in influenza C virus NS1 suggests shared structural features that distinguish influenza C and D virus NS1 proteins from their influenza A and B counterparts.

Title: Engineering and characterisation of AAVS1 FRT cell lines for inducible and dose-dependent gene expression
Authors: Portillo Malumbres, M.; Ellingboe, L.; Roberti, A.; Nashchekina, O.; Sialana, F. J.; Pines, J.; Choudhary, J. S.; Mansfeld, J.; Davey, N. E.
Abstract: Investigating biological function with high reproducibility requires the generation of stable cell lines that offer precise and inducible transgene expression. However, traditional methods often suffer from the limitations of random genomic integration, including unpredictable expression levels, leaky basal activity, and disruption of endogenous loci. To address these challenges, we engineered a versatile RPE1 cell line by integrating a TetOn3G-FRT cassette into the AAVS1 safe-harbour locus using CRISPR/Cas9(D10A) nickase. This platform utilises the Flp-FRT recombination system to facilitate rapid, site-specific "plug-and-play" insertion of transgenes, combined with the Tet-On 3G system for tight, dose-dependent expression control. The resulting RPE1 AAVS1 FRT8 line enables highly consistent transgene induction across independent clones, behaving as a monoclonal population. We highlight the importance of rigorous cell line characterisation through a multi-omics approach. Whole genome sequencing identified precise heterozygous integration at the target locus and de novo genomic duplications on other chromosomes. By integrating WGS with high-resolution proteomics and cell cycle analysis, we confirmed that these alterations did not significantly perturb cellular homeostasis or phenotypic fitness. This work establishes a robust and reliable platform for the efficient generation of inducible AAVS1 FRT stable cell lines, facilitating reproducible research in modern molecular biology.

Title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
Authors: Oterino-Sogo, S.; Mechkouri, N.; Garcia-Ruano, D.; Groppi, A.; Rezvani, H.-R.; Nikolski, M.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has become a central tool in tissue biology, with multiple technologies addressing the issue from a different angle. Each platform imposes its own raw data format conventions, and few workflows address reproducible, scalable, cohort-level analyses while integrating expert-supervised decisions to strengthen computational and biological provenance. In this work, we present SpaceBlocks, a Snakemake workflow for reproducible cohort-level analysis of single-cell resolution-ST data that prioritizes expert supervision over full automation. SpaceBlocks homogenizes heterogeneous platform outputs into a common data format, whose structure is validated to ensure downstream processing. Comprehensive expert supervision is facilitated through per sample quality control and cell type annotation diagnostic visualizations, after which downstream analyses automatically follow. SpaceBlocks also allows the ingestion of technology-agnostic externally formatted data and provides interoperability with existing tools and technologies. We demonstrate the use of SpaceBlocks through the reanalysis of 37 samples from public Visium HD, Xenium 5K and MERSCOPE datasets. SpaceBlocks exhibited processing scalability across the three platforms. This reanalysis identified previously missed cell types in Visium HD and heterogeneous marker gene expression in MERSCOPE, highlighting the need for expert-supervised annotations. Moreover, SpaceBlocks facilitated the identification of differentially expressed genes associated with previously defined multiple sclerosis (MS) spatial domains in MERSCOPE, and transcriptional differences between healthy and malignant colorectal tissues in Visium HD. Together, these findings establish SpaceBlocks as a flexible and reproducible workflow for expert-supervised spatial transcriptomics analysis across technologies and biological cohorts.

Title: MaCADEMIA: a software toolbox for single-molecule fluorescence image quantification
Authors: Alderson, D.; Catchpole, Z.; Crompton, K.; Sanders, K.; Johnson, S.; Smith, K.; Packer, J.; Harris, K. S.; Rodriguez, J.; Leake, M. C.; Wollman, A. J.
Abstract: Single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) is a powerful tool in molecular and cellular biology and part of the broad umbrella of super-resolution microscopy. A distinct feature of SMLM, is its capacity for deep quantification, beyond just spatial information, to copy number, stoichiometry, molecular interaction and dynamics in living cells. The hardware required is increasingly straightforward to implement. However, complexity remains in the image analysis where much remains fragmented across specialised software tools. Here, we present MaCADEMIA (Matlab Computational Analysis of Diffusion, Emitter Molecular Intensity and Abundance), a simple yet powerful toolbox of MATLAB functions and associated documentation to enable straightforward extraction of quantitative single-molecule information. MaCADEMIA performs ensemble particle detection achieving localisation accuracies down to 0.5 pixels Root mean squared error (RMSE) across wide signal-to-noise (SNR) ranges on standardised particle tracking benchmarks, consistently matching or exceeding the performance of 14 leading methods. Our integrated workflow enables molecular counting and stoichiometry determination through stepwise photobleaching analysis, mobility measurement via mean squared displacement, colocalisaton analysis and absolute protein copy number quantification using three-dimensional cellular models.

Title: Ultra-precision 3D Printed Sample Tubes of Complex Cross Section for Enhanced Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Sensitivity of AqueousSamples
Authors: Anilkumar, A.; Wherley, J. T.; Garces, A. M.; Lerch, M.; Klug, C.; Sidabras, J. W.
Abstract: This paper discusses the applications of ultra-precision 3D printing in developing EPR sample tubes for X-band measurements of aqueous samples. The seed idea of this work started from the flat cell idea discussed in Mett and Hyde et al.(2003), Sidabras et al. (2005), and Sidabras et al. (2017), where placing multiple aqueous flat cells perpendicular to the electric field in the microwave cavity reduce RF losses and improve EPR signal sensitivity. In this work, we present the 3D printed aquastar sample holders for dielectric resonators and the aquasun sample holders for cavity resonators. Even though the ultra-precision 3D printing enables the fabrication of complex cross-sections at 25um resolution, the photopolymer material has comparatively higher dielectric losses compared to the conventional materials like glass and PTFE. To reduce the RF losses due to the inherent dielectric properties, we introduced the latticing approach in reducing the amount of plastic without compromising the structural stability. In addition to this, we present the slicing and dielectric approximation approach in reducing the computation cost for these complex cross-sections. The novel sample tubes discussed here present signal improvements through both simulation and experiments, which were validated through power saturation experiments. The sample tube development methodology presented here provide a general framework for designing and implementing 3D printed EPR sample holders, based on resonator electromagnetic field distribution and dielectric properties of the photopolymer material.

Title: Long-PDE4D degradation attenuates left ventricular cardiomyocyte hypertrophic remodelling
Authors: Judina, A.; Shi, Z.; Fu, J.; Sherstnev, I.; Boichenko, V.; Ling, J.; Hussain, M.; Zorn, A.; Sin, Y. Y.; Wang, H.; Li, A.; Korogodski, S.; Torres, E.; Stirling, D.; Chan, K.; Swindlehurst, C.; Kibread, I.; Black, I.; Nicklin, S.; Baillie, G. S.; Gorelik, J.
Abstract: Spatial compartmentalisation enables cyclic AMP (cAMP) to regulate distinct cellular functions, yet selectively targeting disease-associated signalling remains challenging. Phosphodiesterases constrain local cAMP responses, but conventional inhibitors offer limited isoform selectivity. Here we investigate whether targeted degradation of long phosphodiesterase-4D (PDE4D) isoforms can suppress pathological growth while preserving contractile function. Using adult rat and human ventricular cardiomyocytes and human myocardial slices, we show that the proteolysis-targeting chimera KTX-184 enhances compartmentalised cAMP signalling and attenuates hypertrophic remodelling. In rat cardiomyocytes, KTX-184 increases {beta}-adrenergic cAMP responses in the cytosol and at the plasma membrane, including T-tubule and crest regions, and enhances nuclear protein kinase A activity. In contrast, phospholamban- and ryanodine receptor-associated cAMP nanodomains, calcium transients and sarcomere shortening remain unchanged. KTX-184 prevents angiotensin II-induced hypertrophic remodelling, preserves T-tubule organisation and normalises hypertrophic marker expression. In human cardiomyocytes, it increases cytosolic cAMP responses and prevents overload-induced hypertrophy in myocardial slices. These findings identify long PDE4D isoforms as targets for spatially selective modulation of cAMP signalling and support targeted degradation as an approach to suppress cardiac hypertrophy without increasing contractility.

Title: PFOS and GenX Induce Mitochondrial Toxicity and Differentially Alter Respiratory Complex Activities in Liver and Brain
Authors: Boonpraman, N.; Kim, D.-W.; Pai, S.; Kuhn, N.; O'Keefe, J.; Sammi, S.
Abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants associated with adverse health effects, yet the mitochondrial consequences of exposure to individual PFAS and their mixtures remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the individual and combined effects of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (GenX) on mitochondrial respiratory complex activities under acute, sub-chronic, and chronic exposure conditions. Acute effects were evaluated using isolated mouse liver and brain mitochondria, while repeated exposure was assessed in mice treated with PFOS, GenX, or their combination at 0.2, 2, and 10 mg/kg body weight for 1 month or 0.2 mg/kg for 5 months. PFAS distribution in plasma and brain tissues, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) protein expression, and predicted interactions with mitochondrial Complexes III and IV were also examined. Acute exposure inhibited Complex III and IV activities, with combined treatment generally producing greater inhibition than either compound alone. Following sub-chronic exposure, mitochondrial responses varied according to dose, treatment, and tissue, with more pronounced reductions in liver complex activities and comparatively limited changes in brain enzyme activities. Chronic low-dose exposure altered selected brain mitochondrial complex activities, while PFAS measurements revealed differences in plasma concentration and distribution across brain regions. OXPHOS protein expression also varied across brain regions and exposure conditions. Molecular docking indicated distinct predicted interaction patterns, with PFOS generally exhibiting more favorable scores at Complex III binding sites and GenX at selected Complex IV regions. Overall, these findings demonstrate exposure-dependent and tissue-specific mitochondrial responses to PFOS and GenX and highlight the importance of evaluating combined PFAS exposure across multiple exposure durations.

Title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
Authors: Zintel, M. A.; LeBlanc, C. J.; Kotha, S. R.; Soriano, M.; Bansal, R. J.; Aguilera, D.; Majidi, T.; Ornelas, I.; Kirkpatrick, L. D.; Udupa, A.; Hu, G.; Agarwal, P.; Lam, A. W. Y.; Nunez, J. K.; Shih, P. M.; Sozzani, R.; Strader, L. C.; Staller, M. V.
Abstract: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships1. Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

Title: Uncovering disease progression trajectories across multiple timescales with hybrid ODE-mixture models
Authors: de Rooij, M.; Quadt, J. D.; van Riel, N. A. W.; O'Donovan, S.
Abstract: Biological systems are capable of evolving across multiple timescales, yet most modeling approaches capture either short-term physiological responses or long-term disease progression. Additionally, methods that combine these time scales either struggle with inter-individual variation, or require large volumes of data to work. We present Latent Class Parameter Trajectory Analysis (LCPTA), a hybrid framework that combines mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE) modeling of short-term dynamics with latent class trajectory modeling of long-term parameter evolution. To support this approach, we developed TemporalMixtureModels.jl, a Julia package for univariate and multivariate temporal mixture modeling. We evaluated LCPTA in two synthetic longitudinal studies, covering a simulation of a heterogeneous population developing hypertension, as well as a synthetic longitudinal study of 75 virtual individuals followed over 30 years, representing muscle insulin resistance, liver insulin resistance, and healthy trajectories. We compared LCPTA with a conditional neural ODE and a conditional neural network for reconstruction of long-term parameter trajectories and subgroup separation. In both studies LCPTA recovered relevant subgroup structure and trajectory patterns. In the cardiovascular study, the neural approaches were able to distinguish inter-individual differences, but in the insulin sensitivity study, neural approaches failed to represent parameter trajectories faithfully, primarily separating individuals along a single dominant parameter and showing weaker multivariate trajectory reconstruction. In additional experiments with sparse and irregularly sampled unseen individuals, LCPTA maintained strong classification performance. We show that LCPTA is an efficient and interpretable strategy for multiscale modeling of heterogeneous metabolic disease progression, with potential utility for data-efficient digital twin applications.

Title: The Global Phosphorylation Landscape of Acute Heat Stress in Reef-Building Corals
Authors: Ashley, I. A.; Tortorelli, G.; Nguyen, J.; Alba, K.; Majerova, E.; Winters, D.; Carthen, S.; Perez, T.; Rosset, S. L.; Drury, C.; Bouhaddou, M.
Abstract: Warming oceans disrupt the coral-algal symbiosis that sustains reefs, yet the signaling mechanisms initiating bleaching remain poorly understood. Integrating global phosphoproteomics across three reef-building corals with protein structure modeling revealed conservation between coral and human kinases, enabling inference of coral kinase activities and uncovering a shared signaling program induced by acute heat stress. Heat rapidly activated ERK, JNK, and p38 MAP kinases, suppressed cell cycle signaling, and remodeled pathways controlling chromatin, RNA processing, and metabolism. Most strikingly, thermal stress rewired immune receptor signaling networks associated with non-self recognition, suggesting that heat shifts the coral host from tolerance to immune recognition of its algal symbionts. These findings define conserved signaling mechanisms that precede bleaching, revealing actionable molecular targets for enhancing coral resilience.

Title: Caspase-1 and -11 defend against environmental but not host-adapted pathogens in genetically complex mice
Authors: Li, L.; McGlaughon, B. D.; Larson, H. N.; Koller, B. H.; Miao, E. A.
Abstract: Caspase-1 and -11 are inflammatory caspases that trigger pyroptosis, yet in most infection models they confer only a modest survival benefit. We have proposed that caspase-1 and -11 evolved primarily to defend against ubiquitous environmental microbes that have not been under selective pressure to evade them, whereas host-adapted pathogens have evolved evasion strategies. Testing this idea is complicated because the inbred mouse strains used in most infection studies carry mutations in innate immune genes: i.e., C57BL/6 (B6) mice carry a loss-of-function Nramp1 allele, and 129 mice lack functional caspase-11. Here we generated B6 x 129 F1 hybrid mice, which are gene-sufficient at both Nramp1 and Casp11, and used them to measure the fold change in lethal dose ({triangleup}LD100) caused by caspase-1 and -11 deficiency for four pathogens on the B6, 129, and F1 backgrounds. Caspase-1 and -11 conferred little or no survival benefit against the host-adapted pathogens Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella Typhimurium on any of the three backgrounds, apart from a modest benefit at the lowest S. Typhimurium inoculum in F1 mice. In contrast, caspase-1 and -11 were required to survive infection with the environmental pathogens Burkholderia thailandensis and Chromobacterium violaceum, where caspase-1 and -11 deficiency lowered the lethal dose by up to six orders of magnitude. The failure of caspase-1 and -11 against host-adapted pathogens therefore persists on a genetically robust hybrid background, supporting the view that a major evolutionary role of caspase-1 and -11 is defense against environmental microbes that have not been selected to evade them.

Title: A minimal two-residue C-terminal truncation of AID in adult-onset hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2)
Authors: Green, K.; Rovsing, A. B.; Terczynska-Dyla, E.; Jensen, L.; Machalica, K.; Wolff, J. H.; Westerberg, L.; Larsen, C. S.; Lin, L.; Mikkelsen, J. G.; Jensen, J. M. B.; Degn, S. E.
Abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), encoded by AICDA, facilitates class-switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM) in activated B cells. Loss of AID function causes hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2). While typically autosomal recessive, three C-terminal truncation variants have been reported to act in autosomal dominant manner. We describe a novel heterozygous AICDA nonsense variant, c.589G>T (p.G197*), that truncates the final two C-terminal residues of AID and results in adult-onset HIGM2. Single-cell sequencing of primary patient B cells revealed a complete block in CSR and a [~]10-fold reduction in SHM. AICDA mRNA expression was balanced between wild-type and variant alleles, yet AID protein abundance was reduced to [~]56% with normal subcellular localization. Remarkably, inducible germinal center (iGB) cultures restored CSR in purified naive patient B cells. CRISPR-Cas9 editing of healthy donor B cells confirmed that the iGB platform can rescue B cells harboring heterozygous, but not homozygous, AICDA variants. These results demonstrate that even a two-amino-acid truncation at the AID C-terminus is sufficient to disrupt its function and cause HIGM2.

Title: Genomic context tunes sequence-encoded RNA processing
Authors: Nielsen, M. L.; Tyukaev, A.; Garkul, L.; Ulitsky, I.
Abstract: Sequence and genomic position jointly determine RNA processing, but at native loci the two are difficult to separate. Here, we uncoupled them by integrating RNA-processing elements into endogenous transcription units at tens of thousands of mapped positions and different elements at shared positions. Genomic position dominated RNA production levels but differentially influenced RNA processing events. A cryptic polyadenylation site, used natively only upon U1 inhibition, was rarely used ectopically. In contrast, introns partially retained at their native loci remained so across thousands of ectopic positions, with a substantial fraction of transcripts reaching the cytoplasm unspliced. SON depletion reduced splicing of two such introns, preferentially near speckles. Chromatin state, GC content, and speckle proximity tuned this behavior without overriding it, and in opposite directions: speckle proximity improved the splicing of one intron and reduced that of another. Specialized introns are therefore portable modules carrying their own processing information.

Title: Generation of functional adipoids from human induced pluripotent stem cells
Authors: Hinte, L. C.; Okamoto, R.; Jansen, S.; Spirig, S. E.; Tsiepa, S.; Shimobayashi, M.; Hall, M. N.
Abstract: Human adipose tissue models are lacking although essential for metabolic research. Traditional primary cell cultures are poorly scalable and unsuitable for drug screening or modeling of genetic disease. Conventional two-dimensional adipocyte cultures cannot withstand the long-term treatment required to mimic chronic conditions such as obesity and insulin resistance. To overcome these limitations, we developed an accessible protocol to produce three-dimensional human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived adipocyte microtissues, termed adipoids. hiPSC-derived adipoids display long-term stability and viability. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed that adipoids contain mature adipocytes and adipocyte stem/progenitor cells, similar to human adipose tissue. Furthermore, hiPSC-derived adipoids contain unilocular adipocytes, exhibit stimulated lipolysis, and secrete adipokines. Thus, hiPSC-derived adipoids provide a functional, scalable and genetically tractable model to perform large-scale pharmacological screens and to investigate human metabolic disease.

Title: XRN1-dependent RNA homeostasis regulates hepatitis D virus
Authors: Tsukuda, S.; Boutasbih, M.; Wing, P. A. C.; Fedorov, A.; Zhu, X.; Rehwinkel, J.; Balfe, P.; McKeating, J. A.
Abstract: Hepatitis delta virus (HDV) infection causes the most severe form of viral hepatitis, yet the host mechanisms restricting HDV replication remain poorly understood. Although HDV infection activates the MDA5-LGP2 pathway and induces robust interferon (IFN) responses, these antiviral programs have limited impact on viral replication. Here we identify the 5-3 exoribonuclease XRN1 as a key regulator of HDV infection. Loss of XRN1 in hepatoma cells increased double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) levels and induced interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), including MDA5 and MAVS, and limited HDV infection. XRN1 deficiency enhanced ADAR1-mediated RNA editing, revealing a dynamic interplay between endogenous dsRNA metabolism and antiviral sensing. Inhibition of type I IFN signaling restored MDA5 expression and rescued HDV replication in XRN1-deficient cells. To identify the downstream effectors responsible for this restriction, we combined transcriptomic profiling with functional siRNA screening and identified DUSP5 and SIRPA as previously unrecognized ISGs with anti-HDV activity. Together, our findings establish XRN1 as a gatekeeper of dsRNA homeostasis that controls HDV replication through innate immune activation and reveals host antiviral effectors that may provide therapeutic opportunities for chronic hepatitis D.

Title: Single-probe, amplification-free multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH maps bacterial gene expression in intact three-dimensional biofilms
Authors: Barbosa, A.; Smith, H. J.; Parker, A.; Jones, C. J.; Goeres, D. M.; Azevedo, N. F.; Cerqueira, L.
Abstract: Biofilms are spatially structured communities in which local microenvironments drive physiological differentiation, yet mapping gene expression inside intact three-dimensional biofilms remains challenging. Bacterial spatial transcriptomics methods typically rely on tiled probe sets, sequential hybridization rounds, or signal amplification. Here, we show that a single short, directly labelled peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe per target is sufficient to quantify bacterial mRNA in situ without amplification. With all probes designed for a common hybridization condition, a transcript panel is resolved in one hybridization on a standard confocal microscope, in unmodified cells while preserving biofilm architecture. Benchmarked against the biphasic cycle of Legionella pneumophila, multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH recovers the expected transcriptional switch and agrees quantitatively with RT-qPCR in planktonic and biofilm populations. In flow-cell biofilms, it shows that sessile populations do not recapitulate the planktonic program and that transcriptional differences follow cellular aggregation state rather than depth.

Title: Mechanotransduction tuned by intermediate filaments promotes DNA repair in stiff environments
Authors: Dehours, C.; Locatelli, M.; Lepetit, C.; Smelser, A.; Lee, H.; Holmes, J.; Song, Q.; Gabber, M.; Bertho, M.; Lelievre, S.; Bonin, K.; Guthold, M.; Vidi, P.-A.
Abstract: High mammographic density increases breast cancer risk. Dense tissues are rich in fibrillar collagen, forming a rigid extracellular matrix around the epithelium. Although cancer initiation and progression are closely tied to DNA damage and to the DNA damage response, if and how tissue stiffness affects genome maintenance is not fully elucidated. We found that repair factor recruitment is more efficient, and that DNA breaks are repaired faster by cells on rigid substrates. Mechanistically, hemidesmosomal integrins, intermediate filaments, the LINC complex, and YAP are key mediators of this mechanogenomic response. Rigid tissue contexts favor survival of cells with DNA damage, which may lead to the accumulation of somatic mutations, as identified here with RNAseq analyses of normal breast tissue. Our findings provide new insights into how tissue rigidity influences cancer risk.

Title: Spatiotemporal mapping of endothelial proliferative response in acute chemical liver injury
Authors: Rajput, A. S.; Yoon, H.; Travis, K. L.; Hernandez, E. J.; Shah, E. P.; Azizoglu, D. B.
Abstract: Endothelial cells are major contributors to liver injury response, regeneration, and chronic liver disease. Previous studies identified a proliferative endothelial response to acute liver injury; however, a comprehensive characterization of this adaptive response is missing. We have developed a novel pipeline for spatiotemporal analysis of proliferative response in the liver. We demonstrate that endothelial cells enter the cell cycle upon acute centrilobular injury with a delay compared to hepatocytes and in a spatially distinct pattern from hepatocytes. We show that endothelial cycling predominantly occurs in the pericentral zone, while hepatocyte cycling occurs uniformly throughout the lobule. Endothelial cycling in injured livers leads to heightened clonal expansion, and to serial division rarely observed in homeostatic livers. Consequently, injured lobules exhibit endothelial overabundance during regeneration. Our study provides an in-depth characterization of endothelial proliferative response to liver injury and establishes a novel pipeline for spatiotemporal mapping of hepatic cell states.

Title: Conformation governs cellular behaviors of LRRK2 Parkinson's disease variants
Authors: Hatch, K. S.; Surridge, K. J.; Gai, W.; Quan, B.; Kumar, G.; Lattal, N.; Abrisch, R.; Pagani, N.; Leschziner, A. E.; Reck-Peterson, S. L.
Abstract: Gain-of-function of leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is a common cause of Parkinson's disease (PD). In its autoinhibited state, the leucine-rich repeats of LRRK2 block the kinase active site, preventing substrate phosphorylation. Displacing the repeats ('unlatching') primes LRRK2 for activity. Preferential unlatching causes increased substrate phosphorylation of the PD allele LRRK2[R1441H], but not LRRK2[G2019S]. Here, we define a large class of PD-associated 'unlatching' mutations based on their effect on LRRK2 conformation. Unlatching mutants show increased localization to membranes, the site of LRRK2's Rab substrates. Unlatching mutants are also characterized by decreased LRRK2 S935 phosphorylation, which we define as a biomarker of conformation. This framework resolves the mechanism of variants such as I2020T, which structural studies could not predict. Overall, we establish unlatching as a unifying mechanism for most PD-linked variants and describe measurable readouts for identifying LRRK2-driven disease.

Title: Tiled base editing screens uncover rare second-site mutations that rescue a misfolded disease protein
Authors: Rawat, S.; Sarkar, P.; Giavedoni, E.; Pusapati, G. V.; Padmanarayana, M.; Shin, M.; Phillippi, E.; Simmons, T.; Azaria, R.; Shukla, D.; Schultz, M. L.; Rohatgi, R.
Abstract: Therapeutic base editing can directly revert ~30% of disease-causing missense mutations to the wild-type sequence. One strategy to broaden its reach is to install second-site corrector mutations that improve protein stability or function across multiple pathogenic alleles. Here, we use tiled adenine and cytosine base editing screens to identify such corrector mutations in NPC1, a lysosomal cholesterol transporter whose misfolding causes Niemann-Pick type C disease. Tiling mutagenesis of the endogenous NPC1 locus in haploid human cells carrying the prevalent NPC1I1061T disease allele, combined with phenotypic reporters for cholesterol transport and protein abundance, uncovered rare intragenic suppressor mutations distributed across multiple domains. Unexpectedly, we identified a promiscuous second-site variant that can correct many different pathogenic NPC1 mutations. These correctors improve protein stability, promote ER exit and lysosomal trafficking, and restore cholesterol clearance in patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons. Our results establish in situ base editing screens for the discovery of second-site corrector mutations that are actionable for therapeutic base editing when the original mutation cannot be corrected.

Title: HNRNPC-mediated RNA processing promotes VHL-associated excessive vasculogenesis in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome revealed from patient-derived blood vessel models
Authors: Ito, H.; Sato, I.; Matsuo-Takasaki, M.; Shimizu, T.; Noguchi, M.; Nakamura, Y.; Kubo, N.; Takagi, D.; Tamura, M.; K Saito, M.; Takayanagi, S.; Saito, N.; Nakamura, E.; Hayashi, Y.
Abstract: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome (VHLS) is an inherited disorder characterized by excessive vascularization, which contributes to the development of hemangioblastomas and benign or malignant tumors, as well as renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and cysts in multiple organs. VHLS is caused by mutations in VHL tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Although therapeutic agents targeting hypoxia-inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF2A), which is stabilized by VHL loss and promotes tumor angiogenesis, have been approved for clinical use, their therapeutic response remains limited in RCC patients associated with VHLS. Therefore, there is an unmet need for the development of alternative therapeutic approaches independent of HIF2A. Here, we establish a human iPSCs-based model of VHLS-associated excessive vasculogenesis using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from VHLS patients and VHL-edited isogenic iPSC lines. Vascular cells (VCs) differentiated from these VHLS-specific iPSCs exhibited excessive blood vessel formation compared to healthy donor-derived VCs, leading to vascular lesion formation characterized by abundant blood vessels and abnormal cellular growth in vivo. Mechanistically, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were preferentially stabilized in the patient-VCs. Among these RBPs, the stabilization of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (HNRNPC), which is a substrate for pVHL-mediated protein degradation independent of HIF2A expression, was critical for the dysregulated vascularization caused by VHL inactivation in this model. These findings provide an iPSCs-derived vascular platform to elucidate VHLS mechanisms and identify HNRNPC as a potential therapeutic target for VHL-driven vascular lesion formations through an HIF2A-independent mechanism.

Title: Hydrogel crosslinking mechanisms influence the release and functional delivery of lipid nanoparticles
Authors: Schreiber, A. G.; Hauswirth, F.; Reger, L.; Carneiro, S. P.; Merkel, O. M.; Breunig, M.
Abstract: Hydrogels have emerged as attractive vaccine delivery platforms because they enable controlled modulation of antigen availability. However, how different hydrogel environments affect the release and functionality of mRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the release, stability, cellular uptake, and transfection capability of LNPs released from four hydrogel systems representing distinct crosslinking mechanisms: covalently crosslinked poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), ionically crosslinked alginate, thermoresponsive Poloxamer 407 (P407), and protein-based Matrigel/collagen hydrogels. All hydrogel types enabled release of LNPs over days, with lower polymer concentrations generally exhibiting faster nanoparticle release. PEG offered greatest tunability of release kinetics; at the same time the recovery of the LNP-incorporated fluorescent dye DiI was reduced to about 80 %, indicating partial dye leakage. Alginate hydrogels exhibited recovery of DiI below 50 % and broader particle size distributions after release, while P407 hydrogels largely preserved LNP characteristics. CyroTEM analysis revealed that mRNA-LNPs kept at 37 , including those released from hydrogels, exhibited a more compact and electron-dense morphology than mRNA LNPs maintained at 4 . Notably, although quantitative recovery from Matrigel/collagen hydrogels was limited, released LNPs achieved approximately 80-90 % of the eGFP expression compared to mRNA-LNPs that have not been embedded. Importantly, cellular uptake and transfection experiments demonstrated that all investigated hydrogels released biologically active mRNA-LNPs capable of mediating protein expression. Moreover, our findings show that hydrogel composition is a critical determinant of mRNA-LNP release, stability, functional delivery and morphology of the released particles. This work provides design principles for the development of hydrogel-based mRNA delivery systems aimed at sustained antigen availability and prolonged vaccine responses.

Title: Conserved catalytic activity of animal TIR domains functions in TLR4 signaling
Authors: Hurieva, B.; Christ, S. B.; Schwojer, S. J.; Osterman, I.; Bergmaier, A.-L.; Falkovich, A. H.; Yirmiya, E.; Leavitt, A.; Garb, J.; Roth, O.; Amitai, G.; Hornung, V.; Sorek, R.
Abstract: The Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain is important for immune signaling across bacteria, plants, and animals. In animal innate immunity, TIR domains are thought to function as adaptors mediating protein-protein interactions, yet studies in bacteria and plants revealed that TIR domains often act as enzymes that produce immune signaling molecules. Here, we show that catalytic activity is a conserved property of TIR domains across the animal tree of life. We find that TIR domains from evolutionarily diverse animals, including the TIR domain of human TLR4, are enzymes that can produce cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR). We further show that the catalytic residue of TLR4 TIR domain is required for TLR4 signal transduction in human macrophages. Substitution of the catalytic glutamate abolishes LPS-induced inflammatory responses and disrupts Myddosome assembly, revealing a previously unrecognized functional requirement for the TIR catalytic site in TLR4 signaling. Beyond animals, we identify a TIR domain from green algae that produces 3'cADPR, suggesting deep evolutionary conservation of TIR-mediated signaling. Together, our findings establish enzymatic activity as a widespread and evolutionarily conserved property of TIR domains and reveal a functional role for the conserved catalytic site in mammalian innate immune signaling.

Title: A unified photosensitizer platform for in situ DNA, RNA, and protein directed proximity labeling
Authors: Biletch, E. B.; Herlihy, C. P.; Li, L.; Kim, E.; Krebs, M.; Kelly, C. J.; Longhi, N. J.; Weissenfels, O.; Goldberg, H.; Brandt, K.; Grimm, J. B.; Lavis, L. D.; Huttlin, E. L.; Li, M. M. H.; Schweppe, D. K.; Backus, K. M.; Beliveau, B. J.
Abstract: Cells depend on the spatial organization of proteins, RNA, and DNA into discrete subcellular compartments. Previous methods have largely centered on measuring spatial organization based on only one of these biomolecular classes at a time. Here, we demonstrate that POCA photocatalytic proximity labeling can serve as a unified photosensitizer-based platform for profiling the proximal proteomes of protein, RNA, and DNA targets within a single experimental framework. We show that POCA can harness standard immunofluorescence or in situ hybridization workflows to specifically target organic fluorophore photosensitizers to intracellular targets for proximity labeling in fixed cells. POCA-targeted proximity labeling requires minimal cellular input and does not require genetic engineering. Additionally, POCA photosensitizers are selected to also be fluorescent, enabling direct confirmation of on-target localization by imaging prior to proteomic analysis. To demonstrate broad utility, we apply POCA across multiple molecular targets spanning protein, RNA, and genomic DNA, including components of the nuclear pore complex, nucleolus, nuclear speckles, telomeres, and pericentromeric heterochromatin. By anchoring proximity labeling to both a protein and an RNA within the same nuclear compartment, we resolve shared and distinct proximal proteomes from orthogonal molecular perspectives.

Title: TDP-43 amyloid conversion in cells tracks the net charge of a polyampholyte motif, not condensate solidification
Authors: Choi, Y. J.; Kang, Y.; Cho, S.; Jeong, S.; Jung, M.; Pack, C.; Jeong, Y.; Song, K.
Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation of TDP-43 is implicated in ALS and FTLD, yet how its condensates convert into pathological amyloid in living cells remains poorly defined. Here we identify a polyampholyte motif (PAM) in the linker between RRM2 and the amyloid-forming low-complexity domain as a charge-tunable determinant of fibrillization that operates independently of condensate solidification. In budding yeast expressing GFP-TDP-43{Delta}NLS, charge reversal of three PAM arginines (R268E/R272E/R275E; 3R-E) converted liquid puncta into ProteoStat-positive fibrils. Unexpectedly, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching revealed that 3R-E condensates were more mobile than wild-type condensates, whereas the least mobile condensates, in both yeast and human U2OS cells, converted least. Across 24 PAM charge variants, the proportion of fibril-bearing cells scaled linearly with net charge independently of residue identity, and charge neutralization delayed rather than abolished conversion. Phosphomimetic substitution of the PAM serines alone induced fibrils, implicating phosphorylation as a potential physiological modulator of PAM charge.

Title: Covalently Functionalized Click Alginate Cryogels Enable Non-Invasive Near-Infrared Sensing of Gastric pH
Authors: Cherifi, K.; Machuca Parra, A. I.; Kwon, N.; Ding, L.; Bart, L.; Ayad, M.; Rose, C.; Zheng, G.; Matoori, S.
Abstract: Gastric acidity shapes mucosal injury in reflux disease, peptic ulcer, and gastritis, yet is almost never measured. Acid-suppressive therapy, taken by approximately 40% of elderly adults, is therefore titrated on symptoms alone. A gastric sensor must hold onto its reporter in a highly acidic protease-rich environment, conditions that destabilize ionically crosslinked hydrogels and leach physically entrapped dyes. Click alginates, established in biomechanics and drug delivery but not as sensors, meet this requirement with a single chemistry: bioorthogonal tetrazine-norbornene crosslinks are stable in acid and against proteases, and excess norbornene from crosslinking becomes the anchoring site for the pH-sensitive reporter, so network and reporter are installed by the same mechanism. Cryogelation adds macroporosity for rapid gastric fluid influx. A screen identifies IRDye 680RD as the only near-infrared dye responsive across the targeted pH 2-5. Dye release stays below 1.5% in simulated gastric and intestinal fluids, and the pH response remains active after nine months of storage. In rats, the orally administered NIR fluorescent cryogel resolves pH 2.0 from pH 5.0 transabdominally and discriminates esomeprazole- from saline-treated animals, with extra-gastric organ and plasma fluorescence comparable to untreated controls. Ex vivo photoacoustic imaging shows pH-dependent contrast, pointing toward deeper-tissue detection. These results establish covalently functionalized cryogels as a non-invasive sensing platform for hostile physiological environments.

Title: Simulating Bead-Tethered Biomolecules: Force-Probe Coupled Steered Molecular Dynamics (fp-SMD) in Optical Tweezers Force Spectroscopy
Authors: Zhang, G.; Leng, Y.
Abstract: Interpreting single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) data from optical tweezers with steered molecular dynamics (SMD) is hindered by a severe timescale mismatch: SMD trajectories span nanoseconds to microseconds, while SMFS experiments unfold over milliseconds to seconds, forcing SMD to pull six to nine orders of magnitude faster than experiment and systematically distorting rupture forces, molecular pathways, and kinetic intermediates. We introduce force-probe coupled steered molecular dynamics (fp-SMD), which explicitly propagates the force probe (the optically trapped bead) alongside the biomolecule within a single classical Hamiltonian description of the coupled molecule-linker-bead system. A Predict-Correct Trajectory Propagation (PCTP) scheme resolves the resulting computational bottleneck by alternating a bead-propagation step, with the molecular center of mass (COM) held fixed, and a molecular step in which metadynamics and transition-state theory identify the kinetically resolved intermediate reached at each macroscopic time step. On the cholesterol--{beta}-cyclodextrin ({beta}-CD) host-guest complex, fp-SMD reproduces the experimental rupture-force histogram directly at matched conditions, without extrapolation from standard SMD. fp-SMD further resolves how applied force reshapes the molecular escape pathway: we find that cholesterol dissociates via a high-angle route at low force and a direct, small-angle route at high force--providing, to our knowledge, the first direct structural evidence for force-induced pathway switching in a small host-guest system, a mechanism believed to underlie catch-slip bond behavior.

Title: Systems-level imaging reveals assembly and synaptic delivery of a multi-organelle ensemble during T cell killing
Authors: Kumar, A.; Stinchcombe, J. C.; Griffiths, G. M.
Abstract: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) undergo a dynamic intracellular polarisation of their secretory compartments as they recognise and destroy cancerous cells. How multiple organelles are coordinated in space and time during this process is unknown. To enable high-dimensional systems-level imaging of multiple organelles and their relationships at high spatiotemporal resolution we use multispectral super-resolution microscopy and volumetric live-cell imaging of CTLs interacting with their targets. Organelle polarisation is initiated by perinuclear endoplasmic reticulum (ER) contacting the immune synapse, while calcium signalling promotes multi-organelle clustering around the centrosome at the rear of the cell. This creates a multi-organelle ensemble that then translocates around the nucleus to the synapse. We track organelle interactions during dynamic polarisation revealing a shift from ER-dominated to Golgi-dominated contacts as organelles reach the synapse. These findings show that CTL polarity is built through staged, calcium-driven formation of a multi-organelle assembly. More broadly, this work establishes a framework for systems-level imaging of the organelle network in cells as they deliver effector functions.

Title: Molecular crowding differentially regulates magnetic field-dependent fluorescence, recovery kinetics, and photostability of the magnetosensitive protein MagLOV2
Authors: Sridharan, V.; Ross, B. L.; Lodesani, A.
Abstract: Macromolecular crowding and solvent composition can alter protein conformation, diffusion, hydration, and cofactor photophysics, yet their influence on magnetically sensitive flavoproteins is poorly understood. We tested seven molecular environments in MagLOV2-overexpressing Escherichia coli lysate using a custom-built, high-intensity magnetofluorescence platform. Five-point concentration series of Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, PEG6000, PEG3350, glycerol, ethylene glycol, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were measured at 22 mT under continuous 6.12 W/cm2 blue-light excitation. Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, and PEG6000 progressively attenuated the negative magnetic field effect (MFE), whereas PEG3350 shifted toward mild enhancement at higher concentrations. Glycerol and ethylene glycol enhanced the negative MFE despite producing the strongest slowing of recovery upon the field being switched off (OFF-recovery), while BSA modestly enhanced MFE and accelerated OFF-recovery. Across 105 treatment cuvettes, the change in MFE was not globally correlated with changes in the OFF-recovery time constant (r = -0.07, p = 0.449). The initial pre-field illumination period revealed a second phenotype: Dextran and Ficoll increased late fluorescence loss, whereas glycerol and BSA were photoprotective. Pre-field fluorescence loss correlated moderately with MFE change across the full dataset (r = 0.474, p = 3.28 x 10-7) but not consistently within crowder classes. These findings show that MagLOV2 spin-dependent magnetofluorescence is shaped by crowder chemistry, polymer size, solvent environment, recovery kinetics, and photostability rather than by a single generic crowding or viscosity mechanism.

Title: QC-espresso: Brewing quality in proteomics
Authors: Pauperio Lanfredi, G.; Miyamoto, J. G.
Abstract: Data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics has become a standard approach for high-throughput proteomics, with DIA-NN emerging as one of the most widely adopted data-analysis platforms. However, despite the detailed information available in DIA-NN output reports, proteomics researchers may lack a streamlined and reproducible approach for assessing acquisition quality, identification consistency, and quantitative reliability across experiments. QC-espresso addresses this need through an automated, report-centered quality-control workflow implemented in R and Quarto. The tool processes a DIA-NN report.parquet file together with the corresponding FASTA database and generates a structured HTML report containing plots, run-level statistics, and exportable summary tables. Application to three experimental datasets allowed the visualization of lower identification depth related to high contaminant content; a chromatographic transition accompanied by altered retention-time and peak-width behavior; and the co-occurrence of systematic mass-error bias with changes in precursor- and protein-level quantitative-quality metrics. QC-espresso can be executed directly in R or through a portable Windows distribution with a graphical launcher, with both modes using the same analytical modules and report-generation workflow. The resulting report provides a consistent record for local inspection and troubleshooting of quality-control metrics within individual DIA proteomics experiments. QC-espresso is freely available at https://github.com/lanfredig/QC-espresso_DIA.

Title: Selective binders of a cotranslational folding intermediate
Authors: Prakash, O.; Voisin, T. B.; Roeselova, A.; Jorgensen, C. M.; Desmet, J. S.; Nans, A.; Davies, R.; Walport, L. J.; Balchin, D.
Abstract: Drug discovery efforts typically target mature, folded proteins, primarily to inhibit their function or induce their degradation. An alternative strategy would be to target incompletely folded states that are transiently populated during protein biogenesis, but whether these states contain druggable pockets was unclear. Here, we used an mRNA display approach to discover cyclic peptides that recognize a nascent polypeptide at an intermediate point during its synthesis on the ribosome. We identified peptides that bind with low-nanomolar affinity to a model nascent protein, {beta}-galactosidase, but do not detectably bind either the fully-folded protein or ribosomes synthesising different sequences. Hydrogen/deuterium exchange-mass spectrometry and cryogenic electron microscopy revealed the molecular basis for selective binding. We found that the nascent chain folds into an -helix against the ribosome surface during ongoing translation, creating a cryptic pocket together with ribosomal proteins uL23 and uL29 that is exploited by the hit peptides. Our results establish proof-of-concept for selective targeting of protein biogenesis intermediates, and provide a platform for future drug development.

Title: Cross-species structure-mechanics prediction in the intervertebral disc
Authors: Chen, J.; Parmenter, A. L.; Sharma, A.; Henderson, I.; Brunet, J.; Zwingenberger, S.; Raina, D. B.; Urban, T.; Dejea, H.; Marussi, S.; Bele, E.; Pitsillides, A. A.; Lee, P. D.
Abstract: Despite long-standing uncertainty regarding the suitability of animal intervertebral disc (IVD) models for the study of human IVD pathophysiology, few cross-species studies have integrated hierarchical structure with mechanical function. In this study, we present a multiscale structure-mechanics framework combining synchrotron computed tomography (sCT), fibre tracing, digital volume correlation (DVC) with structure-based mechanical inference and finite-element modelling. Rat, mini-pig and human IVDs (n = 3/species) were imaged by sCT, with rat and mini-pig discs additionally subjected to in situ uniaxial compression and DVC. A Structure Index (SI), integrating local structural anisotropy and fibre orientation, was developed to regionally pinpoint the location of mechanically vulnerable regions. Cross-species comparison showed scale-dependent structural conservation: gross disc and lamellar organisation retained common regional features, whereas fibre-bundle architecture exhibited greater species- and regional divergence. Despite these differences, lower SI was consistently associated with elevated deformation in rat and mini-pig discs across multiple strain measures. Structure-strain inverse correlations became tighter within progressively higher-strain domains, reaching Spearman p values of approximately -0.5 to -0.7 for several strain components. Synthetic fibre phantoms confirmed that SI reflects a coupling of fibre orientation and organisation, with additional sensitivity to fibre number in poorly organised configurations. In human discs with varying degrees of degeneration, SI revealed spatial heterogeneity and redistribution of structurally vulnerable regions. Fibril-informed homogenisation provided anisotropic material properties for organ-scale finite-element modelling that independently supported SI-based predictions. Overall, these findings establish a cross-species framework linking hierarchical collagen architecture to mechanical vulnerability and provide a basis for non-invasive, structure-driven biomechanical assessment of human IVD degeneration and mechanical risk.

Title: Bone Response to Mechanical Loading is Highly Heritable and Correlates with Osteocyte Lacunar Morphology in Genetically Diverse Mouse Strains
Authors: Migotsky, N.; Lamia, S.; Shuster, J. T.; Kumar, S.; Farber, C. R.; Silva, M. J.
Abstract: Skeletal loading is a key regulator of bone formation. Studies using in vivo loading of rodent bones have established many mechanical and biological factors that regulate bone response to loading. However, most studies have been performed in a small number of inbred rodent strains, and there are few data on effects of genetic background on the loading response. In the current study we employed two murine models of genetic diversity, the Diversity Outbred (DO) and their eight founder inbred strains, to assess the influence of genetic background on skeletal response to tibial loading. Loading-induced periosteal bone formation rates and formed bone volumes varied significantly among inbred mouse strains. DO mice, which each carry a unique mixture of alleles of the inbred founder strains, were more responsive to loading, on average, than the the inbred founder strains. Additionally, bone response to mechanical loading was highly heritable; broad-sense heritability for measures of periosteal formation were near or above 80%. Furthermore, osteocyte lacunar morphology correlated with loading response across inbred strains. Inbred 129S1 mice had the most elongated lacunae and exhibited the highest magnitude of response on both periosteal and endocortical surfaces. 129S1 also demonstrated a robust transcriptional response to loading, although the pathways induced by loading were largely conserved with lab-standard C57Bl/6. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic background significantly contributes to bone response to loading and establish DO mice as a platform for discovery of genes that regulate skeletal mechanoresponsiveness.

Title: Refining RNA-Seq Transcriptome Profiles with Transcript-Specific Minimal-Shared Regions
Authors: Su, Q.
Abstract: Accurate transcript quantification remains a critical challenge in RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) due to ambiguities in read assignment caused by shared regions among transcripts. Beyond shared exons among homologous isoforms, we identified the widespread presence of extensive undefined shared regions-overlapping sequences common to exons or transcripts of heterologous genes-across diverse species, including animals and plants. To overcome this issue, we developed a minimal-sharing strategy that partitions transcripts into unique sets of k-mers and systematically evaluates overlap across all transcripts. By isolating minimal-shared regions specific to each isoform, our approach reduces mapping uncertainty, thereby minimizing false positives and false negatives in transcript detection. Comprehensive evaluations using both in silico simulations and empirical sequencing data demonstrated that our method outperforms traditional probabilistic model-based quantification methods. This strategy improves isoform abundance estimates, enhances gene ontology annotations, and identifies distinct transcript isoforms critical for understanding biological processes, as exemplified in a Huntington's disease mouse model.

Title: GraphExperiment: infrastructure for high-dimensional quantitative data and associated networks in R/Bioconductor
Authors: Almeida-Silva, F.
Abstract: Networks are widely used to represent relationships among features (e.g. genes, proteins, and microbial taxa) and among observations (e.g. cells, samples, and species) in omics data, as well as their neighborhoods. The Bioconductor ecosystem provides users and developers with modular and interoperable software tools by relying on standard data structures that are reused across packages. However, Bioconductor lacks a standard data structure to store such networks together with the quantitative data from which they are inferred. Here, we present GraphExperiment, an R/Bioconductor package that provides an S4 class extending SingleCellExperiment with containers for feature- level (rowGraphs) and observation-level (colGraphs) networks stored as igraph objects. Networks are kept in sync with assays, row and column metadata, allowing the simultaneous manipulation of quantitative data and graphs. We demonstrate GraphExperiment in seven use cases covering bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics, microbiome, and comparative genomics data, with networks ranging from gene coexpression and protein co-abundance networks to cell-cell communication and phylogenetic networks. GraphExperiment is available on Bioconductor (https://bioconductor.org/packages/GraphExperiment).

Title: Pangenome Graph Node-Phenotype Association shows GWAS-like quality results with only few individuals
Authors: Carrette, C.; Sabot, F.; Muller, C.
Abstract: Purpose: We introduce GraNPA (Graph Node-Phenotype Association), a method that performs a phenotype-sequence association analysis on a pangenome vari- ation graph (PVG). This PVG is built using a small number of individual genome sequences and does not require additional population materials or kinship information for qualitative phenotypes.
