This approach minimizes the number of individuals required for association studies and mitigates the impact of reference bias in variant calling within these types of analyses. Background: A PVG is a representation of the multiple alignment of a set of complete genomes. It contains all variations, ranging from single nucleotide poly- morphisms (SNPs) to large structural variations (SVs), and these are represented as nodes in the graph. By integrating phenotype information within these nodes, we can assign a Score (S ) to each one and identify regions related to the phe- notype directly within the PVG. These regions represent statistically significant shifts in S distribution, indicating their involvement in the phenotype. Finally, GraNPA provides their positions and scores for further analysis. Results: This method was tested using different simulated contexts and two publicly available datasets: the Sub1A gene locus for Asian rice Oryza sativa in a 13 individuals PVG, and the insertion responsible for the white-headed in cattle (Bos taurus) with a PVG of 24 individuals. Source code of GraNPA is available here https://forge.ird.fr/diade/graphgwas/granpa under GNU GPLv3. Conclusion: GraNPA was able to identify the expected area in two simulated datasets, as well as the loci responsible for these two known traits, using only a few dozen complete genomes from these PVGs. Although this method is currently limited to qualitative phenotypes, it paves the way for more efficient methods that rely on PVGs and a small number of individuals.

Title: Probing bacterial fitness in virtual chemostats
Authors: Öcal, K.; Maas, L.; Stumpf, M. P. H.
Abstract: The growth rate of a bacterial population is a fundamental quantity in microbiology, but hard to predict from mechanistic single-cell models. Simulating exponentially growing cell populations is computationally infeasible, and single-lineage estimates are biased as they do not account for phenotypic selection between cells. We present computational algorithms to efficiently estimate growth rates with arbitrary accuracy by combining ideas from branching processes and particle filtering. These can be used with general agent-based cell models at a cost quadratic in the desired accuracy, bypassing the exponential complexity of naive approaches. Applying these methods to single-cell models of Escherichia coli, we study how single-cell heterogeneity in antibiotic responses shapes population dynamics, and how bacterial locomotion and chemotaxis in fluctuating environments affect their long-term growth.

Title: A Reproducible Pre-Transplant γδ T-cell Effector Signature Reveals Immune-Metabolic Programs Associated with Kidney Allograft Rejection
Authors: Kim, S. M.; Sur, S.; Koser, K.; Pineda, S.; Bestard, O.; Koyama, T.; Hoffmann, T.; Sigdel, T. K.; Sirota, M.; Babdor, J.; Spitzer, M. H.; Sarwal, M. M.
Abstract: Despite optimized immunosuppression, acute kidney transplant rejection affects 10-20% of recipients within the first year, and no reliable pre-transplant molecular test exists to identify patients at high risk, independent of the donor HLA matching. Across three independent cohorts of kidney transplant recipients, profiled by bulk RNA-sequencing with T-cell receptor repertoire analysis, flow cytometry, CyTOF with paired metabolomics, we identified a reproducible depletion of {gamma}{delta} T cells associated with rejection: an elevated {beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell ratio in two post-transplant, biopsy-matched cohorts, and depletion of specific {gamma}{delta} T effector clusters in a third, longitudinally sampled cohort. In this third cohort, {gamma}{delta} T cell depletion was already present at the pre-transplant baseline in patients who subsequently developed rejection and remained detectable across the transplant course, indicating that it reflects recipient baseline immune biology rather than a consequence of graft injury. Longitudinal metabolomic profiling in this cohort identified time-dependent metabolic changes, including in amino acid metabolism that co-occur with the {gamma}{delta} signature and converge with it upon multi-omics integration. At the pre-transplant baseline, {gamma}{delta} T-cell marker expression alone showed exploratory discriminatory value for rejection risk (AUC = 0.69), improving marginally when integrated with metabolomic features (AUC = 0.71); larger prospective studies will be needed before clinical translation.

Title: Enzymatic attachment of antigens to probe immune modulation by skin commensals
Authors: Bousbaine, D.; Lalgudi, P. V.; Bauman, K. D.; Tsang, E.; Nguyen, T. T. D.; James, A.; Chiang, M.; Zhao, A.; Terasaki, M.; Swenson, J. M.; Trinh, A.; Fischbach, M. A.
Abstract: The skin colonist Staphylococcus epidermidis induces potent T and B cell responses, which can be redirected against antigens of interest by genetic engineering. However, since many taxa in the microbiome are genetically intractable, the utility of this method is limited. Here, we use recombinant sortase to conjugate antigens to the surface of a wide range of Gram-positive bacterial species, and we show that this non-genetic method can be used to generate protective immunity in vivo.

Title: Draft genome of Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 isolated from marine oil snow in the Churchill Marine Observatory, MB, Canada
Authors: Vidanage, T.; Collins, R. E.
Abstract: An oil-degrading enrichment culture was inoculated from Marine Oil Snow (MOS) collected during an oil-spill experiment at the Churchill Marine Observatory in winter 2024. The complete metagenome-assembled genome for Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 was reconstructed, exhibiting the genetic potential to degrade hydrocarbons, including alkanes and aromatic compounds, as well as the ability to produce surfactants.

Title: Genetics and genomics of enteroarthroconidial development in Coccidioides
Authors: Fleming, K. E.; Christensen, K. C.; Szewczyk, E.; Homer, C. M.; Brem, R. B.
Abstract: The human fungal pathogen Coccidioides causes disease when its infectious spores, enteroarthroconidia, are inhaled from the soil. Spore dispersal depends on the death of a unique developmental form, disjunctor cells, which flank incipient enteroarthroconidia and are unexplored molecularly. Here we used single-cell (sc) RNA-seq to catalog expression across the Coccidioides colony; with gene deletion and protein tagging, we established a role for the pyropoptosis-like cell death pathway in enteroarthroconidial development.

Title: Characterizing nascent readthrough transcripts in human cells
Authors: McShane, A.; Narayanan, I. V.; Paulsen, M. T.; Blinkiewicz, H.; Ashaka, M.; Magnuson, B.; Bedi, K.; Yang, N.; Prasad, J.; Dudley, J. N.; Pitchiaya, S.; Seiden, E.; Grohar, P.; Aiden, E. L.; Wilson, T. E.; Ljungman, M.
Abstract: Termination of transcription by RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is critical to appropriately define transcriptome and proteome identity; yet mechanisms of termination regulation are incompletely understood. Current models suggest critical roles for the exonuclease XRN2, which is posited to "torpedo" out RNAPII after degrading uncapped and RNAPII-tethered nascent transcripts and posit an allosteric model wherein elongating RNAPII loses its processivity downstream of the transcription end site (TES) via unknown mechanisms. Here, we used nascent RNA Bru-seq to interrogate transcription termination across 16 human cell lines of distinct lineages, as part of the ENCODE 4 project, to identify key regulatory modes. We find that > 75% of protein-coding genes engage in readthrough transcription under homeostatic conditions. Exposing human cells to oxidative stress or hyperosmotic conditions or splicing inhibitors cause an increase in readthrough transcripts globally. Using an auxin-inducible degradation approach we find that depletion of BRD4, MED14 or XRN2 increases the extent and pervasiveness of readthrough transcripts while depletion of SUPT16H results in shorter readthrough transcripts. Our study provides a comprehensive view of homeostatic readthrough transcripts in human cells and delineates key components regulating transcription termination.

Title: Molecular basis of Cyclin B1-CDK1 recruitment by MAD1
Authors: Ord, M.; de Martin Garrido, N.; Winters, M. J.; Subbanna, M. S.; Kliche, J.; Benz, C.; Williams, S. L.; Ivarsson, Y.; Greber, B. J.; Pryciak, P. M.; Davey, N. E.
Abstract: The interaction between Cyclin B1-CDK1 and MAD1 recruits kinase activity to the nuclear pore complex and kinetochore corona to sustain spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) signaling. Here, we characterize a short linear motif (SLiM) within MAD1 that mediates its interaction with Cyclin B1. This SLiM peptide is specific for B-type cyclins and lacks the canonical "RxL" cyclin-binding consensus sequence, suggesting a distinct mode of cyclin recognition. Using a combination of deep mutational scanning, structural analysis by cryogenic electron microscopy, and binding affinity measurements, we define the molecular basis of the Cyclin B1-MAD1 interaction. These approaches reveal that a short MAD1 peptide binds as an -helix to the RxL-binding hydrophobic patch of Cyclin B1. The interaction employs hydrophobic contacts that overlap with those used by canonical RxL motifs, but is distinguished by additional contacts and sequence features that confer preferential recognition by B-type cyclins while excluding other cyclin types. We also show that the MAD1 motif is sufficient to confer B-type cyclin-specific substrate phosphorylation in mitotic cells. Together, these findings reveal a non-canonical, B-type cyclin-specific helical binding mode that ensures selective Cyclin B1-CDK1 recruitment at two critical stages of SAC signaling, and suggest potential strategies for selective therapeutic targeting of this interaction.

Title: Msp300 Links Autophagy to Nuclear Morphodynamics
Authors: Sharma, S.; Nezis, I. P.
Abstract: Autophagy is a fundamental cellular process that maintains homeostasis and enables adaptation to stress by degrading damaged or superfluous components. While its core machinery is well characterized, the interplay between autophagy and nuclear architecture remains poorly understood. In this study, we identify the LINC complex protein Msp300 as a novel interactor of the autophagy protein Atg8a in Drosophila melanogaster. Msp300 belongs to the KASH (Klarsicht/ANC-1/Syne Homology) domain protein family, known for its role in nuclear positioning through interactions with the cytoskeleton. The KASH domain anchors Msp300 in the outer nuclear membrane, where it pairs with SUN domain proteins across the nuclear envelope to form the LINC complex, a mechanical bridge between the nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton. Yeast two-hybrid screening revealed an interaction between Atg8a and Msp300 isoforms E and G, mediated by a canonical LC3-interacting region (LIR). Localization studies show Msp300 associates with Atg8a within the cytoplasm and at the nuclear periphery under both basal and elevated autophagy conditions. Functional perturbations through stress assays indicate that this interaction influences event in and around nucleus, establishing a link between autophagy and nuclear architecture. By exploring the role of Msp300 isoforms E and G in shaping not only nuclear organization but potentially endoplasmic reticulum, through autophagy machinery, this study introduces a new dimension to nuclear envelope biology and opens opportunities to explore how steady state homeostasis, stress adaptation and cytoskeletal connectivity are coordinated at the nuclear periphery.

Title: Diet-Related Molecular Evolution Differs between Vertivores, Invertivores, and Combined Carnivores
Authors: Tene, M.; Seaver, A.; Foley, K.; Meyer, W.
Abstract: Mammals have repeatedly evolved specialized diets, including a variety of predatory diets targeting different prey animals. Prior research has found differences in positive selection, gene family evolution and gene functional loss linked with diet, but has focused primarily on trophic level classifications of herbivory, carnivory, and omnivory. Here we divide "carnivores" into vertivores and invertivores, due to the differences in nutrient composition of those food sources. We find significant differences in evolutionary conservation of multiple genes and GO categories between vertivores and invertivores. Conservation relative to herbivores differs among vertivores, invertivores, and the combination of all carnivores. Lineages with predatory diets have increased conservation in lipid and amino acid metabolism relative to herbivores. Notably, we find that results in the combined carnivore-herbivore comparison are much more similar to those of the invertivore-herbivore comparison than the vertivore-herbivore comparison, which suggests that prior studies on carnivory may have been detecting signatures of selection related to invertivory.

Title: Shared and divergent features of the immune response to acute and chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection in mice revealed by cardiac transcriptomics
Authors: Olmo, F.; Jayawardhana, S.; Taylor, M. C.; Kelly, J. M.; Francisco, A. F.
Abstract: Chagas disease is caused by infection with Trypanosoma cruzi and can result in chronic cardiomyopathy. However, the molecular programmes that define infected cardiac tissue, and how they change as the host-parasite relationship moves from acute pathogenic infection to long-term persistence, remain incompletely understood. Here, we used RNA sequencing to characterise host transcriptional responses in cardiac tissue during both acute and chronic infection in a mouse model. Cardiac parasite distribution was defined using bioluminescence imaging and histology, and RNA sequencing was performed on anatomically standardised cardiac tissue samples collected at both stages. Acute infection was associated with a broad interferon-driven immune activation, whereas during chronic infection this network contracted, with preservation of a tightly connected antigen presentation core centred on major histocompatibility complex genes and immunoproteasome components. Genes associated with extracellular matrix remodelling and fibrosis were not broadly activated. These findings indicate that reduced, but sustained immune activation, rather than widespread fibrotic transcriptional remodelling, represents a prominent feature of cardiac tissue in chronically infected mice. They identify a transition from an overtly inflammatory, pathogen-driven acute response to a more restricted chronic host-parasite equilibrium in which immune surveillance remains transcriptionally active despite very low and spatially intermittent cardiac infection. We identified a conserved 20-gene signature shared between acute and chronic stages. This overlap is consistent with continued or episodic parasite-derived stimulation and/or intrinsic host mechanisms that maintain cardiac immune surveillance. Thus, chronic T. cruzi infection can be viewed as a persistent host-parasite association in which biological coexistence does not imply benignity: immune containment and parasite persistence can occur alongside cumulative cardiac injury.

Title: Environment-Aware DNA Language Model for Stress-Responsive Genomic Prioritization in Maize
Authors: Pal, D.; Odell, A.; Singh, A.; Thompson, A. M.; Ross, A.; Thessen, A.
Abstract: Abiotic stresses such as heat and drought severely reduce the productivity of major crops including maize, with adverse implications for agricultural sustainability. Despite progress in characterizing stress resilience, identifying genomic regions associated with stress response remains challenging due to complex genotype-by-environment interactions. Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs), inspired by advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), leverage large-scale self-supervised pre-training on DNA sequences to capture regulatory patterns; however, their adaptation to plant stress-response analysis remains underexplored. In this work, we propose an environment-aware DNA-LLM framework that incorporates stress-specific prompt tokens into AgroNT, a transformer-based plant GFM, using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). The model learns stress-conditioned genomic representations that exhibit distinct structures across environmental contexts. We further formulate a prioritization method that uses stress-induced shifts in these representations relative to the control condition together with stress-token-associated transformer attention patterns to identify putative stress-responsive genomic regions. The framework was evaluated on the Genomes-to-Fields (G2F) dataset, comprising over 4,000 maize hybrids grown across 38 locations over 8 years, using grain yield under heat, drought, and combined heat-drought stress. Flowering traits were used to assess generalizability of the stress-conditioned representations across phenotypes. The prioritized regions were assessed using spatiotemporal differential gene-expression profiles, stress-associated quantitative trait loci, and transcription-factor characterization. Regulatory motif analysis further revealed stress-associated motifs enriched within the prioritized sequences as well as model-emphasized high-attention regions. Functional annotation of genes proximal to prioritized regions highlighted roles in transcriptional regulation, signaling, and metabolic pathways relevant to abiotic stress adaptation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the potential of stress-conditioned transformer-based sequence modeling for environment-aware genome-to-phenome analysis in crop improvement.

Title: A Plasmid-Derived Machinery Drives Chromosomal Replication Initiation in the Colorectal Cancer-Associated Bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum and Its Close Relatives
Authors: Brezellec, P.; Pasek, S.
Abstract: Chromosome replication initiation in bacterial genomes typically occurs at a single origin, called oriC, through the binding of the DnaA initiator protein to specific chromosomal repeats known as DnaA-boxes. Here, relying on comparative genomics, we show that the family Fusobacteriaceae, which belongs to the order Fusobacteriales alongside the family Leptotrichiaceae, deviates from this paradigm. Our analysis revealed a stark contrast between the two lineages: while dnaA flanks oriC in Leptotrichiaceae, it is notably missing from Fusobacteriaceae genomes. Adjacent to oriC in Fusobacteriaceae, we identified a gene encoding replication initiator protein A (RPA). We characterized RPA as a Rep-type initiator involved in plasmid replication that likely originated from an iteron-containing plasmid, iterons being the plasmid analogues of DnaA-boxes. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicates that the gene encoding RPA was acquired together with its associated iterons and subsequently domesticated by the Fusobacteriaceae ancestor, successfully displacing the ancestral chromosomal dnaA gene at the origin of replication. This shift to a plasmid-derived replication system may represent an adaptive trait of the Fusobacteriaceae, potentially offering new insights into the biology of Fusobacterium nucleatum, a member of this family known to be a major driver of colorectal cancer progression within the tumor microenvironment.

Title: A respiratory microdomain links ubiquinone biosynthesis to succinate dehydrogenase in an apicomplexan mitochondrion lacking Complex I
Authors: Baierna, B.; Moreno, S. N. J.
Abstract: Mitochondrial complex I (CI) is a major entry point for NADH-derived electrons and an important site of redox regulation in most eukaryotes. However, apicomplexan parasites, including Toxoplasma gondii, lack CI, raising a fundamental question of how mitochondrial respiration is organized in these parasites. Here, we identify a parasite-specific mitochondrial microdomain that physically and functionally couples ubiquinone (UQ) biosynthesis to succinate dehydrogenase (SDH). Using proximity labeling, membrane-based yeast two-hybrid analyses, reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations, and blue native PAGE, we show that UQ biosynthesis proteins associate with parasite-specific SDH subunits and co-migrate as a high-molecular-weight assembly. Knockdown of TgCoq4, a component of the UQ biosynthesis pathway, reduced SDH activity, and adding exogenous UQ to the assay did not restore it, indicating that UQ availability is not sufficient for efficient succinate oxidation. FCCP stimulates malate- and TMPD/ascorbate-supported respiration to maximal capacity but fails to do so with succinate as the substrate. This result, combined with reactive oxygen species (ROS) data, suggests that succinate causes over-reduction of the UQ pool, limiting further electron flow. We also find that CIII associates with the UQ synthesis machinery, suggesting a larger protein assembly. Together, these findings reveal that UQ biosynthesis and electron transport are physically and functionally integrated in T. gondii, defining a previously unrecognized organization of mitochondrial respiration in an organism lacking CI.

Title: A compact three-way junction oligonucleotide probe for widefield and super-resolution imaging of RNAs and proteins
Authors: Nguyen, P.; Ma, H.; Chen, M.; Sun, X.; Li, S.; Soloff, A.; Yang, D.; Liu, Y.
Abstract: Molecular imaging of RNAs and proteins requires methods that preserve nanoscale organization while enabling large-scale tissue analysis. However, weak or low-abundance targets often need signal amplification, which can increase labeling size, background, or signal spread and compromise super-resolution imaging. Here, we report a compact three-way junction (3WJ) oligonucleotide probe platform for multiscale RNA and protein imaging. The design couples paired target recognition with junction assembly and recruitment of preassembled amplifier complexes, while tunable amplification balances signal strength and labeling size. Using DNA origami and single-molecule localization microscopy, we show enhanced signal while retaining the ability to resolve nanoscale target patterns. The platform improves RNA detection and supports simultaneous RNA-protein super-resolution imaging in cells. It also enhances protein detection in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues under low-numerical-aperture, large-field imaging conditions. Together, this programmable 3WJ platform enables sensitive RNA and protein detection across scales, supporting super-resolution analysis of molecular organization and large-field tissue mapping.

Title: A cytotoxicity dataset for data-driven design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles
Authors: Liu, N.; Zhu, Q.; Lu, Z.-R.
Abstract: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are widely used to deliver nucleic acid therapeutics, but the design of safe LNPs remains challenging due to the complex activity relationships among structure, composition, and physicochemical properties. Here, we present a curated dataset, the Lipid Nanoparticle Cytotoxicity Database (LNPCD), which aggregates 1,413 LNP cytotoxicity measurements across 1,288 unique ionizable lipids drawn from 11 high-throughput combinatorial studies. Lipid structures were generated computationally from the published libraries and manually verified against the original publications. Each record pairs a machine-readable SMILES representation of the ionizable lipid with its measured viability endpoint and the associated experimental descriptors, including cell line, dose, and cargo type. The dataset provides a traceable resource for examining how ionizable lipid structure and experimental conditions relate to in vitro cell viability, and for developing and evaluating computational models of lipid nanoparticle cytotoxicity.

Title: Fibronectin-Assisted Coating of Low-Molecular-Weight Fucoidan Creates a Biomimetic Interface for Endothelialization of Cobalt-Chromium Stents
Authors: SAADI, M.; HADDAD, R.; ZEAITER, N.; HADDAD, O.; PRABHAKAR REDDY, D.; BAUMANN, J.-S.; FALENTIN-DAUDRE, C.; IRKI, F.; BAMBA-FUNCK, J.; SUTTON, A.; BASSAND, K.; BOISSON VIDAL, C.; HLAWATY, H.
Abstract: Incomplete or delayed endothelialization after stent implantation compromises vascular healing and increases the risk of restenosis and late thrombosis. To address this limitation, Cobalt-Chromium (Co-Cr) stents were modified with a biomimetic coating combining Low-Molecular-Weight Fucoidan (LMWF), a sulfated polysaccharide with glycocalyx-mimetic properties, and fibronectin, to promote endothelial repair while preserving vascular homeostasis. The morphology, chemical composition, wettability and stability of the coating were characterized using complementary physicochemical approaches. The behavior of human endothelial cells cultured on this dual fibronectin-LMWF-coated stent was then assessed. Our results showed that fibronectin-LMWF-based coating achieved a ten-fold higher surface density on the stent than LMWF alone (0.29 {+/-} 0.04 vs 0.03 {+/-} 0.01 {micro}g/mm2) and retained 0.27 {+/-} 0.03 {micro}g/mm2 of the coating after 168 h, compared with 0.01 {+/-} 0.01 {micro}g/mm2 for LMWF alone. Although wettability remained similar to that of uncoated stents, the combined coating markedly enhanced endothelial cell adhesion, spreading, lamellipodia formation, proliferation, and MMP-2 secretion. These effects were accompanied by enhanced F-actin organization and redistribution of membrane-associated VE-cadherin, integrins {beta}1 and 6, and syndecans-1 and -4, without major changes in their total expression. Importantly, the coating induced these responses without detectable cytotoxicity or significant inflammatory activation. Overall, the fibronectin-LMWF-based coating provides a stable biomimetic interface that enhances endothelialization through coordinated remodeling of adhesion, cytoskeletal, and glycocalyx-associated structures, while maintaining endothelial homeostasis on Co-Cr stent. This strategy offers a promising platform for next-generation glycocalyx-like stent coatings designed to improve vascular healing and limit restenosis.

Title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
Authors: Haiss, S.; Skoog, E. J.; Herbert, J.; Ding, C.; Weidenbach, K.; Tufail, M. A.; Schlaich, S.; Molitor, B.; Schmitz, R. A.; Schoelmerich, M. C.
Abstract: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.

Title: PhoPQ is an upstream regulator of quorum sensing in small colony variant subpopulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Authors: Simanek, K. A.; Mendoza, A. G.; Kurtz, A. F.; Schumacher, M. L.; Pope, A. N.; Paczkowski, J. E.
Abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic human pathogen that is hospital-endemic, forming biofilms on medical equipment and causing thousands of hospital-acquired infections each year. The success of P. aeruginosa as an opportunistic pathogen is linked to its phenotypic and genotypic adaptability. Relatedly, P. aeruginosa forms a small colony subpopulation in response to stresses like oxygen limitation and antibiotic exposure. Additionally, P. aeruginosa coordinates population-level decisions using a mechanism of cell-cell communication called quorum sensing. P. aeruginosa is notorious for these signaling pathways to control virulence factor production and biofilm formation in the host. We show that certain quorum-sensing mutations promote phenotypic switching; specifically, deletion of lasR and autoinducer modulating mutations in rhlI enhanced small colony formation in a time course-dependent manner. Using transcriptome analyses of isogenic small and large colony variants, we show that small colony formation is driven in part by the PhoPQ two-component signal transduction system in quorum-sensing mutant backgrounds. Specifically, our data show that unphosphorylated PhoP represses rhlR gene expression, and that subsequent de-repression of quorum sensing contributes to the production of virulence factors and the small colony phenotype. In total, these findings provide insight on how mutations evolved by clinical strains might serve as a bet-hedging strategy to promote the formation of a small colony phenotype and alter quorum-sensing signaling within a subpopulation of a given community.

Title: A comparative analysis of BrdU and EdU genotoxicity shows that trypanosomatids exhibit unique responses to the presence of these thymidine analogs in their DNA
Authors: de Oliveira, M. A. F.; da Silva, V. L.; Teixeira, T. L.; Gerolamo, F. M.; Gaziri, T. J. N.; Black, J. A.; Silva, F. d. J.; Chaimovich, H.; Cuccovia, I. M.; da Silva, M. S.
Abstract: The thymidine analogs 5-bromo-2'-deoxyuridine (BrdU) and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) are widely used to monitor DNA synthesis. Although studies have reported EdU toxicity in certain cell types, no reports to date describe genotoxic effects associated with BrdU/EdU use in trypanosomatids, etiological agents of neglected tropical diseases. This lack of studies raises two possibilities: either these nucleotides are not toxic to these parasites, or the observed genotoxicity was not relevant under the experimental conditions used. Here, we assessed the potential toxicity of BrdU and EdU across three pathogenic trypanosomatids: Trypanosoma cruzi, Trypanosoma brucei, and Leishmania major. Our findings show that EdU has greater genotoxic potential than BrdU. Nevertheless, trypanosomatids respond markedly differently to DNA alterations caused by this analog: T. cruzi cells stop replicating and accumulate in S phase, T. brucei tolerates the DNA lesions generated, while part of the L. major population appears to display an altruistic behavior that benefits the survivors. Furthermore, in silico assays suggest that, once incorporated into DNA, the ethynyl group increases the EdU's polarity, thereby altering DNA structure more strongly than BrdU does after the first round of DNA replication. Together, our findings suggest that using thymidine analogs in trypanosomatids should be preceded by rigorous preliminary analysis, especially when using EdU. Otherwise, the data may be biased by a BrdU/EdU-triggered DNA damage response. We believe this study may serve as an atlas to guide the initial selection of thymidine analog concentrations and exposure periods.

Title: The self-renewing lymphoid-biased hematopoietic stem cells support long-term lymphopoiesis in mice
Authors: Ma, Y.; Li, X.; Li, X.; Wang, L.; Xu, Y.; Zhai, J.; Wang, J.; Lan, Y.; Zhou, B.; Cheng, T.; Ema, H.; Dong, F.
Abstract: Lymphopoiesis is profoundly impaired during ageing largely due to ageing-susceptible changes of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). How to maximize the preservation of lymphopoiesis during ageing remains unknown and whether there exists a specific population with life-long lymphoid potential not intensively affected by ageing is of substantial scientific and translational significance. Here, we identified a self-renewable, lymphoid-biased hematopoietic stem cells (Ly-biased HSCs) subset within the EPCR+CD150-CD48-LSK (HSC2) population, phenotypically termed EPCR+MPP6 (CD34-CD135-HSC2), that not only displayed comparable multi-lineage potential with HSC in young mice, but also maintained similar lymphoid-biased reconstitution during aging. The lymphoid-biased characteristics of EPCR+MPP6 were also supported by immune associated program at transcriptome and proteomic levels. Notably, EPCR+MPP6 and HSCs rarely generated one another following the first cell division in vitro and under homeostasis in vivo indicating the most likely independent relationship between them and an earlier-than-thought bifurcation of the lymphoid differentiation pathway, which may function as a backup source to support lymphopoiesis. Collectively, this newly defined Ly-biased HSCs represent a promising cellular target for both mechanistic studies and therapeutic strategies concerning age-related immune decline.

Title: Structural Basis for Inhibition of Human Anion Transporter SLC26A6/PAT-1
Authors: Chi, G.; Bohstedt, T.; Adamson, R.; Pike, A. C. W.; Shrestha, L.; Cil, O.; Anderson, M. O.; Izadiar, M.; Williams, E.; Burgess-Brown, N. A.; Elkins, J. M.; Duerr, K. L.; Sauer, D. B.
Abstract: PAT-1, encoded by the gene SLC26A6, is an exchanger of small organic and inorganic anions including oxalate and chloride in the kidney and the intestines. PAT-1 dysfunction is implicated in nephrolithiasis and hyperoxaluria, and its modulation is a potential therapeutic strategy to treat cystic fibrosis. PAT-1 has two small molecule inhibitors: DIDS, a non-specific anion exchanger inhibitor; and PAT1inh-B01 which is highly specific to PAT-1. In this study, we report high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of the human PAT-1 homodimer in complex with these inhibitors to reveal their different inhibition mechanisms. These structures also uncover the complex interactions between the transmembrane, STAS and N-terminal domains, with implications on its ion exchange function. Hence, this study provides mechanistic insight into PAT-1 molecular function and inhibition, and contributes to our understanding of SLC26 transport mechanisms.

Title: irAEGIS: Pathway-guided interpretable prediction of immune-related adverse events
Authors: Budhkar, A.; Guo, S.; Zhang, X.; Su, J.; Song, Q.
Abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are major complications of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy and remain difficult to predict prior to treatment initiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a unique opportunity to characterize immune states associated with future irAE development. However, translating single-cell measurements into accurate and biologically interpretable patient-level risk predictions remains challenging. Existing approaches typically aggregate cellular profiles into patient-level summaries, thereby obscuring cell type specific signals, or rely on complex deep-learning architectures that offer limited insight into the biological pathways and mechanisms underlying their predictions. Here, we present irAEGIS, a pathway-guided interpretable model for predicting irAE risk from pre-treatment scRNA-seq data. irAEGIS incorporates prior biological knowledge through gene set constrained representation learning, aggregates pathway activities within individual cell types, and integrates cell type specific risk signals through a hierarchical prediction framework. This design enables predictions to be decomposed into contributions from individual cell types, pathways, and genes, providing interpretable explanations across multiple biological resolutions. Across simulated datasets and independent pre-treatment ICI cohorts, irAEGIS consistently outperformed seven existing methods. Beyond predictive performance, irAEGIS identified biologically coherent immune programs associated with irAE risk. In non-small cell lung cancer, irAEGIS highlighted neutrophil-associated inflammatory pathways linked to future irAE development, whereas in melanoma, it identified apoptotic and immune activation pathways in CD8+ NKT-like cells associated with severe irAEs. These findings were independently supported by pathway enrichment, cell-cell communication, and trajectory analyses. Together, irAEGIS provides a biologically informed and interpretable model for linking single-cell immune states to patient outcomes, enabling both accurate risk prediction and mechanistic insight into immune-related adverse events. More broadly, irAEGIS establishes a general strategy for interpretable phenotype prediction and biological discovery from single-cell transcriptomic data.

Title: A validation approach for RNA structures based on deep-learning 3D-structure predictions
Authors: Voorspoels, A.; Simpkin, A. J.; Keegan, R.; Chojnowski, G.; Rigden, D. J.
Abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of life depends on accurate macromolecular structures. RNA, in particular, poses a particular challenge for structural biology due to its inherent flexibility and dynamic nature. The challenging nature of structure determination experiments and their interpretation have led to the development of validation approaches to prevent or fix errors in solved structures. Existing methods for RNA structure validation can, as with proteins, be broadly split into two types. Map-based validation tools seek to detect discrepancies between the experimental data and the determined structure. They are excellent for fixing all types of errors, but only when high-resolution experimental data are available.Model-only validation methods, which usually focus on molecular geometry, are excellent for fixing short-length-scale issues even when experimental resolution is low. Conkit-validate is a mapless method for protein validation, which is not based on chemical plausibility, but rather on the similarity between experimental models and structure predictions for the same protein. By comparing contact patterns, this tool leverages evolutionary covariance information, learned by state-of-the-art structural prediction models, into a mapless validation method capable of detecting sequence assignment issues, with notable success in detecting register errors. Here, we extend the conkit-validate method to work on RNA.The results show performance similar to that previously achieved for proteins. %We also show how this new method can detect errors missed by map-based approaches when the experimental data is of low resolution. In a scan of the PDB, its detection rate does not depend on the local resolution of the density, so it remains applicable where map-based approaches are not, and case studies show it can identify register errors where the density alone cannot decide between models.Together, this highlights the complementary value of a contact-prediction based validation approach using information orthogonal to map- and geometry-based approaches to ensure the quality of deposited RNA structures against varying criteria.The performance of the method can be expected to track ongoing improvements in RNA structure prediction methods.

Title: FoxO1 and HNF1α cooperatively remodel nucleosome architecture and mechanical stability to activate transcription
Authors: Florez Ariza, A. J.; Yang, Z.; Sosa, R. P.; Diaz-Cellis, C.; Richter, H. J.; Ramani, V.; Bustamante, C. J.; Nogales, E.
Abstract: How different transcription factors (TFs) cooperate to bind nucleosomal DNA targets remains unclear. Cryo-EM and force spectroscopy show that the pioneer factor FoxO1 binds superhelical location (SHL) +2 of nucleosomes assembled on the human IGFBP1 promoter, enhances distal DNA unwrapping, destabilizes the histone core, and reduces nucleosome mechanical stability. TF HNF1 binds SHL +5/+7 as a dimer, induces extensive DNA unwrapping without perturbing the histone core, and reshapes nucleosome disassembly dynamics. FoxO1 enhances HNF1 recruitment, and together they stabilize the nucleosome during its mechanically-induced disassembly trajectories. In-cell nucleosome footprinting on active promoters shows that FoxO1 binding enhances unwrapped nucleosomes and subnucleosomes presence, while HNF1 increases stabilized and breathing nucleosomes and reduces the subnucleosome population. Combined, they display an intermediate nucleosome phenotype. Our data leads to a model where FoxO1 destabilizes the nucleosome and enhances HNF1 recruitment, and together they remodel nucleosome architecture both in vitro and in native chromatin.

Title: Organelle Aging Predicts Human Disease
Authors: Ying, K.; Roh, K. K.; Chen, K. L.; Bot, V. A.; Ding, D. Y.; Farinas, A.; The Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC),  ; Ma, C.; Oh, H. S.-H.; Isakova, A.; Wyss-Coray, T.
Abstract: Aging affects cellular organelles differently, but whether subcellular aging predicts human disease remains unknown. Here, we integrated organelle-enriched proteins in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid proteomes from 61,931 individuals to model aging of 10 organelles across the human lifespan. Organelle aging was heterogeneous with lysosomes, plasma membranes, and Golgi compartments accelerating rapidly after age 60. Individuals with four or more prematurely aged compartments exhibited up to 22-fold higher kidney disease risk and up to 8-fold higher mortality risk. Major diseases are characterized by distinct organelle aging signatures and disease risk increased with the number of accelerated organelles. APOE-{varepsilon}4 dosage was associated with lysosomal and mitochondrial aging and reduced PDP1 levels, implicating altered energy metabolism. Decomposition of organelle signature coefficients into biological programs further showed that diseases are associated with distinct subcellular patterns. These findings establish organelle-resolved aging as a measurable dimension of human biology, revealing subcellular mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility and resilience.

Title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
Authors: Vidanage, T.; Desmond, D.; Collins, R. E.
Abstract: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell-Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 {degrees}C and 20 {degrees}C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas, and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 {degrees}C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.

Title: A candidate HNRNPU-CHD2 RNA-processing axis in neurodevelopmental disease
Authors: Tang, H.; Xiao, Z.; Wang, R.; Babarinde, I. A.; Huang, S.; Hutchins, A. P.; Ma, G.
Abstract: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPU, which encodes a nuclear RNA-binding scaffold protein, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, intellectual disability and brain malformations, but the programs that link HNRNPU dosage to neuronal dysfunction remain poorly defined. We depleted HNRNPU in Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells, profiled gene expression and alternative splicing, intersected the two datasets, and asked which of the resulting genes already carried a neurodevelopmental annotation. Knockdown produced 5,643 differentially expressed genes and 21,728 high-confidence splicing events; 1,222 genes changed at both levels, and two pre-specified neurodevelopmental panel genes were among them: CHD2 and DYRK1A. In K562 eCLIP experiments, 107 reproducible HNRNPU peaks were detected across the CHD2 gene body, and three of the four regulated exons introduce a reading-frame shift whose premature termination codon lies far upstream of the final exon junction, predicting nonsense-mediated decay. Public K562 knockdown data reproduced the rise in CHD2 mRNA and the same skipped-exon change, and CHD2 depletion in the neural line SH-SY5Y altered cell-cycle, DNA-repair and neural gene programs. HNRNPU therefore constrains a frameshift-prone splicing switch in CHD2, a candidate route from HNRNPU haploinsufficiency to loss of functional CHD2 if these transcripts are degraded.

Title: LplA-mediated rescue of lethal myopathy and cardiomyopathy in mitochondrial lipoylation-deficient mammalian caused by Lipt1
Authors: Yu, J.; Hu, Z.; Liu, Z.; Yang, R.; Zeng, A.
Abstract: Inherited mitochondrial metabolic disorders impair cellular energy generation and often lead to fatal metabolic crises. Mitochondrial lipoylation defects represent a severe case of such disorders that can lead to lethality but lacks effective treatment so far. In this study, we generated a viable mouse model with muscle-specific deficiency of the lipoyltransferase coded by Lipt1 to provide an in vivo preclinical model that overcomes embryonic lethality. Using this model, we examined a bacterial lipoate protein ligase A (LplA)-mediated gene therapy via adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery. By introducing LplA alongside lipoic acid supplementation, we reconstituted a salvage pathway that bypasses the mammalian endogenous lipoylation pathway. The intervention rescued premature lethality, recovered motor function and reversed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the Lipt1-deficient mouse model. Mechanistically, AAV-LplA reconstitutes mitochondrial protein lipoylation and oxidative phosphorylation in situ. This energetic rescue suppresses phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt hyperactivation, thereby restoring autophagic clearance and subsequently contributing to the recovery of the pathological phenotype. This study established AAV-LplA as a promising gene-delivery strategy for rescuing lethal mitochondrial lipoylation disorders.

Title: An oral protein cocktail therapeutic for C. difficile infection
Authors: Zhao, H.; Dodds, M.; Pollock, A.; Gewe, M.; Martinez, A.; Keeney, K.; Jester, B.; Hutton, M.; Tabakh, H.; Zhang, M.; Heinnickel, M.; Paddock, T.; Ertel, S.; Aggarwal, K.; Amendola, C.; Tasch, M.; Brady, C.; Sanjaya, N. R.; Kahwaty, M.; Cruickshank, K.; Struyvenberg, S.; Dang, J.; saveria, t.; Shanitta, C.; Park, Y.; Doughty, D.; Poirot, J.; Pensak, C.; Adame, T.; Ferrara, J.; Read, A.; Heil, D.; Shibuya, S.; Henderson, J. C.; Fletcher, D.; Charron, T.; sigmar, k.; Aw, E.; Ruiz, R.; Yoshino, K.; Lo, J.; Strong, D.; Goetsch, L.; Gamble, C.; Shephard, S.; Zhong, Y.; Antolock, R.; Loper, C.; Guzma
Abstract: Here we show that transgenic spirulina may solve key challenges of developing effective monoclonal protein therapeutics for diseases afflicting gastrointestinal (GI) tissues. We describe, as a paradigm for this novel approach, LMN-201: an investigational four-component treatment for Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) infection comprising four monoclonal protein therapeutics produced and delivered within spirulina biomass. Three antibody-like moieties within LMN 201 were rationally designed using a multiplicative potency framework, termed synthetic avidity, that increased in vitro toxin neutralization potency by >200-fold relative to the individual components. The fourth moiety, a lysin enzyme protein, adds direct, toxinotype-agnostic antibacterial activity. In rodent challenge models, species-relevant LMN-201-like cocktails reduced disease burden and mortality. In a human GI pharmacokinetic study, LMN-201 was present at concentrations 100- to 1,000-fold above the estimated minimally effective therapeutic threshold at the distal intestine. In Part A of a Phase 2 study, participants with C. difficile infection (CDI) were treated for seven days with LMN-201 plus standard-of-care antibiotics. The primary endpoints of safety and tolerability were assessed favorably. An interim analysis of efficacy in pre-planned coordination with the data and safety monitoring board showed an initial clinical cure rate of 21/21 (100%) and sustained clinical cure rate through four weeks of 19/21 (90.5%). These findings support LMN-201 with standard-of-care antibiotics as a viable treatment option for CDI, validate spirulina as a scalable platform for oral biologics, and establish a generalizable strategy for engineering high-potency combination protein therapeutics for diseases with a GI tissue nexus.

Title: NPlasmid-seq: Cas9-encoded terminal signatures enable molecule-level nanopore quality control of vector and IVT-template plasmids
Authors: Xu, Y.; Wen, W.; Sun, D.; Yin, Y.-X.; Ma, X.-Y.; Ren, J.-X.; Zhang, S.-M.; Chang, J.-Q.; Pang, S.-C.; Wang, S.-D.; Zhang, X.-B.; Zhang, J.-P.
Abstract: Consensus-based plasmid quality control can overlook structural heterogeneity within a preparation. We developed NPlasmid-seq, a Cas9-guided nanopore workflow that encodes sample identity through paired terminal signatures generated at predefined backbone positions, without sample-specific oligonucleotide barcodes. We cleavage-validated 24 sgRNAs. In five representative assigned read bins, each bin showed its strongest sequence agreement with its cognate reference. Contaminant detection was evaluated with a single class-specific classifier applied both to computational read mixtures and to physical DNA mixtures, placing the two designs on a common scale. In computational read mixtures of 5,000 reads, a contaminant was detected in all 20 independent subsamples at each of 0.2%, 0.5%, 1% and 5% abundance and in 13 of 20 subsamples at 0.1%; precision was 1.000 in all 100 subsamples, with no false-positive calls among 493,200 reads from the declared target plasmid. In physical DNA mixtures carried through cleavage, pooled library preparation and sequencing, a contaminant was detected in all six samples prepared at 0.5 mol% input and all six at 1 mol%. Observed read fractions did not distinguish the 0.5 and 1 mol% input levels. Instead, they differed systematically by 4.0-fold between preparation pools, a larger effect than the difference between the two input levels. We therefore interpret the workflow as a detector, not a quantifier, of sub-percent contamination. Read-level analysis identified a recurrent 93-bp deletion in 61.7% of reads from a preparation that had passed consensus-based quality control. Sanger genotyping of 24 colonies identified deletion-type profiles in 10 colonies and intact-type profiles in three. The remaining 11 colonies showed double peaks at the diagnostic locus, consistent with coexistence of both sequence forms within individual clones. In in vitro transcription template plasmids, longer poly(A) tracts were associated with higher multimeric-read fractions. Across ten matched A90 culture pairs, propagation at 30 degree reduced these fractions relative to 37 degree (paired t-test, P = 0.0098). These measurements describe recovered read populations, not absolute molecular abundances. NPlasmid-seq therefore complements consensus validation by revealing sequence and structural heterogeneity within a preparation and by identifying a culture condition associated with a lower multimeric-read fraction.

Title: Single Molecule Diffusion Studies Reveal Rapid Translations Across Target Membrane Surfaces for both p40Phox PX domain and Class III PI3K VPS34 Complex 1, the Autophagy Lipid Kinase
Authors: Lizardos, L.; Ohashi, Y.; McCombs, A. M.; Knight, J. D.; Williams, R. L.; Falke, J. J.
Abstract: Single molecule analyses are providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms by which peripheral membrane proteins approach and translate across a target bilayer surface before stable docking. Here we compare and contrast the translational movements of four diffusers on a representative supported lipid bilayer: (i) the fluorescent lipid LRB-(DO)PE, (ii) the G-protein Rab1A anchored to (DO)PE; (iii) the PI(3)P sensor p40Phox PX domain, and (iv) the autophagy lipid kinase VPS34 Complex 1. The latter enzyme is a Class III PI-3-Kinase and its unusual architecture exhibits two distinct membrane-docking "feet" unique to Class III PI3Ks. Notably, the membrane contact surfaces of the PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase each possess multiple positive charges suitable for electrostatic interactions with their anionic target membrane. The present single molecule tracking studies reveal that both the fluorescent lipid and the lipid-anchored G protein Rab1A exhibit 2-dimensional translation typical of simple lipid diffusion in the bilayer. Single molecule density measurements indicate both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit significantly reduced membrane docking when the bilayer negative charge is decreased, confirming the importance of their protein-bilayer electrostatic interactions. Single molecule tracking studies reveal that both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit hopping movements across the bilayer surface during their initial bilayer contacts, yielding a significantly higher frequency of long range displacements than allowed by lipid 2-D diffusion. After transitioning from hopping to a stable bilayer-docked state, both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit 2-D diffusion slower than lipid diffusion indicating the appearance of increased frictional drag against the bilayer due to new protein-bilayer contacts. PX domain requires its target lipid for the transition from electrostatic hopping to stable bilayer docking, while autophagy lipid kinase can dock spontaneously to anionic lipid bilayers even in the absence of its substrate lipid. In principle, the slowly diffusing, bilayer-docked states of PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase could be interrupted by unbinding-hopping-rebinding events. However, such events are not detected for PX domain in the presence of target lipid (DO)PI(3)P nor for autophagy lipid kinase in the presence of substrate lipid (DO)PI. Instead, unbinding-hopping-rebinding events are only observed for autophagy lipid kinase in the absence of substrate lipid, indicating that the presence of a specific binding lipid reduces the frequency or spatial amplitude of such events. Overall, the findings provide evidence that p40Phox PX domain possesses a search mechanism involving electrostatic hopping that speeds its acquisition of target lipid, as previously observed for PH domains. The evidence indicates that the autophagy lipid kinase also exhibits electrostatic hopping/skating behavior that is proposed to play a functional role by speeding regulatory encounters with autophagy lipid kinase activators and effectors. Moreover, the ability of the lipid kinase to spontaneously dock to anionic membranes without a target lipid could facilitate its distribution across broad regions of the growing autophagosome. Finally, the autophagy lipid kinase exhibits multiple translational modes that we hypothesize are enabled by its two membrane docking feet.

Title: Discovery of P1-P2 depeptidized boronic acid based Plasmodium falciparum SUB1 inhibitor
Authors: Kazia, A.; Lidumniece, E.; Withers, C.; Donnelly, O.; Fidock, D. A.; Blackman, M.; Jirgensons, A.
Abstract: The Plasmodium falciparum subtilisin-like serine protease 1 (PfSUB1) is an essential enzyme required for parasite egress from host red blood cells and represents a promising target for antimalarial drugs. Peptidic boronic acids are potent reported PfSUB1 inhibitors, however their drug-likeness is limited by their pronounced peptidic character. Based on molecular docking studies using peptidic boronic acids, we designed a series of partially depeptidized PfSUB1 inhibitors by replacing the P1-P2 dipeptide fragment with a 3-aminomethylphenylboronic acid core. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) investigations targeting interaction with active-site residue Lys138 revealed that introducing a meta-carboxylate group (compound 3a) markedly enhanced inhibitory activity, yielding a low-nanomolar PfSUB1 inhibitor (IC50= 10.2 nM). Bioisosteric replacement of the carboxylic acid demonstrated that an N-acylsulfonamide group (compound 4k) retained high enzymatic potency (IC50= 13.5 nM)). In cellular assays against blood-stage P. falciparum (3D7 strain), the leading depeptidized boronic acids exhibited growth inhibition with values in the low-micromolar range suggesting that further structural modifications are needed to enhance membrane permeability across host and parasite membranes to reach exonemes prior to egress. Overall, this study validates the P1-P2 depeptidization of boronic acid scaffolds and provides key SAR insights for the rational design of non-peptidic PfSUB1-targeted antimalarials.

Title: Gentamicin impairs nephron development in iPSC-derived kidney organoids and disrupts proximal tubular lysosomal function
Authors: Sendino Garvi, E.; Piorunska, W.; Böhl, L.; Sparidans, R. W.; Masereeuw, R.; van Genderen, A. M.
Abstract: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used to treat Gram-negative bacterial infections. However, its clinical use is limited by nephrotoxicity, affecting approximately 10 - 20% of treated patients. Nevertheless, gentamicin remains widely used due to its high potency, low cost, and low incidence of bacterial resistance and hypersensitivity. Importantly, gentamicin crosses the placental barrier and is administered to neonates, including preterm infants in whom nephrogenesis is still ongoing, raising concerns about its effects on kidney development. Current knowledge of this risk relies largely on rodent studies, which fail to fully recapitulate human kidney physiology. Here, we developed human-relevant in vitro models to investigate the impact of gentamicin on kidney development and to unravel the dynamic cellular responses underlying gentamicin-induced impairment. Kidney organoids differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) and magnetically sorted proximal tubule cells were used to model immature kidney and immature proximal cells, respectively. Organoids were continuously exposed to gentamicin (0.25 - 1.5 mM) throughout development (d7+18), while megalin-expressing proximal tubule cells were exposed for 24 hours to explore the cellular mechanisms underlying gentamicin toxicity. Intracellular concentrations of the gentamicin congeners C1, C1a, and C2/C2a/C2b were quantified by LC-MS/MS. Gentamicin exposure impaired organoid growth, and nephron formation and maturation. Additionally, gentamicin induced lipid accumulation and reduced lysosomal area in proximal tubule cells, indicating disrupted cellular metabolism and homeostasis. In conclusion, iPSC-derived kidney organoids provide a suitable platform to further investigate gentamicins impact on kidney development and studying co-treatments to mitigate its adverse effects.

Title: Anti-TGFβ peptide P144 augments CAR-T cell efficacy through neutrophil recruitment and TME remodeling in malignant mesothelioma
Authors: Bugda, R.; Hawkins, E.; Box, G.; Secchiari, F.; Leboreiro Babe, C.; Tan, R. S.; Dimou, P.; D'Souza, R. R.; Klampatsa, A.
Abstract: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare, aggressive and highly desmoplastic cancer characterised by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its activity against solid tumours such as mesothelioma remains limited, in part through transforming growth factor-beta (TGF{beta})-mediated immunosuppression. To address this barrier, we engineered murine CAR-T cells that simultaneously target tumour antigen and deliver TGF{beta} blockade to the tumour. We first compared two anti-TGF{beta} peptides, the beta glycan-derived P144 and the phage-display-derived P17, in vitro; both attenuated TGF{beta}-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and reporter activity, but P144 suppressed canonical Smad3 phosphorylation more effectively and was selected for downstream work. Murine CAR constructs targeting either mesothelin (M11) or fibroblast activation protein (FAP) were modified to secrete P144, and the resulting products were assessed in co-culture assays and in the syngeneic AE17m model of mesothelioma. P144 secretion did not alter transduction efficiency, expansion or antigen-specific cytotoxicity, but markedly increased antigen-driven IFN{gamma} production, most notably at low effector-to-target ratios. In vivo, both M11-P144 and FAP-P144 CAR-T cells-controlled tumour growth better than their parental, peptide-free counterparts, although complete tumour resolution was not achieved. Flow cytometric profiling of the tumour immune infiltrate showed that P144 delivery increased intratumoral neutrophil frequency approximately three-fold, and neutrophils recovered from these tumours were substantially more cytotoxic ex vivo than those from control tumours. Antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion attenuated the additional benefit conferred by P144 while leaving parental CAR-T activity largely intact, indicating that neutrophils contribute functionally to the effect. Local, CAR-T-delivered TGF{beta} blockade therefore remodels the mesothelioma TME and engages a tumoricidal neutrophil response, offering a modular strategy for enhancing adoptive cell therapy in desmoplastic solid tumours.

Title: Genetically restricted human antibodies recognize a conserved β-hairpin in postfusion influenza hemagglutinin
Authors: Finney, J.; Park, J.; Dodes Traian, M.; Kuraoka, M.; Towers, D.; Moody, M. A.; Georgiou, G.; Kelsoe, G. H.; Harrison, S.
Abstract: A public class of broadly protective, human antibodies (Abs) binds a conserved {beta}-hairpin exposed in the postfusion conformation of influenza virus hemagglutinin (HA). We here describe use of in vitro immunoassays and high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy analysis of Ab:HA complexes to explain the apparent genetic restriction of these Abs and the wide range of influenza A and B subtypes they recognize. We show that recognition of the {beta}-hairpin epitope requires 1) germline-encoded residues unique to certain alleles of the human immunoglobulin heavy chain gene IGHV1-2, 2) a short (<14-residue) HCDR3 to avoid steric clash with HA, and 3) several Ab light chain residues that are germline-encoded by various IGLV2-family genes or IGLV7-46. Despite the genetic restrictions, the capacity to make {beta}-hairpin Abs is widespread among humans. We recovered examples of these Abs from 14 genetically unrelated donors, and a previously reported analysis of the IGHV genotypes of ~2,500 individuals sampled from major ethnic populations estimates that >75% of people have the necessary IGHV1-2 alleles to make these Abs. We conclude that an immunogen that displays the {beta}-hairpin epitope might reliably elicit broadly protective influenza antibodies in most humans.

Title: Identification of Cryptococcus neoformans capsule-associated protein antigens that mediate B cell-dependent vaccine protection in mice and elicit antibody responses in humans with cryptococcosis
Authors: Hester, M. M.; Carlson, D.; Oliveira, L. V. N.; Hastings, Z.; Sahu, S.; Hargarten, J.; Anjum, S.; Ostroff, G. R.; Williamson, P. R.; Specht, C. A.; Levitz, S. M.
Abstract: Infection with the encapsulated fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans causes substantial global disease burden in persons with compromised T cell function. Previously, we demonstrated that vaccines containing adjuvanted recombinant cryptococcal proteins protected mice against lethal infection by mechanisms dependent on CD4+ T cells. For the present study, we hypothesized that vaccines containing protein antigens naturally located on the surface of the cryptococcal capsule would contribute protective B cell responses. We found that B cell-deficient mice exhibited reduced survival following vaccination with any of four capsule-associated antigens: Blp4, Cpd1, Lhc1, or Krp1. To further elucidate the role of antibodies in protection, we tested serum from mice vaccinated with a live-attenuated strain (cda123) and then challenged with a virulent C. neoformans strain for IgG responses to a panel of 26 cryptococcal recombinant proteins. Strong reactivity was detected against Blp4, which we focused on because it is capsule-associated and protects mice when administered in adjuvanted subunit vaccines, by mechanisms partly dependent on B cells. Blp4 antibodies were consistently present in surviving mice, including those vaccinated with unrelated proteins or those challenged with diverse clinical isolates. Additionally, serum from Blp4-vaccinated mice promoted macrophage opsonophagocytosis of C. neoformans. Finally, IgG antibodies against Blp4 were detected in 20 of 21 serum samples from patients who survived cryptococcosis, compared with only 4 of 14 samples from healthy controls. Together, these data identify Blp4 as an antigen that elicits protective B cell responses and is a strong candidate for inclusion in subunit cryptococcal vaccines.

Title: Serotype specific anti-capsular polysaccharide IgG associated with colonizing and invasive group B streptococcus in pregnant woman-newborn dyads
Authors: Amar, N.; Hall, T.; Bentley, E.; Chakroun, A.; Ben-Taleb, H.; Saïle, R.; Le Doare, K.; Chamekh, M.
Abstract: Maternal IgG against group B streptococcus (GBS) capsular polysaccharide (CPS), is the principal placental mediator of neonatal protection, yet naturally acquired anti-CPS immunity has not been characterized in North African populations. To address this gap, we conducted a prospective study in a Moroccan mother-newborn cohort to quantify the serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG levels in relation to colonizing versus invasive GBS serotypes. Additionally, we assessed the transplacental transfer of anti-CPS IgG and identified potential correlates of invasive disease. We examined serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG (serotypes Ia-V) in the plasma from maternal and cord blood of 103 GBS-colonized pregnant women, 35 uncolonized controls and their paired newborns (90 paired colonized dyads, including five newborns with invasive GBS disease) using a standardized six-plex immunoassay. Transfer ratios were compared with 1.0 and cord concentrations with published serotype- and onset-specific risk-reduction thresholds. Maternal anti-CPS IgG concentrations varied by serotype, with the highest median for serotype II(1.36g/mL) and the lowest for serotype Ib(0.003g/mL). They were higher in GBS-colonized than uncolonized mothers for serotypes Ia, Ib and II. Maternal and cord blood IgG concentrations were correlated across serotypes, but placental transfer was incomplete, with median ratios of 0.50-0.80. Among 77 newborns, 13.0%(n=10) reached early-onset and 44.2%(n=34) achieved late-onset disease risk-reduction thresholds. The serotype IV was the most identified among neonatal infection disease cases, and this was associated with sub-protective anti-serotype IV antibody. This suggests that while naturally acquired anti-serotype II antibodies were predominant, the low level of anti-serotype IV antibodies could contribute to neonatal infection diseases in mother-newborn pairs.

Title: Serial intravascular labeling resolves dynamic decidual NK residency and gestational remodeling toward T-bet-Low states
Authors: Mohamed, M. A.; Vazquez, J.; Cordero, M. A.; Beaulieu, S.; Finnerty, E. C.; Chen, X. Y.; Hasan, R.; Virumbrales-Munoz, M.; Stanic, A. K.
Abstract: Decidual natural killer (dNK) cells are the predominant immune population at the maternal-fetal interface during early pregnancy. However, how vascular trafficking, tissue residency, proliferation, and apoptosis-associated activity are coordinated to establish and maintain the dNK population throughout pregnancy remains unclear. We hypothesized that gestational remodeling of the dNK compartment reflects coordinated changes in these cellular processes in association with progressive T-bet downregulation. We combined serial intravascular labeling (SIVL), flow cytometry, BrdU incorporation, active caspase-3 detection, spatial imaging, and Tbx21 fate mapping to examine NK cells in virgin mice and across gestation. Pregnancy altered CD49a/CD49b-defined dNK-cell composition and redistributed dNK cells among SIVL-defined vascular-accessibility states, supporting a model of dynamic dNK-cell tissue residency. Trafficking-associated marker scores displayed continuous gradients of tissue retention, circulatory/egress potential, and chemokine responsiveness rather than defining a single resident state. Spatial imaging demonstrated greater dNK-cell density in the mesometrial decidua and preferential CD31 vessel contact by recently intravascular dNK cells during early and mid-gestation. BrdU incorporation and active caspase-3 positivity peaked during early pregnancy and varied across SIVL-defined states. Tbx21 fate mapping identified a progressive and selective shift from current T-bet expression toward ex-T-bet and non-fate-mapped Eomes dNK states. T-bet-low states preferentially maintained proliferation at mid-gestation, whereas current T-bet expression was associated with greater circulatory/egress potential. However, active caspase-3 was not selectively increased in current T-bet-expressing cells. Collectively, these findings identify pregnancy-induced dNK-cell remodeling as a coordinated process integrating dynamic tissue residency, vascular accessibility, local proliferation, and apoptosis-associated activity, alongside a progressive shift toward T-bet-low dNK states.

Title: Integrated transcriptomic and metabolite analyses link DMSP cleavage to acetate overflow in the coral symbiont Endozoicomonas ruthgatesiae
Authors: Chen, Y.-C.; Yen, J.-H.; Hsu, T.-C.; Liao, W.-T.; Chang, H.-F.; Lu, C.-Y.; Lin, L.-R.; Chuang, P.-S.; Tang, S.-L.
Abstract: Endozoicomonas, a dominant bacterial symbiont of corals, degrades dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) and produces dimethylsulfide (DMS), a key compound in the global sulfur cycle. By contrast, the carbon backbone of DMSP has received far less attention. Using Endozoicomonas ruthgatesiae strain 8E as a model, we exposed cultures to DMSP at 25 and 31, simulating an ambient condition and thermal stress, respectively. Using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to monitor DMS and acetate production, we observed a significant increase in acetate efflux from 8E during DMSP metabolism in a growth phase-dependent manner. This increase in acetate was not observed when the native compound was replaced with 13C-labeled DMSP, suggesting that the additional acetate originated from DMSP. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that DMSP exposure upregulated dddD expression and triggered a reconfiguration of 8E's central carbon metabolism, with upregulation of genes associated with the glyoxylate shunt-associated genes, and down-regulation of the TCA cycle and the Pta-AckA pathway. These findings suggest that DMSP-derived acetate overflows when its assimilation into biomass is restricted. Notably, elevated temperature diminished DMSP cleavage activity of 8E, indicating thermal sensitivity of this bacterial metabolic activity. Together, our results indicate that exposure to DMSP redirects carbon flow in Endozoicomonas, resulting in overflow of DMSP-derived acetate.

Title: Bispecific VSV-G Engagers: A Platform for Cell-Type-Specific Delivery of Viral Vectors
Authors: Nenavath, G. N.; Gataulin, D.; Eisenstein, M.; Schreiber, G.; Hasan, M. S.; Packiriswamy, N.; Jain, P.; Kadungure, T.; Anantharama, H.; Chin, C.-H.; Kancharla, A.; Salimi, H.; Lech, P.; Blancas-Mejia, L.; Munoz-Alia, M.; Peng, K.-W.; Russell, S.; Rubinstein, M.
Abstract: VSV-G-pseudotyped lentiviral vectors (LVVs) enable highly efficient ex vivo gene delivery through the broadly expressed LDL receptor (LDLR) but lack the cell-type specificity required for in vivo applications. To provide cell-type specificity, we developed reversible engagers consisting of a cell-specific ligand or antibody fused to the ~40-amino-acid VSV-G-binding domains of LDLR. Following endocytosis, the engager dissociates, releasing unmodified VSV-G for efficient delivery of the vector cargo. An engager comprising the CEACAM8 N-terminal domain enables selective transduction of CEACAM6-positive epithelial cells. A trimeric CEACAM8-based engager matching the VSV-G homotrimeric spike blocked non-specific VSV infection through LDLR with an IC50 of 16.7 pM, while enabling effective VSV-mediated lysis of CEACAM6-positive tumor cells. An anti-CD3-based trimeric engager selectively transduced non-preactivated T cells in human PBMCs with high transduction efficiency. Engager-mediated in vivo CAR T cell generation resulted in sustained control of human OPM2 multiple myeloma tumors in NSG mice. This platform may further advance in vivo gene therapy, including in vivo CAR T-cell therapy and tumor-directed oncolytic virotherapy.

Title: Classical guinea pig coat phenotypes are associated with variants in FGF5 and CELSR1
Authors: Halley, M.; Bierle, C. J.; Hsieh, P.; Zaidi, A. A.; Albert, F. W.; Cetera, M.
Abstract: Classical Mendelian coat phenotypes in the domestic guinea pig, Cavia porcellus, were central to early studies of mammalian genetics, yet their molecular bases remain unresolved. Long fur is characterized by elongated hair, and rough coat by whorled patterns of fur orientation. Here, we performed genome-wide association mapping using exome and whole-genome sequencing data to identify the genetic basis of both phenotypes. Mapping of long fur identified a locus containing FGF5 and resolved the association to a premature stop codon, independently confirming a previously proposed candidate variant. Mapping of rough coat identified a locus containing CELSR1, an atypical cadherin and core component of the planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway, resolving the association to an in-frame proline insertion in its extracellular domain. The variant is associated with a dominant rough-coat phenotype, unlike previously characterized recessive mouse Celsr1 alleles, which produce a similar hair-patterning phenotype only when homozygous. The mouse alleles are also associated with severe developmental abnormalities, including open neural tube, which are not observed in rough-coat guinea pigs. This dominant, tissue-specific phenotype suggests that the insertion alters CELSR1 function in a previously undescribed manner. Consistent with this possibility, the rough-coat variant localized normally to cell-cell junctions in cultured mouse keratinocytes and retained its ability to recruit Fzd6 and Vangl2, demonstrating preserved molecular interactions involved in PCP junction assembly. These findings resolve the molecular basis of two classical guinea pig coat phenotypes and identify a naturally occurring, dominant CELSR1 allele associated with a mode of PCP disruption distinct from previously characterized alleles.

Title: Inherited maternal memory T cells protect offspring from respiratory viral infection through disease tolerance
Authors: Toure, H.; Jimena, B.; Caban, M. E.; Lederer, E. E.; Rico, D. M.; Medlin McFadden, A.; Abideen, S.; Kokati, P.; Harrington, W. E.; Koch, M. A.
Abstract: Maternal immune transfer is a powerful mechanism for early-life protection from infection, yet the full repertoire of protective factors remains unknown. We discovered that maternal memory T cells are both necessary and sufficient to protect offspring from lethal respiratory infection. This antigen-specific protection operated independently of maternal antibodies and offspring T cell responses and required IL-10 produced by maternal T cells. Transfer of protective maternal T cells reduced offspring inflammatory responses and lung tissue damage without affecting viral burdens, indicating that maternal memory T cells directly suppress pathogenic innate inflammatory responses to preserve offspring health. Critically, maternal vaccination similarly protected offspring in a T cell-dependent manner. These findings reveal maternal antigen-specific T cell transfer as a complementary immunological defense mechanism to protect offspring against pathogens that escape maternal antibodies, with broad implications for maternal vaccination strategies.

Title: Transcriptomic Analysis of Innate Immune Responses to Toxoplasma gondii in Bat Cells
Authors: Yarovinsky, P.; Kwok, S. F.
Abstract: Bats exhibit remarkable tolerance to numerous viral infections, a phenotype associated with distinctive adaptations in innate immune and inflammatory pathways. Whether these adaptations also shape responses to nonviral intracellular pathogens remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the interaction between the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii and epithelial cell lines derived from the black flying fox (Pteropus alecto). We found that both type I and type II strains of T. gondii readily invaded and replicated in bat cells, demonstrating a high degree of cellular permissiveness to infection. Surprisingly, transcriptomic analysis revealed remarkably limited early host responses despite progressive intracellular parasite replication. A pronounced transcriptional response emerged only at later stages of infection, coinciding with extensive parasite replication and cellular damage, and was characterized by changes in genes associated with inflammatory signaling, metabolic adaptation, and tissue remodeling. Together, these findings reveal an unusual interaction between bat cells and an intracellular protozoan pathogen, characterized by efficient parasite replication and markedly delayed host transcriptional activation. Our results suggest that distinctive regulation of cellular responses to intracellular infection may extend beyond viral pathogens and represent a broader feature of bat immune biology.

Title: CTLA-4 checkpoint signalling modulates germinal centre dynamics and antibody avidity during Borrelia burgdorferi infection in mice.
Authors: Mäkinen, V. J.; Alinikula, J.; Fair-Mäkelä, R.; Sundqvist, P.; Salmi, M.; Mattila, P.; Pietikäinen, A.; Hytönen, J.
Abstract: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme borreliosis, persists in mammalian hosts despite robust activation of innate and adaptive immunity. A hallmark of murine infection is the production of low-avidity antibodies, yet the immunological mechanisms underlying this defective humoral response remain poorly understood.   Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing of draining lymph node cells from Borrelia-infected mice at days 7 and 14 post-infection, comparing transcriptional profiles with those from mice immunised with heat-killed Borrelia or with a potent germinal centre-inducing protein immunisation. Borrelia infection induced a rapid germinal centre response, however, light zone B cells displayed diminished expression of co-stimulatory and T-B cell interaction molecules while maintaining core germinal centre identity markers, suggesting impaired positive selection. T follicular helper cells upregulated multiple inhibitory checkpoint receptor genes, most prominently Ctla4, alongside an active germinal centre engagement programme.
