Foxp3? regulatory T cells upregulated genes associated with follicular-homing and suppressive function, including those implicated in CTLA-4-mediated trans-endocytosis.   To test whether inhibitory signalling contributes to the impaired humoral response, infected mice were treated with anti-CTLA-4 blocking antibody. CTLA-4 blockade significantly increased plasma cell numbers and enhanced both the magnitude and avidity of Borrelia-specific IgG responses, including the induction of complement-fixing IgG2a. These findings reveal that CTLA-4-dependent inhibitory signalling contributes to defective antibody quality during Borrelia infection, identifying a mechanism by which dysregulated T cell responses may facilitate impaired humoral control of a persistent spirochaetal pathogen.

Title: GxE and changes to the genetic architecture of flowering time in an overwintering environment
Authors: Peake, A. L.; Stinchcombe, J. R.
Abstract: Characterizing how the expression of genetic variation changes across environments is essential for understanding evolution in complex environments, the evolution of phenotypic plasticity, and the genetic architecture of adaptation. We investigated how the phenotypic distribution, large-effect loci, and polygenetic architecture of flowering time in Arabidopsis thaliana changes when grown in an ecologically realistic environment compared to standard chamber conditions. We grew 479 A. thaliana accessions in an overwintering common garden that have previously been phenotyped in growth chambers by the 1001 Genomes Project (2016). Our findings suggest there is extensive GxE for flowering time between the overwintering common garden and the growth chamber environments. None of the large effect loci that we identified using a multivariate Genome Wide Association Study (GWAS) were shared across growth conditions. We find evidence of allelic differential sensitivity, conditional neutrality, and antagonistic pleiotropy contributing to GxE for flowering time between growth conditions. Our results also suggest that the effects of genetic variation across multiple flowering time regulatory pathways is revealed when grown in a more ecologically realistic environment. The effect sizes for the most significant 1% of SNPs are moderately correlated between the outdoor and growth chamber conditions which indicates a partially shared genetic basis. Overall, our findings highlight how making inferences about the genetic basis and evolution of complex traits may be dependent on conducting experiments in ecologically realistic environments.

Title: Sedimentary ancient DNA analysis from the Iron Age courtyard and cooking pit site of Rodskjaer in Troms, Northern Norway
Authors: Lucas, M.; Cerbing, M.; Fischer, C.-E.; Wickler, S.; Alsos, I. G.; Lammers, Y.; Gusarova, G.; Beaulieu, M.; Brown, A. G.
Abstract: Courtyard sites, which are Iron Age structures unique to Norway, are often associated with cooking pit fields suggesting feasting practices, but little is known about the main purpose of these sites. To address this, a framework for sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) metabarcoding sampling was undertaken at the site of Rodskjaer, northern Norway. Of the 63 sediment samples from cooking pits, fire pits, a hearth, a fireplace, the natural shell-sand and topsoil, 52 successfully detected plant and animal sedaDNA. The plant diversity was high with 41-100 taxa. SedaDNA identified archaeologically significant taxa that were not detected by other methods, including Avena (oats), Quercus (oak), Equus (horse), and Salmo salar (salmon). Additionally, from inter-sample comparison, and with reference to worm sedaDNA we identified the archaeological contexts that were affected by partial bioturbation and root penetration that restricted interpretation of spatial or temporal differences in use of these features. This pioneering study shows the importance of taking many samples from modern and natural sediments as well as using multi-proxy analysis when conducting sedaDNA metabarcoding studies at open-air archaeological sites. If these factors are taken into consideration, sedaDNA from cooking pits can be a valuable resource for investigating uses of courtyard and cooking pit field sites.

Title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
Authors: Moene, C. J. I.; Eder, M.; Dauban, L.; Yanez-Cuna, J. O.; Kocher, A. A.; Eschauzier, L.; Verkuilen, M.; Franceschini-Santos, V. H.; van Steensel, B.
Abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position ("launch site"), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

Title: GNG2-MRAS interaction regulates SHOC2-dependent RAF activation and MAPK signaling
Authors: Navale, G. R.; Towolawi, B.; Christoff, C.; Malasani, S.; Liu, Z.; Wang, Z.
Abstract: Dysregulation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway is a hallmark of many human cancers and RASopathies. The SHOC2-MRAS-PP1C; (SMP) holophosphatase complex is a crucial regulatory node of this pathway. It activates the MAPK pathway by dephosphorylating the inhibitory phosphoserine on RAF kinases and thereby relieving RAF autoinhibition. Although GNG2, the {gamma}-subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins, has recently emerged as a negative modulator of MAPK signaling, its molecular mechanism of action remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify GNG2 and its truncated variants as inhibitors of SMP complex assembly by directly targeting MRAS. Using NanoBiT live-cell bioluminescence, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), biolayer interferometry (BLI), and molecular dynamics simulation studies, we demonstrate that full-length GNG2 (residues 1-71aa) and two helical fragments ({Delta}1, residues 1-29aa and {Delta}2, residues 30-71aa) bind MRAS, disrupt SMP complex formation, and therefore prevent RAF dephosphorylation. Expression of the truncated GNG2 variants significantly reduced phosphorylation of ERK in cells, consistent with inhibition of pathway activation. Furthermore, a short peptide synthesized from the GNG2 {Delta}2 sequence effectively disrupted SMP complex formation in both purified protein systems and live cells and potently attenuated MAPK signaling. Molecular dynamics simulation studies revealed that GNG2 variants engage with the Switch I/II regions of MRAS, sterically interfering with SHOC2-PP1C association. Together, these findings establish GNG2 as a direct regulator of SMP complex assembly and demonstrate that GNG2-derived peptides represent a promising strategy for disrupting SHOC2-MRAS interactions and suppressing MAPK signaling in RAS/RAF-driven pathologies.

Title: Mapping the sequence determinants of constitutive activity in GPCRs
Authors: Howard, M. K.; Whiteman, S.; Rockefeller Grimes, P.; Macdonald, C. B.; Manglik, A.; Coyote-Maestas, W.
Abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) signal not only in response to ligands but also in their absence. This basal, or constitutive, activity has distinct physiological consequences and is the only functional measurement available for orphan receptors. It is also hard to compare receptors because each is reported relative to its own baseline. Here, we measure basal activity on a single scale across the human GPCR family. Pairing a barcoded library of all human GPCRs with a transcriptional cAMP reporter, we scored 901 receptor constructs in one pool experiment. Basal activity forms a continuous distribution, and many of the highest-scoring recipes have prior reports of ligand-independent activity, with orphan being strongly represented. We then exhaustively mutated one of them, GPR161, and measured its effects on protein abundance, surface expression, and cAMP signaling. Of the 528 positions, only 10 specifically alter signaling independent of expression. Constraints on basal signaling are dominated by reepotro biogenesis, which requires multiphenotype scanning to resolve. Together, these datasets place basal activity on a common scale across the GPCR family and provide a template for dissecting it at residue resolution.

Title: Development and cross-cohort evaluation of a multimodal deep-learning model for ER, PR and HER2 status classification in breast cancer
Authors: Tran, B. M.; Nguyen, V. A.; Dang, Q. A.; Nguyen, N. M. H.; Nguyen, Q. A.; Tran, H. N.; Tran, D. H.; Nguyen, T. B. V.
Abstract: Background. Estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2 status guide systemic treatment in breast cancer. Multimodal models are rarely benchmarked against key biomarker molecular baselines or evaluated for cross-cohort calibration. We assessed incremental value, dependence on label-proximal HER2 transcripts, and transport of discrimination and calibration. Methods. A model combining whole-slide images, transcriptomes, age and stage was developed in TCGA-BRCA (1051 patients; ER/PR/HER2 analysis sets: 1001/998/1006) and evaluated in CPTAC-BRCA (120 patients; 118/113/95). CPTAC had been observed during earlier development and included 13 HER2-positive cases. Analyses included paired model comparisons, transcript removal, alternative loss functions and recalibration. Internal discrimination used pooled out-of-fold predictions; external discrimination used fold-mean estimates, with ensemble calibration reported separately. Internal calibration and macro-AUC uncertainty were interpreted as exploratory. Results. Internal AUCs were 0.943 for ER, 0.901 for PR, and 0.860 for HER2; external AUCs were 0.952, 0.937, and 0.918, respectively. External macro-AUC was 0.936 for the multimodal model and 0.957 for logistic regression using ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 (difference -0.021). Removal of the extended 29-transcript 17q12-q21 region changed HER2 AUC by -0.035 [-0.058 to -0.013] (95% CI) internally and by -0.042 [-0.089 to -0.007] externally relative to the baseline multimodal model. For external 15-model ensemble predictions, recalibrated HER2 expected calibration error (ECE) was 0.236, exceeding the ECE reference ceiling of 0.125, while calibration-in-the-large was -1.657 [-2.373 to -1.023] (profile-likelihood 95% CI), indicating systematic overprediction. ER and PR also showed overprediction. In paired fold-mean comparisons, HER2 ECE and Brier score favoured the three-transcript model (ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2). Conclusions. A multimodal deep-learning model achieved high discrimination across cohorts but did not demonstrate clear incremental value over a parsimonious three-transcript baseline, while cross-cohort calibration remained a substantial challenge. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating incremental value, calibration, and clinical utility alongside discrimination when assessing AI-based prediction models for medical use.

Title: TileScope quantifies spatial gene expression relationships beyond colocalization
Authors: Macha, N.; Arrieta-Lobo, M.; Lillo, S.; Dartigues, B.; Chalopin, D.; Saleh, M.; Daubon, T.
Abstract: Gene expression patterns within the same tissue region can exhibit similar correlation or enrichment, but still differ in their organization within regions and at their boundaries. We present TileScope, a framework for analysing genes and transcriptional programs within predefined tissue regions, their components and their contacts with neighbouring regions. TileScope combines regional enrichment, within-region correlation, cross-correlation over distance and expression differences near specific boundaries. Repeated spatial partitions and consensus aggregation show how these measurements depend on the grouping of spots or cells. Across 30 controlled constructions derived from glioblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma data representing ten spatial expression scenarios, combined measurements separated arrangements that individual statistics left ambiguous, including coincident patches, gradients and expression localised at region boundaries. In 30 human glioblastoma sections, TileScope distinguished shared regional enrichment from internal covariation and identified hypoxia-associated expression localised at region boundary despite negligible within-region correlation. In newly acquired Visium profiles of control and myeloid-targeted MCT1-knockout (KO) orthotopic GL261 mouse gliomas, proliferation and myeloid programs were enriched in tumour peripheries but showed opposite within-periphery-region correlations. Proliferation was higher near the tumour-facing boundary in both samples, whereas myeloid expression was higher near the tumour-facing boundary in the control and farther within periphery in the KO condition. Xenium applications on glioblastoma and breast cancer samples demonstrated feasibility with irregularly spaced individual cells and different regional annotations. TileScope provides spatially explicit descriptions of gene and program relationships, linking their organization within tissue compartments to their sensitivity to aggregation.

Title: Genome-wide loss of chromatin accessibility coexists with selectively elevated RNA abundance in nutrient-starved U2OS cells
Authors: Qi, X.; Al Refaai, S. A.; Muslinov, S.; Panov, K.
Abstract: Background Chromatin accessibility is widely used as a proxy for regulatory potential and is often interpreted together with RNA-seq to infer gene-regulatory responses. However, the quantitative relationship between chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance may become difficult to interpret, particularly under acute cellular stress. Metabolic challenges such as nutrient deprivation are known to induce extensive chromatin remodelling and transcriptional reprogramming, raising the question of whether changes in transcript abundance are directly governed by chromatin accessibility in these contexts. Clarifying this relationship is critical for interpreting epigenomic data under stress conditions, and requires careful distinction between Tn5 accessibility, relative steady-state RNA abundance and transcriptional output. Results We integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses in human U2OS osteosarcoma cells following 18 h of severe nutrient deprivation. We found that starvation was associated with a genome-wide reduction in accessibility and almost all significantly altered accessible regions showed reduced signal relative to actively growing cells. This decrease affected promoter- and enhancer-associated regions alike, including housekeeping-gene promoters and CTCF-motif sites. In contrast, RNA-seq revealed a more selective change in relative steady-state RNA abundance: only a minority of expressed genes were differentially regulated, and approximately 64% of differentially expressed genes showed increased relative RNA abundance. Changes in accessibility and transcript abundance were modestly correlated at promoters (Pearson r = 0.25) and weakly at enhancers (r = 0.10), and together explained only ~6% of the variance in transcript abundance changes. The relationship was graded: genes with the smallest promoter losses were about four times as likely to show increased RNA abundance as genes with the largest losses, independently of baseline promoter accessibility. Within-condition analyses similarly showed only modest relationships between promoter accessibility and RNA abundance in both actively growing and starved cells. Pathway-level analysis of mRNA abundance revealed the expected repression of biosynthetic and growth-related programmes, including ribosome biogenesis, translation and cellular growth, together with a less anticipated relative activation of stress-adaptive programmes, including extracellular matrix organisation, lipid and cholesterol metabolism, small GTPase signalling and developmental processes. For genes within these activated programmes, increased steady-state mRNA abundance was observed despite reduced ATAC-seq accessibility at associated regulatory regions. Exon-intron analyses of RNA-seq data indicated that these changes predominantly reflect altered RNA production. Metabolic labelling of nascent RNA at selected loci confirmed increased transcription of genes involved in adaptive programmes despite reduced promoter and enhancer accessibility, alongside with reduced production of biosynthetic transcripts and rRNA. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that chromatin accessibility and steady-state RNA abundance are only modestly coupled during severe nutrient deprivation, against a baseline of similarly modest promoter accessibility-abundance coupling. This underscores the limited ability of ATAC-seq accessibility to predict transcript abundance under this stress condition and supports a model in which chromatin accessibility acts as a permissive rather than deterministic layer of gene regulation. The selective induction of adaptive programmes, confirmed here at the level of RNA production, shows that transcriptional activation can occur despite genome-wide loss of ATAC-seq accessibility. Because ATAC-seq reports Tn5 accessibility rather than physical chromatin compaction, we interpret compaction as a plausible mechanistic model compatible with the current observations, which will require direct orthogonal validation.

Title: Resonant Recognition Model analysis of cGAS: conserved spectral frequencies and a divergent naked mole-rat phase signature
Authors: Hernandez-Caceres, J. L.; Vega-Hernandez, M.; Iglesias Fuster, J.; Dorohova, A.; Padron-Diaz, I.
Abstract: Background: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) is a cytosolic DNA sensor with additional noncanonical nuclear functions, including suppression of homologous recombination (HR) in humans. In the naked mole-rat (NMR), cGAS instead promotes HR through a FANCI-RAD50-dependent mechanism, a functional reversal attributed to four C-terminal amino acid substitutions. Whether such functional divergence is reflected in primary-sequence-derived spectral features is unknown. Methods: We applied the Resonant Recognition Model (RRM) to cGAS sequences from fourteen mammals and to FANCI sequences from eight species. Sequences were converted to numerical series using EIIP values and analyzed by discrete Fourier transform; consensus spectra were generated by point-wise multiplication of individual power spectra. Phase differences between cGAS and FANCI were computed at frequencies of interest. Spectral amplitudes at the dominant shared frequency were correlated with body mass, lifespan, and lifespan-to-body-mass ratio. RRM frequencies were converted to electromagnetic wavelengths using the Cosic formulation ({lambda} = 201/f_RRM). Results: The cGAS consensus spectrum contained four prominent peaks (f = 0.0392, 0.0765, 0.2539, 0.4229), with 0.2539 dominant. Three FANCI peaks (0.04138, 0.2479, 0.4332) were close to cGAS peaks, and the combined cGAS+FANCI consensus retained peaks at 0.2539 and 0.04077. Spectral amplitude at f = 0.2539 correlated with body mass (r = 0.647, p < 0.05) and with lifespan-to-body-mass ratio (r = -0.677, p < 0.01); the NMR showed the lowest amplitude. Human cGAS-FANCI phase difference was 3.1297 rad, 0.0118 rad from opposition, satisfying the RRM interaction criterion; the NMR cGAS-FANCI pair gave 1.7319 rad, approximately {pi}/2, which does not satisfy the criterion. Conversion of the dominant frequency yielded a predicted wavelength of 792 nm (378.5 THz), in the near-infrared range. This prediction is testable in transparent vertebrate models: zebrafish respond to NIR light, and red-light pre-treatment has been reported to improve survival after lethal gamma irradiation in zebrafish embryos. Conclusions: RRM identifies conserved spectral features in cGAS consistent with a cGAS-FANCI relationship, and amplitude at the dominant frequency varies with life-history traits. The phase analysis does not support a direct interaction signature for NMR cGAS-FANCI, a negative result consistent with a chromatin-mediated mechanism. The cross-species phase comparisons suggest that NMR FANCI, not only NMR cGAS, may contribute to the distinctive interaction mode. The predicted 792 nm wavelength provides a concrete, experimentally accessible parameter for testing whether RRM-derived frequencies can modulate radiation resistance in a transparent vertebrate model. These results are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation.

Title: Sodium arsenite requires redox sensitization to cause developmental dopaminergic neurotoxicity in Caenorhabditis elegans
Authors: Huayta, J.; Espinoza Tapia, W.; Jhaver, J.; Meyer, J.
Abstract: Environmental pollutants can disrupt mitochondrial function through many pathways and mitochondrial dysfunction is often linked to neurotoxicity, particularly of dopaminergic neurons. However, there are many mechanisms of mitochondrial toxicity. Remarkably, despite the centrality of the Krebs cycle to mitochondrial bioenergetics, there is very limited evidence regarding whether pollutants that inhibit the Krebs cycle can cause neurotoxicity. We exposed Caenorhabditis elegans through its whole development to Krebs cycle inhibitors sodium arsenite and fluoroacetic acid, and evaluated neuronal morphology and function as well as dopaminergic ATP levels and redox state. Both chemicals impaired growth and reproduction, but neither caused morphological damage nor functional deficits in dopaminergic, glutamatergic, or cholinergic neurons at concentrations causing mild organismal toxicity. Sodium arsenite, but not fluoroacetic acid, decreased dopaminergic ATP levels; neither caused significant changes in mitochondrial redox state. However, developmental exposure to sodium arsenite caused dopaminergic neurotoxicity when mitochondrial quality control or redox stress response was compromised by loss of pink-1/PINK1 or sod-2/SOD2, by co-exposure to rotenone, antimycin A, or buthionine sulfoximine, or secondary challenge to 6-hydroxydopamine. These conditions also led to dopamine-associated behavioral deficits. Thus, developmental exposure to sodium arsenite required an additional mitochondrial or redox stress challenge to cause dopaminergic neurotoxicity, and we did not find evidence that inhibition of the Krebs cycle broadly defined causes developmental neurotoxicity.

Title: Antibiotics drive immunometabolic rewiring of human immune responses
Authors: Hen-Avivi, S.; Bossel Ben-Moshe, N.; Avera, R.; Adin, I.; Kitsberg, Y.; Lyskov, S. K.; Navon, S.; Zalmanovich, A.; Yardeni, T.; Ben-Ami, R.; Avraham, R.
Abstract: Antibiotics are routinely evaluated for their antimicrobial activity, potential host toxicity, and disruption of the microbiome. Certain antibiotics can also impact cell-intrinsic host processes, including evolutionarily conserved processes in the mitochondria. These raise the possibility that antibiotics can directly impact host immunity, which relies on mitochondrial function for their immunometabolic activation. However, the immunological consequences of most antibiotics in current use have not been systematically examined. Here, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the effects of clinically used antibiotics on activation of primary human immune cells. We uncovered an underappreciated antibiotic-specific modulation of immune function in healthy individuals and infectious disease patients. Focusing on the immunomodulatory antibiotic ciprofloxacin, we found altered mitochondrial gene expression across multiple immune populations, driving distinct, lineage-specific responses and heightened sensitivity of T-cells. Ciprofloxacin impaired primary human T-cell expansion and activation and altered mitochondrial function and metabolism. We further demonstrated immunomodulatory effects of selected antibiotics in response to inactivated bacteria and during live viral infection. Finally, to test the implications of our findings in vivo, we showed that immune activation is altered shortly after a single dose of antibiotic administration in mice. This work established a widespread impact of antibiotics on immune-cell function, and identified mitochondrial perturbation as one underlying mechanism, with implications for host-pathogen interactions and antimicrobial therapy.

Title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
Authors: Oeller, M.; Vasconez Grunauer, S.; Sitron, C. S.; Mahul Mellier, A.-L.; Diedrich, L.; Schuele, A.; Ruf, V.; Oliinyk, D.; Kuttler, F.; Dransfeld, U.; Prassler, J.; Ben-Moshe, S.; Rodriguez, E.; Heymann, T.; Ugur, E.; Madden, K.; Sun, Y.; Ulrich, C.; Jasiqi, Y.; Lashuel, H. A.; Hartl, F. U.; Mann, M.
Abstract: -Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson's disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell's proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic. Inclusions took up whole assemblies, with subunits moving together in 421 of 438 complexes, and the V-ATPase alone was enriched in all three systems. Degradation cargo stayed with the receptors that route it, consistent with sequestration and failed degradation acting together. Neuritic and somatic inclusions differed, the former rich in UBQLN2 and the latter in intermediate filaments. In the cell line, phosphorylated -synuclein was tenfold higher in the inclusion than in the rest of the cell, with about one third of the rise already present before an inclusion was visible. Measured against its host, the composition of an inclusion becomes a readout of how it formed and a source of candidate markers and therapeutic targets.

Title: Singular Value Decomposition for the Automated Analysis of NMR Fraction Libraries
Authors: Esselman, C.; Edison, A. S.; Prestegard, J. H.
Abstract: Identifying and quantifying molecular components of biological fluids offers great potential for the diagnosis of disease, detecting environmental contaminants, and process monitoring. The use of simple 1D 1H NMR spectra to accomplish this task offers advantages in terms of broad applicability and quantitative output. However, it also encounters obstacles in extracting individual components from complex superimposed spectra and in compound identification through comparison with limited database entries. Here, we present a new protocol that includes automatically separating component spectra using singular value decomposition (SVD) and matching them to database entries that carry both chemical shift and scalar coupling information. The procedure is illustrated by application to a fungal extract from Neurospora crassa that is chromatographically fractionated to form a two-dimensional spectral fraction library. Results are compared to a previous analysis that used a semi-manual curation of separated spectra followed by chemical shift matching.

Title: Targeted cancer ablation via programmable sensing of amplified oncogenic RNA
Authors: Zhang, M.; Hu, Y.; Yamada-Hunter, S. A.; Sotillo, E.; Dai, H.; Call, C. C.; Tousley, A. M.; Kim, S. J.; Liu, W.; Winslow, M. M.; Mackall, C.; Gao, X. J.
Abstract: Selectively eliminating cancer cells based on their oncogenic drivers holds great promise but remains challenging for targeted cancer therapy. Here, we present ORCA (Oncogenic RNA-triggered Cancer Ablation), a programmable and modular platform that couples RADAR-based detection of oncogenic RNA with conditional expression of therapeutic payloads in cancer cells. We identify RADAR sensors targeting the transcripts of endogenously amplified oncogenes, including MYC, FGFR2 and wild-type KRAS in colorectal and gastric cancer cells. Focusing on colorectal cancer (CRC) driven by extrachromosomal DNA-amplified MYC, we demonstrate targeted ablation of high-MYC cancer cells using two orthogonal strategies: anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy and enzyme-prodrug therapy. In vivo delivery of ORCA using adeno-associated virus (AAV) suppresses tumor growth in a subcutaneous xenograft model and prolongs survival in a CRC liver metastasis model. ORCA establishes oncogenic RNAs as actionable inputs for targeted cancer therapy via programmable RNA sensing, thus offering a strategy to target tumors through the transcripts of otherwise difficult-to-drug oncogenes such as MYC.

Title: ExPert infers causal perturbations from cell states across biological and clinical contexts
Authors: Schwartz, L.; Schlamowitz, J. L.; Kuznets-Speck, B.; Johnson, C. W.; Das, D.; Grody, E. I.; Bai, T.; Sun, H.; Senthilkumar, I.; Primavera, G.; Jung, J.; Kuusik, B.; Grant, R. A.; Rojas, E.; Abdrabou, A. M.; Peiffer, B.; Sun, Z.; Diehl, A. M.; Marr, C.; Chandel, N. S.; Mithal, D. S.; Weinberg, S. E.; Adli, M.; Kalsotra, A.; Prashnani, E.; Goyal, Y.
Abstract: Pooled single-cell CRISPR screens have driven substantial effort toward models predicting the response to a perturbation. We posed the inverse question: which perturbation produced an observed cell state? Here we developed ExPert (Extracting Perturbations), which learns one prototype per perturbation in a latent space shared by 12 cellular contexts, trained on 8,964 perturbations and 19.5 million cells, and ranks 19,895 candidate genes per query, over half absent from training. ExPert more than doubled held-out-context recall over the best existing method with 1,000-fold less compute, and transferred without retraining to drugs, protein degradation and combinations. In alcohol-associated liver disease it implicated mRNA export, unchanged in expression, and we experimentally confirmed nuclear poly(A) retention and isoform switching. In primary mitochondrial disease it recovered the affected complex from blood, localized the signal to monocytes, and flagged a misdiagnosed control. Perturbation atlases can thus be queried in reverse, from state to likely driver.

Title: New perspectives in assessing environmental risks for birds: a simple TKTD framework to link growth and reproduction energy budget to chemical stress
Authors: Baudrot, V.; Kaag, M.; Charles, S.
Abstract: Assessing the risk of pesticides to birds requires models that can extrapolate laboratory data to realistic exposure scenarios. In this work, we propose a new modeling framework BIRDkiss (Bird - Impact on Reproduction via Diet, keep it simple and suitable). This framework integrates a simplified Dynamic Energy Budget (DEBkiss) of organisms and the toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic (TKTD) of chemical substances according to a trait-based approach, thereby reducing the number of parameters to identify and strengthening the statistical robustness of the critical endpoints. The BIRDkiss model describes how food intake and toxicant exposure affect growth and egg production in birds over time. The model is fully embedded within an R package, including routines for calibration, validation and prediction under single-compound scenarios performed via Bayesian inference using standard data from the OECD avian reproduction tests. The BIRDkiss model also allows the simulations of scenarios under both varying food availability and multi-compound exposures based on the two classical mixture-toxicity paradigms: Concentration Addition (CA) and Independent Action (IA). The results of calibration for single compounds show good results matching with observed weights and egg counts. From these calibrations, predictions for new exposure scenarios can be readily generated. For mixtures, the IA algorithm is simpler and does not require to scale variables as in CA. Simulations indicate that high food levels do not further increase egg production (saturation), whereas substantial food reductions markedly decrease reproduction because energy is reallocated to maintenance. Exposure to chemicals combined to low food availability amplify the decline in reproductive output. The ready-to-use mechanistic, open-source BIRDkiss tool enables predicting the impact of pesticides on avian reproduction under realistic dietary exposure profiles. The implementation of CA and IA models is a first step toward mechanistic assessment of chemical mixtures, although validation still requires empirical mixture data. The model highlights the importance of food availability and shows that chemical stress can exacerbate the negative effects of nutritional stress. Integrating such models into regulatory frameworks could improve the ecological relevance of risk assessments.

Title: A noncanonical function of Dicer fuels self-dsRNA-driven inflammation
Authors: ter Haar, L. R.; de Lange, S.; Gravekamp, D.; Kooij, A. R.; de Wolf, J. W.; Asschert, Y.; Oosenbrug, T.; Paul, M. W.; van Veelen, P. A.; van Roon-Mom, W. M. C.; Mei, H.; Van der Veen, A. G.
Abstract: Self-derived double-stranded RNA (self-dsRNA) acts as potent triggers of autoinflammation and damage-associated molecular patterns in cancer and infection. However, the upstream processes controlling self-dsRNA homeostasis remain unclear. We uncover a non-canonical role for human Dicer in driving cell-intrinsic immunity to self-dsRNAs that arise from editing or splicing defects, epigenetic deregulation or mitochondrial stress. Dicer loss abolishes type-I interferon induction, PKR activation, and OAS-RNase L activation in response to self - but not exogenous - dsRNA in multiple cell types, including a clinically-relevant hiPSC model of neuroinflammation. Dicer interacts with G3BP1 and LGP2 to regulate self-dsRNA availability and recognition, respectively, independently of miRNAs. As immunostimulatory self-dsRNAs fail to accumulate and activate dsRNA sensors in absence of Dicer, these findings position Dicer as a central regulator of self-dsRNA sensing.

Title: Loss of cell-identity DNA methylation tracks division history, not DNA damage
Authors: Sagy, N.; Benedek, N.; Bar, D. Z.
Abstract: One influential proposal holds that DNA damage drives aging by degrading the epigenome, so that a cell loses the information that specifies what it is. We test that specific proposed driver, not the broader idea that aging involves a loss of epigenetic information. Cell-type-unique CpGs are a direct place to test it. They are the sites where a cell's methylome differs most from every other cell type, so they are where its identity information can be accurately measured. We built such a panel for human skin fibroblasts against twenty primary cell types, and found that most of its 9,150 CpGs behave as a record of proliferation rather than identity. Their methylation state in fibroblasts is shared with continuously proliferating cell lines, consistent with the bulk hypomethylation of late-replicating chromatin that accumulates in culture, and this layer must be separated from identity marks before identity loss can be tested. We then expressed every perturbation as the fraction of the panel's identity information lost beyond baseline-matched background CpGs, using a Bernoulli cross-entropy between the fibroblast code and a generic comparator cell. In 24 matched fibroblast cultures, replicative exhaustion cost 24.3% of the identity information (95% CI 20.2 to 28.7) and RAS activation cost 5.4% (4.6 to 6.1), both at p = 1.2 X 10^-7;. A senescence-inducing dose of X-rays cost nothing: -0.5% (-0.7 to -0.2), with identity CpGs if anything moving slightly further from other cell types than matched background did. The design could detect a loss of 0.4%, about one sixtieth of the exhaustion effect, so the X-ray result is a bounded negative rather than an absence of power. Doxorubicin-induced and irradiation-induced senescence did not move the panel either. Clones that kept dividing after irradiation moved further from other cell types rather than collapsing toward them. In human fibroblasts, loss of identity information tracks prolonged division, not acute DNA damage.

Title: Monounsaturated fat prevent, whereas saturated fat promote, cholesterol crystals in cytoplasmic lipid droplets
Authors: Njoku, U.; Siedlecki, S.; Li, L.; Quirk, A.; Widenmaier, S. B.
Abstract: Objective: Metabolic dysfunction associated steatohepatitis (MASH) may, in part, result from excessive storage of cholesterol in hepatic lipid droplets that transition into a crystalline state. The mechanism by which crystals form in lipid droplets of hepatocytes and other cells such as macrophage is incompletely understood. Recently, we showed cholesterol must be esterified for crystals to form in lipid droplets. As the physicochemical properties of saturated cholesteryl ester render it more susceptible to crystallize than unsaturated cholesteryl ester, we investigated whether lipid droplet crystals are composed of saturated cholesteryl ester. Method: Lipid droplet crystals were measured in cholesterol-loaded Hep3B hepatocyte-like and RAW 264.7 macrophage-like cells co-treated with vehicle, monounsaturated fat, or agents that increase cellular saturated fat level. Lipidomics was used to quantify cholesteryl ester species. We also used Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectromicroscopy on livers of mice with MASH to determine the molecular identity of crystals in hepatic lipid droplets. Results: Cholesterol loading increased cholesteryl ester content and lipid droplet crystals. Monounsaturated fat treatment (e.g., oleate) increased the ratio of unsaturated to saturated cholesteryl ester and this corresponded with a substantial reduction in lipid droplet crystals. Treatments increasing saturated fat level did not exhibit this effect. (FTIR) spectromicroscopy identified cholesteryl palmitate as the prominent molecular constituent of hepatic lipid droplet crystals in mice with diet-induced MASH. Conclusion: Hepatic lipid droplet crystals in mice with diet-induced MASH are composed of saturated cholesteryl ester and unsaturated fat intake supports the cellular capacity to sustain non-crystalline liquid disordered cholesteryl ester in lipid droplets.

Title: Mitochondria-Coupled Hitchhiking Drives Vimentin Intermediate Filament Transport
Authors: Renganathan, B.; Moore, A. S.; Adam, S. A.; Lippincott-Schwartz, J.; Gelfand, V. I.
Abstract: Vimentin intermediate filaments (VIFs) undergo active microtubule-dependent transport throughout the cell, with trajectories resembling those of motor-driven organelles, yet our recent work showed that only a small subset of VIFs lies close to microtubules. How VIFs engage the microtubule-based transport machinery, and whether additional transport routes contribute, remain unresolved. We hypothesized that VIFs move indirectly, by hitchhiking on motile organelles, and tested this using mitochondria. Live imaging showed mitochondria and adjacent VIFs moving together, and volume electron microscopy revealed VIFs closely following mitochondrial surfaces at sites distinct from microtubule contacts. Depleting the mitochondrial motor adaptor TRAK1 to inhibit anterograde mitochondrial transport shifted both mitochondria and VIFs toward the nucleus. Driving mitochondria toward the cell periphery with a tailless kinesin-1 in cells lacking endogenous kinesin-1, or toward the cell center with a minus-end-directed motor, redistributed a subset of VIFs in the same direction. Thus, VIF transport to a large extend is accomplished by hitchhiking on motile mitochondria.

Title: Sex-specific bone marrow populations regulate skeletal phenotype and identify CD74-marked osteoclast precursor subsets
Authors: Koroth, J.; Karkache, I. Y.; Vu, E. K.; Manser, J. C.; Mitchell, S.; Shimak, M. J.; Robertson, N.; Patterson, E.; Kiraguri, S.; Mansky, K. M.; Bradley, E.
Abstract: While there are clear differences in bone accrual and maintenance between men and women due to hormonal regulation, the potential cell-intrinsic factors governing this difference are poorly understood. To investigate this, we performed bone marrow transplantation assays using male or female bone marrow transplantation into male hosts. Micro-CT analyses of lethally irradiated 8-week-old male mice transplanted with female bone marrow exhibited increased vertebral body trabecular and cortical bone mass. To identify cell types mediating these effects, we performed comparative single cell sequencing analyses and identified several CD11B+CD74+ myeloid cell clusters. Male donor BM chimeric mice had a higher proportion of Cd74-expressing clusters compared to female donor BM chimeric mice. We confirmed that males have greater numbers of bone marrow-resident CD11B+CD74+ cells under physiological conditions. Elevated expression of X-linked genes Tlr7 and Kdm6a marked a population of CD11B+CD74+ cells. Lastly, we show that female CD11B+CD74+ cells exhibit diminished osteoclastogenesis. These findings demonstrate that male and female bone marrow-resident cells have cell-intrinsic differences that regulate bone mass and that CD74 marks a subset of osteoclast precursor-enriched myeloid populations.

Title: cGAS integrates Toll-like receptor signaling in platelets to promote thromboinflammation
Authors: Bidias, A. R.; Arsenault, L.; Fleury, S.; Wellman, M.; Osouf, M.; Germain, M.; Pernet, E.; Lordkipanidze, M.; Pepin, G.
Abstract: Thromboinflammation is driven by innate immune signaling and promotes tissue injury during sepsis. Activation of platelets by bacterial products and alarmins amplifies inflammation, coagulation, and thrombotic dysfunction. However, the mechanisms by which these diverse inflammatory signals converge to elicit common platelet responses remain largely undefined. Mitochondria are key integrators of cellular stress responses and can activate innate immune pathways through the release of mitochondrial DNA and engagement of the DNA sensor cGAS. We therefore hypothesized that stimulation of innate immune receptors generates endogenous cGAS ligands within platelets, providing a unifying mechanism by which distinct inflammatory cues converge on cGAS-STING signaling. Here, we demonstrate that activation of TLR4, TLR1/2, and TLR5 engages a platelet-intrinsic mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis that promotes platelet activation. In a model of endotoxemia, genetic deletion of cGAS reduced platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, pyroptosis and the early systemic inflammatory response. Platelet transfer experiments further established that platelet-intrinsic cGAS is sufficient to amplify inflammatory responses in vivo. Mechanistically, we demonstrated that cytosolic accumulation of mtDNA and activation of cGAS-STING signaling pathway in platelets are dependent on mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) and correlated with the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. In contrast, canonical platelet agonists activated platelets independently of cGAS and failed to induce substantial cytosolic mtDNA accumulation. Importantly, this signaling architecture was conserved in human platelets, where TLR1/2-mediated activation required MCU- and STING-dependent signaling, whereas responses to thrombin receptor-activating peptide and collagen-related peptide remained largely unaffected. Together, these findings identify cGAS as an intracellular signal integration node that allows diverse innate immune receptors to converge on a common platelet activation pathway through sensing of mitochondria-derived DNA, allowing a rapid platelet response to microbial products.

Title: Exclusion from DNA double-strand breaks is a pervasive feature of the hnRNP family
Authors: Vincendeau, E.; von Ondarza, L.; Klaric, J.; Venkatesh, N.; Ceraolo, C.; Panier, S.
Abstract: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) are abundant RNA-binding proteins that have been linked individually to the DNA double-strand break (DSB) response, but their behaviour at damaged chromatin has only been examined one protein at a time and under disparate conditions. Here, we compare the core hnRNP family side by side by laser microirradiation and live-cell imaging. We find that 13 of 14 members are excluded from damaged chromatin, 10 directly and 3 after a transient phase of recruitment, establishing exclusion rather than accumulation as the predominant behaviour of this family. We characterised this behaviour in detail for hnRNPH1, which has not previously been linked directly to the DSB response. Its exclusion is sustained for several hours and also occurs at nuclease-induced breaks at a defined genomic locus. Importantly, exclusion is independent of the signalling pathways that drive protein recruitment to breaks and of transcriptional elongation, and instead requires the GYR low-complexity domain, with RNA binding contributing redundantly through three quasi-RNA recognition motifs. Finally, tethering hnRNPH1 to breaks through the RNF8 FHA domain selectively impairs 53BP1 accumulation without affecting {gamma}-H2AX, MDC1 or RPA, and hnRNPH1 is excluded from 53BP1 nuclear bodies in unchallenged cells. Together, these findings establish protein exclusion as an active component of the DSB response and show that the presence of an hnRNP at damaged chromatin can determine which repair factors assemble at DNA break sites.

Title: Novel Regulators of Sugar-dependent Food Consumption in Drosophila melanogaster
Authors: Opoola, M. A.; Fitzgerald, L.; Ahmed, S.; Wright, M.; Alli, S.; Wright, N.; Hwangbo, D.-S.
Abstract: Diet and genetic background interact to influence food consumption, yet the genetic basis of diet-dependent feeding behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we used genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) to investigate the genetic regulation of sugar-dependent food consumption in Drosophila melanogaster. Food intake was quantified in 176 lines of the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) using the Con-Ex (Consumption-Excretion) assay on low- and high-sugar foods. Flies showed compensatory feeding, consuming more low-sugar food than high-sugar food, and this behavior was largely maintained across genotypes. Additionally, the magnitude and overall consumption varied several-fold among lines, with broad-sense heritability of 0.53 to 0.66 across sexes and diets. Association analysis across six sex- and diet-specific phenotypes identified 161 variants mapping to 118 candidate genes, which shared almost no loci between dietary conditions, indicating that consumption on the two foods is largely under separate genetic control. RNAi knockdown of candidate genes identified CG42673 and Tmtc2, whose knockdown increased consumption across sexes and diets and was reproduced in independent experiments. Together, these findings show that natural genetic variation contributes substantially to diet-dependent feeding and identify candidate regulators of sugar-based food consumption in Drosophila.

Title: Removal of maternal compensation reveals retinal-specific roles for Pomgnt1 in zebrafish
Authors: Oliveira, C. D.; Flannery, K. P.; Simhon, L. M.; Shi, N.; Liu, D.; Burbano, D.; Manzini, M. C.
Abstract: Genetic variants in Protein O-mannose N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1 (POMGNT1) result in a broad spectrum of disorders, ranging from severe congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and ocular malformations to non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa. Despite POMGNT1's established role in the glycosylation of the transmembrane glycoprotein &alpha-dystroglycan (&alpha-DG), the mechanistic basis for this clinical variability remains poorly understood. Previous work in a zebrafish pomngt1 knock-out (KO) line identified retinal degeneration at 6 months post-fertilization (mpf). However, potential involvement of other tissues was not characterized, and compensation from maternal transcripts which can occur in the zebrafish oocyte was not tested. Here, we analyzed maternal-zygotic pomgnt1 KOs (MZKOs) to determine whether maternal compensation influences the onset and severity of pomgnt1-associated phenotypes. We assessed survival, gross morphology, locomotor activity, behavioral patterns, and retinal organization across multiple timepoints. MZKOs survived to adulthood and exhibited no morphological or locomotor deficits up to 5 mpf. Retinal abnormalities were found as early as 2 mpf in MZKOs, demonstrating that maternally provided factors of pomgnt1 delay the onset of retinal pathology. Additionally, MZKOs displayed a novel wall-hugging behavioral pattern that may be consistent with visual impairment or anxiety. These findings demonstrate a strong tissue-specific phenotype following loss of pomgnt1 in zebrafish showing evolutionary divergence in the necessity for Pomgnt1 function in the muscle. However, this strain provides a useful system for investigating the mechanisms underlying the retinal vulnerability observed in POMGNT1-related retinitis pigmentosa.

Title: Genomic identification and multi-tissue transcriptomic profiling of vitamin D3-related genes in Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Authors: Saito, T.; Saele, O.; Wischhusen, P.; Adam, A.-C.
Abstract: The metabolic pathway of vitamin D3 is well characterized in mammals, but its genetic basis in teleost fish remains poorly defined. We identified 16 vitamin D3-related genes in Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), 14 orthologs of pathway genes and two albumins as candidate carriers, and profiled their expression in a 14-tissue atlas and in seven independent RNA-seq studies. Phylogenetic analysis resolved seven paralog pairs from the salmonid whole-genome duplication. Atlantic salmon and three other euteleost fishes lacked a gc gene, and the genes that flank gc in other fishes were adjacent in their genomes. The proteins annotated as GC in three Oncorhynchus species were albumins. Skin expression of dhcr7, which converts the precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol, was low and differed between studies. The activating enzyme cyp27b1 was barely expressed in five kidney and 21 head kidney samples, including those of the atlas, whereas cyp27b1.a was expressed in the brain and cyp27b1.b in the liver. In northern pike, which lacks this duplication, cyp27b1 was not detected in the kidney either. The catabolic enzyme cyp24a1 was only weakly expressed in the kidney and the head kidney. These transcript data suggest that vitamin D3 activation in Atlantic salmon may not depend on renal cyp27b1 expression under the conditions sampled, and that albumins or lipoproteins may carry vitamin D metabolites. Both hypotheses need to be tested with protein, enzyme activity, and metabolite measurements. The curated gene set provides a basis for studies of vitamin D3 metabolism and dietary vitamin D3 requirements in salmonids.

Title: Synthetic MPRA perturbation supervision improves variant-effect prediction in sequence-to-function models
Authors: Wang, L.; Galvin, J.; Vaz, E.; Keener, R.; Battle, A.
Abstract: Deep learning sequence-to-function (S2F) models learn to predict functional readouts, such as gene expression, from genetic sequence. However, these models are trained predominantly on the reference genome and struggle to accurately predict the effect of genetic variation on gene expression. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) explore the direct impact of genetic variation on gene expression, but saturation-mutagenesis MPRAs that measure variant effects directly remain limited, thereby restricting their use for fine-tuning S2F models. In this work, we investigate fine-tuning Borzoi, a state-of-the-art S2F model, on model-generated synthetic MPRA variant-effect data as a scalable alternative to overcome limits on the availability of supervised training data for genetic variation. First, we trained an ensemble of 16 models on 110,359 K562 MPRA measurements. Then, we distilled their predictions into a single student model using MPRA elements associated with 1,000 genes. The distilled model was subsequently used to generate synthetic variant-effect labels across increasing numbers of genes (50 to 1,000), with 600 variants per gene, to fine-tune Borzoi. Performance improved as we included more genes in training. In data-limited settings, training on more genes with fewer variants per gene performed better than training on fewer genes with more variants per gene, given the same number of total variants. Compared to pre-trained Borzoi, Borzoi fine-tuned on 600,000 synthetic samples across 1,000 genes increased Pearson correlation from 0.28 to 0.54 on CAGI5 promoter variants and from 0.39 to 0.46 on 903 GTEx fine-mapped whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs). Importantly, these improvements were achieved while preserving the pre-trained performance across all 7,611 output tracks. Furthermore, fine-tuned Borzoi recovered regulatory motifs identified by the MPRA model in genes unseen during training, suggesting that learned regulatory features can generalize across loci. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that model-generated synthetic supervision can improve variant effect prediction in S2F models while preserving their original pre-trained capabilities, offering a scalable strategy toward capturing the impact of genetic variation on gene regulation.

Title: Maternal diet and genetics shape the human milk metabolome
Authors: Johnson, K. E.; Duan, Y.; Youssef, A.; Aristizabal-Henao, J. J.; Johnson, A.; Kiebish, M. A.; Nagel, E. M.; Palmsten, K.; Pierce, S.; Wernimont, S.; Bode, L.; Lock, E. F.; Isganaitis, E. M.; Fields, D. A.; Albert, F. W.; Blekhman, R.; Demerath, E. W.
Abstract: Human milk contains a diverse array of metabolites that contribute to infant nutrition, immune development, and microbial colonization. The maternal factors shaping the milk metabolome, and the relative contribution of genetics or diet vs. other factors, remain poorly understood. Here, we profiled 458 milk metabolites in 349 one-month postpartum human milk samples and integrated metabolomic data with maternal diet, clinical, transcriptomic, and genomic measurements. Maternal diet was broadly associated with milk metabolite composition, with significant correlations identified between dietary features and 323 metabolites. Coffee consumption strongly predicted milk quinic acid and 1,3-dimethyluric acid abundance, while high-fiber dietary patterns were associated with metabolites including proline-betaine and N-acetylornithine. Integration of milk transcriptomic and metabolomic data via machine learning identified biologically plausible gene-metabolite pairs, including associations between QPRT expression and quinolinic acid, and DPEP1 and cysteine-glycine dipeptide. Genome-wide association analyses identified nine study-wide significant metabolite quantitative trait loci, including novel milk-specific associations near PDE6A affecting purine metabolites and near GNE affecting free sialic acid. Comparison with plasma metabolite studies demonstrated both shared and milk-specific genetic regulation of metabolites. Finally, we found that of all tested maternal features, diet explained the largest proportion of variation in the milk metabolome. Together, these findings demonstrate that the human milk metabolome reflects both maternal exposures and mammary gland-specific biology. This work establishes a framework for understanding how genetic and environmental factors shape milk composition.

Title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
Authors: Cantat, A.; Guerin, C.; Morel, N.; Vianay, B.; Mogilner, A.; Thery, M.; Blanchoin, L.; Colin, A.
Abstract: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment. The scalability of these structures depends on how strongly they deplete monomers from a shared pool, and tuning the disassembly rate is sufficient to shift their scaling regime. Scaling principles also hold for multiple competing structures, with greater competition imposing stronger constraints on the monomer pool. Together, these results establish a mechanistic framework in which a structure's capacity to adapt is set by how much it draws down shared resources as it grows, a principle that may extend to other intracellular structures that scale with the cells that build them.

Title: Reference-Guided De Novo Retrieval of 3D Chromatin Organizational Features with Representation Learning
Authors: Moran, S. P.; Liu, J.
Abstract: Chromosome conformation maps reveal spatial genome organization through recurring contact patterns, some associated with established architectural features and others with less understood biological processes. Identifying instances of a pattern across these maps is necessary to investigate its biological associations and recurrence across experimental settings. However, conventional feature callers typically target predefined patterns, offering limited support when researchers can provide examples of a feature of interest but lack a dedicated detection method. We introduce Chromatin Fetch (C-Fetch), a reference-guided retrieval framework that uses examples of a desired feature and a contrasting class to rank and assign contact-map patches at provided candidate coordinates. C-Fetch learns a reusable representation through weakly KL-regularized 3D autoencoding of structurally related, non-temporal Hi-C and Micro-C patches without architectural feature labels. We demonstrate retrieval of biologically defined contacts, visually specified patterns, and established architectural features. Polycomb-guided retrieval identifies contacts enriched for PRC2-associated signals, exceeding enrichment from loop-guided assignments at 5 kb, while queries resembling condensed domains retrieve patches with progressively stronger rectangular enrichment at higher ranks. Loop-guided retrieval increases aggregate focal enrichment relative to complete Mustache proposal sets across four held-out maps, and selected contacts show greater focality loss after cohesin depletion than matched remaining candidates. Retrieval also extends to Region Capture Micro-C and HiChIP, with ranking agreement retained across biological replicates and reduced sequencing depths. Together, these results establish reference examples as a flexible means of specifying contact-map features of interest, enabling biological investigation, exploration of visual patterns, and refinement of existing calls across datasets and technologies.

Title: Decision benchmarking of cryo-EM re-refinement
Authors: Yi, X.; Zhang, X.; Zhang, L.; Yi, J.
Abstract: Map fit is widely used in cryo-EM re-refinement. We benchmarked selection against retaining the deposited model (no operation), using packed-side-chain agreement with higher-resolution references. In a prespecified 3.0-3.6 [A] cohort (167 entries, 131 sequence groups), highest-correlation selection increased {chi}1 disagreement by 2.4{degrees} (95% interval 2.1-2.7{degrees}), with positive loss in 91% of groups. Group-weighted fractions with >20{degrees} increases and decreases were 7.2% and 3.7%; the fraction exceeding 1 [A] local side-chain RMSD rose by 2.4 percentage points. Selection by a half map withheld from re-refinement increased disagreement (2.29{degrees}; 1.70-2.97{degrees}; 99 entries). In 53 prespecified within-study low/high-resolution pairs, loss was 3.43{degrees} (2.85-4.02{degrees}), positive in 50 pairs; half-map loss was 2.35{degrees} (1.60-3.21{degrees}; 44 pairs). Primum provides fixed cohorts, residue sets and scoring tools to benchmark refiners and selection rules against no operation.

Title: 2D U-NET Deep Learning Architecture for Atherosclerotic Lesion Segmentation and Quantification
Authors: Giles, W.; Venetianer, Z.; Patel, N.; Neughebauer, M. B.; Abramson, A. M.; Granger, A. T.; Tustison, N. J.; Shi, W.
Abstract: Mice are commonly used for experimental atherosclerosis research, and a common procedure involves morphometric analysis of atherosclerotic lesions on Oil Red O-stained cross-sections of the aortic root. However, manual measurement of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on numerous histological sections is tedious and time-consuming. Here, we developed a deep learning model based on convolutional neural network to quantify atherosclerotic lesions in cross-sectioned aortic roots of mice. Microscopy images were taken from cross-sectioned aortic roots of genetically diverse F2 mice derived from BALB/cJ and LP/J Apoe knockout mice and fed 12 weeks of a Western diet. Aortic cross-sections were stained with Oil Red O and hematoxylin and images captured. Atherosclerotic lesions were manually segmented in 2553 images using Zeiss AxioVision. These images were split into 1,533 for training the U-NET model, 510 for validation, and 510 images for testing. The developed model was evaluated for its performance to measure atherosclerotic lesions by comparing with manual measurement in test images. The model achieved a high degree of accuracy, with an F1 score of 0.82, a Jaccard score of 0.72, a Recall of 0.80, a precision of 0.87, and a correlation coefficient value of 0.98. While manual lesion measurement took approximately 5 minutes per image, the model performed the task in ~3.35 seconds, reducing measurement time by 98.9%. The developed 2D U-NET model provides a new platform for rapid and accurate quantification of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on Oil Red O-stained sections.

Title: SPaRTA: Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis
Authors: Dutta, A.; Ghosh, S.; Prado, K.; KhudaBukhsh, A.; Sarkar, H.
Abstract: Spatial-omics technologies provide clinicians, pathologists, and biomedical researchers with high-resolution maps of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic activity within tissues. However, querying these complex datasets often requires specialized computational expertise, limiting their accessibility to domain experts without programming experience. In the current manuscript, we develop SPaRTA (Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis), a natural-language interface that translates free-text questions into executable spatial SQL queries over such data. We release SPaRTA-Bench, comprising dataset-specific database schemas, explicit query conventions, and 7,500 question-SQL pairs validated through LLM-assisted verification and targeted human review, spanning breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and melanoma tissue sections, and identify 15 failure modes in which a query runs but returns a wrong answer. Open-weight large language models (LLMs) of the Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and Phi families reach 10-40% execution accuracy zero-shot, and at most 61% with reasoning and execution feedback. Fine-tuning raises them to 63-77%, and they lose at most 6 percentage points on a tissue unseen in training. Execution feedback repairs queries that fail to run, but rarely queries that run and return a wrong answer.

Title: Stochastic gene expression drives state switching and phenotypic heterogeneity in RNA repair
Authors: Hindley, H. J.; Lara Molina, R.; Weisse, A. Y.
Abstract: Bacterial populations often exhibit variability in cellular responses to antibiotics which can affect treatment success and survival outcomes. This heterogeneity suggests that genetically identical cells can occupy different states of susceptibility within the same population. Better understanding of these dynamic responses is essential for determining how cells respond to stress and survive antibiotic-induced damage. In this work, we investigate heterogeneity in antibiotic responses driven by the Rtc RNA repair system in E. coli. We develop a stochastic model of Rtc-mediated RNA repair to identify the drivers of heterogeneity at the single-cell level. We observe bimodality in cellular translational capacity and a transient memory in predicted responses to RNA damage, demonstrating how intrinsic stochasticity in Rtc-regulation can lead to phenotypic heterogeneity. Classifying single-cell trajectories, we predict drivers of state switching between the resistant and susceptible states, finding that stochastic expression of the rtc regulator determines entry into a resistant cell state, while dilution drives the system back into a susceptible state. These results indicate that heterogeneity in RNA repair emerges from stochastic switching between states, offering a route to understanding how individual cells survive in the presence of translation-targeting antibiotics.

Title: Computational Analysis of Antioxidant Effects on Stress Response Mechanisms in Candida albicans
Authors: K R, H.; G, S.; S, A. N.; S, S.; Shenoy, R.; Bhat, S.
Abstract: Candida albicans was used as a eukaryotic model to study aging and oxidative stress response pathways focused on NAD dependent deacetylases, Sir2 and SIRT3. A significant gene expression regulation of both Sir2 and SIRT3 was observed under sublethal hydrogen peroxide treatment towards their association with stress adaptation. Natural ligands known for antioxidant properties were docked against Sir2 and SIRT3 structures. Binding free energy of most components fall in the range of -5.0 to -11 kcal/mol. The best candidates pterostilbene, quercetin and naringenin formed stable hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds within catalytic and NAD binding pockets confirmed by visualization. Detailed ADME profiling shows most of the ligands passed the Lipinski rule of five and revealed a very good gastrointestinal absorption. PASS (Prediction of Activity Spectra for Substances) and SOM (Sites of Metabolism) predicts antioxidants, anti-aging properties, toxicity profiles, with key metabolic hotspots. This integrated in-silico approach highlights naringenin and quercetin as promising modulators of Sir2/SIRT3 mediated metabolic pathways in Candida albicans, warranting further validation with the help of in-vitro and in-vivo methods.

Title: KDM6A is enzymatically active at the Golgi apparatus where it is necessary for maintenance of Golgi apparatus morphology
Authors: Worth, C. S.; Conforti, J. M.; Nambiar, A. M.; Malone, J.; Budhathoki, R.; Ziegler, A. M.; Polavarapu, K.; Lilley, H.; Climer, L.; Simmons, D. D.; Kelber, J.; Gallagher, E. S.; Taube, J.
Abstract: KDM6A and KDM6B, lysine demethylases, play a central role in regulation of transcription through their demethylation activity towards H3K27me3 and have also been shown to be dynamically regulated upon epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). In particular, KDM6A has been implicated in a variety of malignancies and is frequently mutated in cancers including those in kidney, bladder, colorectal, and breast. KDM6A and KDM6B function as part of the COMPASS-like protein complex (CLC) which includes methyltransferases KMT2C/KMT2D and the regulatory WRAD-subcomplex. KDM6A total protein is known to be suppressed by TGF-{beta} in MCF10A breast cells; however, our examination of protein localization by immunofluorescence and LC-MS/MS reveals that KDM6A expression is lost in the nucleus but retained in the Golgi apparatus, independent of other CLC complex members. Importantly, KDM6A isolated from a biochemically-separated subcellular membranous fraction possesses the catalytic JmjC domain and is enzymatically active, indicating that KDM6A may have non-nuclear substrates. Further, knockdown of KDM6A and treatment with TGF-{beta} similarly alter Golgi apparatus morphology, in a cell type specific manner, suggesting context-dependent regulatory functions. These findings support a model in which KDM6A is necessary to maintain Golgi apparatus morphology and is enzymatically active outside of the nucleus.

Title: The role of the fruitless P3 transcript in development in Drosophila melanogaster
Authors: Kulinski, S. A.; Yeung, W.; Moehring, A. J.
Abstract: The generation of multiple transcripts from a single gene through alternative promoter usage and alternative splicing is a major source of functional diversity in eukaryotic genomes. The fruitless (fru) gene of Drosophila melanogaster is a classic example of transcript complexity, producing at least 15 transcript isoforms through the use of alternative promoters and terminal exons. While transcripts derived from the sex-specifically spliced P1 promoter have been extensively studied for their roles in sex determination and courtship behaviour, the functions of most non-sex-specific fru transcripts remain poorly understood. Previous studies suggested that transcripts originating from the P3 and/or P4 promoters may contribute to developmental viability, but their individual roles could not be resolved because available mutations disrupted multiple transcript classes simultaneously. Here, we used transcript-specific RNA interference (RNAi) and the Gal4/UAS system to investigate the function of fru P3 transcripts. Loss of P3 expression significantly increased developmental time to pupariation and resulted in complete lethality during pupal development despite normal survival to pupariation. Most mortality occurred during early and mid-pupal stages, indicating a critical requirement for P3-derived transcripts during metamorphosis. Notably, P3 knockdown did not phenocopy complete loss of fruitless, as knockdown individuals survived substantially later into development than fru null mutants, suggesting that additional fruitless transcript classes contribute essential functions during earlier developmental stages. Together, these findings establish an independent developmental role for the fru P3 transcript class and demonstrate that transcript-specific functions contribute substantially to the biological complexity of the fruitless locus.

Title: Varied forms of mutant tRNA mistranslation produce distinct phenotypes across multiple model organisms
Authors: Charles, B. S.; Moehring, A. J.
Abstract: Mutant tRNA mistranslation is a phenomenon in which specific tRNA gene mutations cause translational errors wherein amino acids incorporated during translation differ from those coded by mRNA sequences. The biological consequences of mutant tRNA mistranslation are highly complex and contextual, but are often deleterious. Importantly, many variables exist that are likely to affect the outcomes of any one mutant mistranslating tRNA; biochemical characteristics of the exchanged amino acids, frequency of use, identity of mistranslated products, and so on. Here, we generate a carefully curated array of tRNA mutants to assess which characteristics of mistranslating tRNA variants are most predictive of deleterious phenotypes. We find that toxicity often arises from mutant tRNAs that induce dramatic changes in biochemical properties between exchanged amino acids, as well as mistranslation that occurs more frequently. Importantly, exceptions are also observed to each of these general rules, implying instead that some deliriousness may arise from more granular, product-specific mechanisms. Additionally, quantification of mistranslation via mass spectrometry demonstrates a weak relationship between quantity of mistranslated products and severity of toxic phenotypes. Lastly, despite previous establishment of mutant mistranslating tRNA models in Drosophila melanogaster, incorporation of higher frequency mistranslating tRNA variants was largely unsuccessful, and incorporation of lower frequency mistranslating tRNA variants produces no detectable developmental phenotypes. These experiments support the notion that although general rules may be capable of reasonably predicting their consequences, each mistranslating tRNA variant warrants individual consideration and investigation for thorough understanding of its biological outcomes and precise mechanisms of toxicity.

Title: Chromosome folding encodes mechanisms of cohesion maintenance
Authors: Yan, X.; Tortora, M. M. C.; Goloborodko, A.; Fudenberg, G.
Abstract: After DNA replication, sister chromatids are physically linked by the cohesin complex. These cohesin linkages must be maintained for many hours for faithful chromosome segregation and DNA repair. Cohesin interacts with multiple rapidly exchanging cofactors, including SORORIN, which is often described as a molecular lock for cohesin on chromatin. How such transient SORORIN binding can protect cohesin over much longer timescales remains mechanistically unclear. Furthermore, how loop-extruding cohesins interact with and influence the positioning of sister-linking cohesins remains largely unknown. Here we show that changes in sister chromatid folding over time and after perturbations encode distinct signatures of the underlying mechanisms of cohesion maintenance. By integrating biochemical kinetics with polymer modeling, we infer cohesin turnover, motion, and encounter rules from these folding signatures. Repeated transient sequestration by SORORIN enables long-lasting protection yet acts as a quantitative modulator, rather than a binary switch for cohesion maintenance. Prolonging cohesin residence time by WAPL depletion exposes additional mechanisms shaping sister chromatid conformation, including pushing of sister-linking cohesins and diffusion of loop-extruding cohesins. Together, these results reveal how transient cofactor interactions regulate long-lived cohesin maintenance and establish sister chromosome organization as a quantitative readout of otherwise hidden molecular mechanisms.

Title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
Authors: Zhang, X.; Luo, H.; Li, G.; Zhang, X.; Wang, S.; Liu, L.; Guo, M.; Tan, Q.; Domeniconi, C.; Chen, J.; Wang, J.; Yu, G.
Abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.

Title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
Authors: Yang, M. M.; Auyeung, V. C.; Kim, S. M. C.; Flynn, E.; Naikawadi, R. P.; Bazarov, A. V.; Lea, A.; Deiter, F.; Neely, J.; Kukreja, J.; Matthay, M. A.; Jones, K. D.; Greenland, J. R.; Sirota, M.; Wolters, P. J.
Abstract: Rationale: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives: To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results: Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1 endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1 fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1 fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-{beta} signaling in UIP. Conclusions: Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-beta signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

Title: The Braarudosphaera bigelowii genome reveals cellular remodeling around a nitrogen-fixing organelle
Authors: Coale, T.; Mak, W. K. E.; Turk-Kubo, K. A.; Hagino, K.; Cornejo-Castillo, F. M.; Fussy, Z.; Zehr, J.
