Abstract: Braarudosphaera bigelowii hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial organelle UCYN-A, or the nitroplast, but the absence of a reference genome has limited investigation of the genomic features accompanying this association. Here, we present nuclear and organellar genome resources for the cultured B. bigelowii strain FR-21. The assembly comprises a 472.1-Mb nuclear genome together with representative nitroplast, chloroplast, and mitochondrial genomes of 1.49 Mb, 107 kb, and 44 kb, respectively. The four genomic compartments have strongly differentiated GC compositions, consistent with their distinct evolutionary origins. The large nuclear genome does not appear to reflect a corresponding expansion of protein-coding capacity. Repeat annotation indicates that approximately 77% of the nuclear assembly is repetitive, leaving approximately 108 Mb of nonrepetitive sequence containing roughly 16,000 predicted protein-coding genes. Phylogenomic analysis places B. bigelowii within the expected diversity of haptophytes, indicating that its unusual diazotrophic lifestyle is not associated with an anomalous phylogenetic position. Comparative analysis of nitrogen metabolism genes reveals extensive remodeling of host nitrogen acquisition and assimilation. B. bigelowii lacks major components required for nitrate and nitrite assimilation and has reduced capacity to use urea, cyanate, and several internally recycled nitrogen sources. In contrast, ammonium transport and the glutamine synthetase-glutamate synthase pathway are retained. This combination suggests reduced flexibility in nitrogen use and a host metabolism increasingly centered on ammonium supplied by the nitroplast. B. bigelowii also encodes an expanded set of flavodoxin and cryptochrome genes. Eleven of 14 flavodoxin candidates and 21 of 39 cryptochrome candidates contained motifs linked to nitroplast targeting. Together with previous evidence that some of these proteins are abundantly imported into the nitroplast, these expansions point to host-encoded roles in nitroplast redox metabolism and diel regulation. These genome resources establish a foundation for investigating nitroplast protein import, host-organelle metabolic integration, and the genomic consequences of acquiring an intracellular nitrogen-fixing compartment. They further show that the evolution of the B. bigelowii-UCYN-A relationship involved substantial remodeling of genome architecture and nitrogen metabolism in both partners.

Title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
Authors: Hao, Y. A.; Liu, M.; Nori, D.; Brixi, G.; Lau, T.; Ramakrishnan, C. A.; Chang, D.; Park, R.; Allen, W. E.; Hie, B.
Abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

Title: A trustworthy semantic knowledge network linking data-driven cell phenotypes to diseases and drugs
Authors: Xu, B.; Deslattes Mays, A.; Diller, M.; LeClair, R.; Pankajam, A. V.; Spear, W.; Osumi-Sutherland, D.; Arvind, K.; Chatterjee, S.; Diehl, A. D.; Islam, M. M.; Kelly, C.; Khalil, R.; Khare, J.; Lopez Candelaria, R.; Peng, B.; McDonald, L.; Pintard, D.; Rotenberg, N.; Zweibaum, D.; Zhang, Y.; Scheuermann, R. H.
Abstract: Genome-wide association and other genetic studies have identified genes involved in disease pathogenesis, and their encoded proteins have provided therapeutic targets. However, little is known about which cells are the functional home of these disease-associated genes and proteins. Single-cell technologies are enabling high-resolution profiling of cell phenotypes and revealing cellular contexts of disease, yet much of the resulting knowledge remains embedded in individual datasets and scientific literature. To address these gaps, the National Library of Medicine has developed Cell Knowledge Network (NLM-CKN, https://nlm-ckn.org). Reproducible computational workflows have generated cell phenotype knowledge for 2,585 cell sets and 5,139 selectively expressed genes from 88 datasets covering 10 human organs. Mapping of these cell sets to cell types grounds Cell Ontology terms in experimental evidence. This experimental knowledge is integrated with external knowledge of anatomical and cell-type hierarchies, gene-disease associations, and therapeutic interventions. A semantic schema defines node types and relations, enabling knowledge to be transformed into triple assertions and loaded into an ArangoDB database with provenance and quantitative evidence. The NLM-CKN interface supports graphical exploration of the cellular constituents of healthy human tissues. Finally, topological analyses generate insights into cellular contributions to disease pathogenesis, cellular contexts for therapeutic intervention, and drug-repurposing hypotheses.

Title: A biomimetic SPARC platform coupling adaptor recruitment and BRS-Lck condensation for enhanced NK/T cell combination therapy
Authors: Wang, Q.; Wu, S.; Qiu, Y.; Lou, J.; Lou, C.; Chen, H.
Abstract: Immune cell engineering has proven to be a promising therapeutic strategy for cancers and autoimmune diseases. Compared to classical CAR therapies, engineered T cells with modified TCRs (such as STAR-T and TRuC-T) exhibit lower tonic signaling and higher persistence. Inspired by this, we developed novel Synthetic Parallel Antigen Receptor Complexes (SPARC) based on the NK cell receptor 1 (NCR1) and the TCR chain. These SPARCs can recognize target cells via engineered extracellular domains and transduce signals by recruiting endogenous adaptor proteins (CD3{zeta}/FcR{gamma}). In NK cells,SPARCs confer high antigen specificity against lymphoma and enables NK cells to specifically recognize and kill tumor cells. Mechanistically, the cytoplasmic domain of NCR1 forms condensates with Lck kinase through two conserved basic-rich sequences (BRS), thereby promoting receptor clustering and enhancing NK cell cytotoxicity. Our findings indicate that SPARCs can also be applied to other immune cells expressing CD3{zeta} and FcR{gamma}. Incorporation of costimulatory domains further improves the performance of SPARCs. Furthermore, combining SPARC-engineered T cells and NK cells showed superior efficacy compared to either cell type alone. This biomimetic design preserves low basal signaling, overcomes the recognition limitations of endogenous receptors, and provides a versatile platform for engineering other membrane complexes.

Title: Characterization of intermolecular base pairing using AMT crosslinking in mammalian cells during oxidative stress
Authors: Liao, J. N.; Betances, I.; Shen, E.; Trcek, T.
Abstract: Intermolecular base pairing is essential for normal gene regulation but can also cause neurodegeneration when dysregulated. Despite its importance, intermolecular base pairing remains poorly characterized in cells. We coupled AMT crosslinking with RNA pulldown to probe intermolecular base pairing in mammalian cells under oxidative stress, a state that drives G3BP1/2-dependent stress granule assembly, translational repression, and increased exposure of RNA sequences available for intermolecular interactions. AMT captured intermolecular base pairing interactions among reporter RNAs in vitro and the known interaction between the U3 snoRNA and pre-18S rRNA in cellulo. Although detection sensitivity was limited for endogenous mRNAs, we found that base pairing among inducibly expressed reporter mRNAs is sensitive to RNA sequence, oxidative stress, and G3BP1/2. Furthermore, chemical probing revealed that base accessibility to DMS within non-translated regions of candidate RNAs remains similar between stressed and unstressed cells, and those lacking G3BP1/2, indicating that RNAs remained state under these conditions. Our findings establish an approach for studying RNA base pairing in cells and suggest that intermolecular base pairing may act together with RNA structure to preserve RNAs during oxidative stress.

Title: Multiparametric Extracellular Vesicle Profiling Identifies a Distinct Circulating Signature of Bicuspid Aortic Valve Disease
Authors: Weiss, L.; Harrison, A.; Chelvanambi, S.; Kasai, T.; Turner, M. E.; Blaser, M. C.; Billaud, M.; Aikawa, M.; Singh, S. A.; Aikawa, E.
Abstract: Background: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) resulting in life-threatening aortic stenosis, heart failure and death, develops earlier and progresses more rapidly in patients with bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) than tricuspid aortic valves (TAV), yet the circulating molecular drivers remain poorly understood. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) capture disease-relevant cellular activation and offer a powerful window into a BAV-specific pathophysiology. Methods: Circulating large extracellular vesicle (LEV) abundance and morphology were characterized by complementary single-vesicle nano-flow cytometry and super-resolution microscopy. Proteomic profiling further delineated LEV molecular cargoes and associated biological pathways between patients with BAV and TAV. Results: We demonstrate that patients with BAVs exhibited fundamentally altered circulating LEV profiles compared to TAVs. Super-resolution imaging revealed BAV-specific organization of platelet- and leukocyte-associated adhesion molecules into discrete EV membrane microdomains. Proteomic profiling identified distinct LEV cargoes between BAV and TAV, including a BAV-specific, previously unrecognized neutrophil-associated signature enriched for proteins involved in neutrophil degranulation and innate immunity. Consistent with this phenotype, BAV displayed alterations in platelet- and neutrophil-associated LEV populations, suggesting enhanced (thrombo-)inflammatory activity. Lastly, distinct associations between LEV populations and clinical parameters in BAV and TAV suggest that LEV profiles reflect morphology-specific aspects of disease severity. Conclusions: Comprehensive single-vesicle analysis and bulk proteomic profiling identified a distinct circulating LEV signature in BAV-associated CAVD, characterized by endothelial activation and reciprocal platelet-neutrophil interactions. These findings reveal previously unrecognized differences in circulating LEVs between BAV and TAV and highlight their potential as biomarkers of valve morphology-specific pathophysiology.

Title: The AP-1 clathrin adaptor has a conserved role in recycling resident proteins of the trans-Golgi network
Authors: Valbuena, F. M.; Lessard, M.; Krahn, A. H.; Pantazopoulou, A.; Lee-Smith, C. F.; Fromme, J. C.; Adarska, P.; Bottanelli, F.; Glick, B. S.
Abstract: Although the AP-1 clathrin adaptor has been studied for decades, its role in membrane trafficking has been ambiguous. Here, we systematically investigated the localization and function of mammalian AP-1. This adaptor associates with the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and with TGN-related recycling endosomes. Disruption of the 1A subunit of AP-1 has only a mild effect on the Golgi export of secretory cargoes, but it causes depletion from the Golgi of multiple transmembrane TGN proteins. Live-cell imaging and a cell surface labeling assay indicate that when TGN proteins are unable to bind AP-1, they exit the Golgi to the plasma membrane. Our interpretation is that the vesicles generated with AP-1 recycle transmembrane TGN proteins, thereby keeping those proteins in the Golgi during cisternal maturation. The clathrin adaptor epsinR seems to function as a partner for AP-1 in recycling a subset of TGN proteins. These results closely align with studies of AP-1 function in yeast, suggesting that the conserved core role of AP-1 is the intra-Golgi recycling of TGN proteins.

Title: Microtubules coordinate with actin assembly and disassembly to elongate cortical actin cables
Authors: McCartney, B.; Chou, W.-C.
Abstract: The coordination of actin filament elongation, bundling and turnover within bundled actin structures is poorly understood. Nurse cells extend bundles of actin filaments (cables) from the cortex during Drosophila oogenesis. We previously showed that cable assembly requires a developmentally-regulated microtubule (MT) network. Here we demonstrate that MTs coordinate with actin filament assembly and disassembly to promote the persistent elongation of actin cables. Disrupting the MT network caused actin cables to detach from the cortex and become free in the cytoplasm. The subsequent fate of those free cables, shrinking over time or maintaining a stable length, depended on the MT manipulation. Furthermore, maintaining cortical continuity and persistent cable elongation requires a regulated imbalance between filament assembly and disassembly. Favoring disassembly caused cable detachment and shrinkage while reducing disassembly allowed free cables to continue elongating in the cytoplasm. Our results also suggest that both filament assembly and disassembly occur at the cortical filament barbed-ends protected from excessive disassembly by Capping Protein.

Title: A DNM1L GTPase Effector Domain Deletion Causes Intermediate Defects in Peroxisomal and Mitochondrial Dynamics and Reveals a Targetable Metabolic Vulnerability
Authors: Srivastav, S.; Jangam, S.; Andrews, J.; Theodorou, E.; Briere, L. C.; Quintana, G. D.; Gomes, I. L.; Saute, J. A.; Bhagwat, P.; Subramaniam, A.; Roy, N.; Macnamara, E.; Sanchez-Valle, A.; Gordillo, C.; Bellen, H. J.; Yamamoto, S.; Lalani, S.; High, F. A.; Walker, M. A.; Simao Medeiros, L.; Sweetser, D. A.; Wangler, M. F.
Abstract: DNM1L encodes dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1), a key GTPase regulating mitochondrial and peroxisomal dynamics. Pathogenic DNM1L variants are associated with a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders, with phenotypic severity varying by affected protein domain. While variants in the GTPase domain are typically associated with milder phenotypes and middle-domain variants with severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, the functional impact of GTPase effector domain (GED) variants remains less defined. Here, we describe four individuals harboring a recurrent heterozygous GED deletion (L700del) presenting with movement disorders and lacking severe infantile encephalopathy, consistent with an intermediate clinical phenotype. Patient-derived fibroblasts exhibited tubular peroxisomes and enlarged mitochondria, while Drosophila models demonstrated that DNM1LL700del has intermediate functional effects that were more pronounced than those of a GTPase-domain variant A192E but less severe than those of the middle-domain variant G350R. Comparison with another GED variant, Y691C, further demonstrated variant-specific differences in severity within the GED. Metabolic stress assays showed that L700del fibroblasts exhibited impaired growth under galactose conditions, consistent with increased vulnerability under conditions dependent on mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Bezafibrate, a PPAR agonist that promotes mitochondrial biogenesis, partially rescued this growth defect. Together, these findings support a functional allelic spectrum in DNM1L-associated disease in which protein domain contributes to, but does not completely determine, functional severity. L700del represents an intermediate-strength allele associated with a movement-disorder phenotype and a pharmacologically modifiable metabolic vulnerability.

Title: Large-scale AI-guided discovery of antifreeze peptides reveals functional tandem-repeat architectures
Authors: Li, Y.; Wang, C.; Liu, J.; Song, M.; Zhang, L.; Sun, S.; Li, W.; Qiu, J.; Qin, Y.; Yao, J.; Zhao, L.; Yu, H.; Wang, X.
Abstract: Despite growing demand for biocompatible materials that regulate ice crystallization in cryopreservation, antifreeze peptide discovery remains constrained by limited candidate sequence diversity and reliance on known protein scaffolds. Here, we establish an AI-guided discovery framework integrating multimodal antifreeze protein prediction, generative sequence expansion and local sequence-pattern analysis. AFPFusionLM combines protein sequence and structure-aware representations, achieving an AUROC of 0.937 and an AUPRC of 0.957 on an independent reference set. Antifreeze-domain-adapted protein sequence generation and multimodel consensus screening of UniProt, glacier metagenomes and generated sequences yielded 87,305 candidate protein records. Large-scale sequence analysis revealed recurring periodic sequence architectures across multiple candidate protein clusters, enabling the identification of short-peptide families with shared repeat features and their natural variants. Experimental evaluation revealed ice recrystallization inhibition activity in multiple peptides from repeat-associated families, with inhibitory effects comparable to or greater than those of reference peptides reported in the literature. Cell-based experiments using a representative peptide-containing formulation also supported its cryoprotective potential under reduced-DMSO conditions. These findings show that large-scale sequence exploration can reveal function-associated peptide sequence architectures, providing a research framework for the systematic discovery and subsequent optimization of antifreeze peptides.

Title: Model-Agnostic Decomposition of the Difference in Mean Response Between Two Groups via Game-Theoretic Attribution with Minimum-Switching-Distortion Coupling
Authors: Koh, H.
Abstract: The difference in mean response between two groups can arise from differences in covariate-response relationships, covariate distributions, or both. We propose a model-agnostic decomposition (MAD) of this difference into structure and composition effects. We formulate a cooperative switching game with a model-switch player and individual covariate-switch players, organized into model and covariate unions. MAD employs the Owen value, whose quotient game yields the aggregate structure and composition effects and whose internal game allocates the aggregate composition effect across covariates, and thereby inherits its fair allocation properties. In the internal game, partial covariate switches create hybrid covariate vectors whose joint distributions are not determined by the group-specific covariate distributions alone. To resolve this indeterminacy, we propose a minimum-switching-distortion (MSD) coupling, formulated as an optimal-transport problem. The MSD coupling satisfies admissibility conditions of identity at coincidence, transposition equivariance, and coordinate equivariance, and its sparse support reduces allocation cost. Because MAD imposes no particular functional form, it accommodates machine-learning models that adapt to complex nonlinear and interactive relationships, thereby yielding more accurate decompositions. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of MAD and the MSD coupling in terms of decomposition accuracy, coupling admissibility, and computational cost. As an illustration, we decompose the difference in mean body mass index between UK and US males aged 30-70 years using microbiome data, at the aggregate level and across microbial genera.

Title: SQANTI-evidence: isoform-resolved, evidence-tiered structural annotation of unannotated genomes from long-read RNA-seq
Authors: Atienza Lopez, P.; Conesa, A.
Abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures full-length transcripts, yet current annotation pipelines fail to properly curate the data for gene prediction. We present SQANTI-evidence, a workflow that annotates a genome from long reads alone, without a reference annotation or protein database. SQANTI3-curated transcripts enter the annotation as observed, with isoforms and untranslated regions; AUGUSTUS predicts genes at loci without read support. In benchmarks, the curated layer was the most precise gene set in five of seven species, recovered twice as many exact isoforms as BRAKER in mammals and placed 3' ends nearest the poly(A) site. We annotated 13 ERGA datasets.

Title: NeuroWeave-3D: Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Completion for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing MRI Modalities
Authors: Miller, D.; Weber, L. A.
Abstract: Multi-parametric MRI segmentation models are accurate when all prescribed sequences are available but can be brittle under missing or corrupted modalities. We propose NeuroWeave-3D, a 3D glioma segmentation framework that treats missing modalities as uncertain evidence rather than deterministic channels to reconstruct. The model combines spatial modality routing, probabilistic latent feature completion, complete-to-missing consistency, and voxel-level uncertainty estimation. A curriculum over all non-empty MRI modality subsets trains one network for arbitrary sequence availability. We define a BraTS-centered evaluation that reports complete-input accuracy, macro and worst-case missing-modality performance, corruption robustness, calibration, and failure detection.

Title: SPARC Reveals Distinct Osteoclastogenesis-Associated Malignant States in Metastatic Osteosarcoma
Authors: Wu, S.; Walker, W. C.; Nirala, B. K.; Martin, C.; Yustein, J. T.; Samee, M. A. H.
Abstract: Single-cell studies of metastatic cancer have revealed extensive transcriptional heterogeneity and cellular plasticity as malignant populations establish themselves in distant organs. The growing availability of paired single-cell profiles from primary tumors and matched metastases offers new opportunities to investigate how malignant-cell states evolve during metastasis in relation to progression within the primary tumor. Static comparisons between these sites have identified differences in cellular composition and molecular programs, but can reduce heterogeneous populations to site-level summaries and overlook changes in gene-expression programs along possible routes of metastatic progression. Investigating these dynamics calls for trajectory inference that reconstructs state progression within each condition and transitions between conditions. However, existing trajectory inference tools have limitations in jointly modeling these relationships under biological ordering constraints. Traditional and widely used trajectory inference tools, such as Monocle 3 and Slingshot, do not impose direction constraints based on biological knowledge or the sampling design during graph construction. Optimal transport-based tools, such as moscot, incorporate temporal order to infer cross-condition correspondences, but these mappings alone do not reconstruct progression within each condition. More recent methods, including CStreet and CellRank 2, incorporate both transition types, but construct the two components separately through distinct modeling or graph-construction strategies. Here we introduce SPARC (Shortest Path Algorithmic Reconstruction of Cross-state Evolution), a unified graph-based optimization framework that evaluates both types of relationships under a common connectivity formulation to reconstruct complete, directionally constrained candidate trajectories. Across benchmarks, SPARC improved recovery of candidate metastatic precursors and complete progression routes in simulations, showed strong directed-trajectory reconstruction in conventional time-course settings, and performed competitively in real tumor lineage-tracing datasets. To examine metastatic progression in a model where lung lesions arise through spontaneous dissemination, we generated, to our knowledge, the first paired scRNA-seq dataset of primary osteosarcoma tumors and spontaneous lung metastases from the same mice, together with the first patient-derived osteosarcoma Visium HD dataset. The biological analyses revealed differences among metastatic tumor states in their association with osteoclast-like myeloid populations and candidate supportive signals, suggesting that certain malignant states may preferentially promote osteoclastogenesis. Together, SPARC provides a framework for investigating biologically ordered cell-state progression and identifying state-specific programs associated with metastatic disease.

Title: Accelerating antibiotic discovery from Earth's isolated habitats through protein language models and microfluidics
Authors: Kang, Z.; Zhou, Q.; Zhang, H.; Liu, J.; Liu, K.; Zhou, K.; Zhang, Y.; Wang, Y.; Chen, P.; Liu, B.-F.; Ning, K.
Abstract: The antibiotic potential of Earth's isolated habitat microbiomes remains largely unexplored. Accessing this resource requires reliable prioritization across divergent peptide sequences and efficient experimental validation. Here we present MicroSPEAR, an end-to-end framework for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery integrating SPEAR, a sequence-structure-aware ensemble predictor, with MicroGrad, a microfluidic testing platform. SPEAR generalized to low-homology peptides and prioritized potent candidates despite training on binary activity labels. MicroGrad simplified liquid handling and shortened susceptibility testing from approximately 18 h to 4 h. Applied to a catalogue derived from 4,480 metagenomes spanning 15 isolated habitat types, SPEAR identified 383,027 non-redundant candidate AMPs, 63.1% of which lacked detectable homologues in reference databases. Of 85 synthesized candidates, 79 exhibited antibacterial activity at [≤]64 M;. Mechanistic analyses revealed distinct modes of membrane disruption. Four broad-spectrum candidates with low toxicity significantly reduced bacterial burdens in a mouse thigh infection model. MicroSPEAR connects underexplored microbial diversity with experimentally validated antibiotic leads and provides a foundation for lab-in-the-loop discovery.

Title: Marker-specific pixel attribution for single-cell protein quantification with PixAQ
Authors: Zha, Y.; Liang, C.; Lin, Y.; Li, G.; Zhang, C.; Huang, Z.; Wang, Z.; Zhang, L.; Tong, M.; Jiang, W.; Xiao, X.; Yu, R.
Abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) typically quantifies all markers within the same cell mask, although their signals have distinct spatial distributions. This quantification method may omit relevant signals or include signals from neighboring cells. We present PixAQ, which improves single-cell protein quantification in IMC through marker-specific probabilistic pixel attribution. PixAQ combines spatial proximity with anchor-group intensity models to assign pixel-marker observations among neighboring cells and an explicit residual component. Original intensities are averaged over marker-specific supports. Across three cohorts (680 regions), comparisons in 366 patients showed improved agreement with predefined population-marker relationships, with cohort-median patient-paired gains of 1.99 to 4.83 percentage points in expected-marker share over shared-mask quantification. Ablation analyses showed that both spatial and intensity evidence contributed to these gains. Conventional and high-resolution IMC images linked supports to visible local and intracellular signal structures. PixAQ improves single-cell protein quantification by determining which local signals contribute to each marker measurement without changing cell segmentation.

Title: Top2All: Benchmarking sparse-to-transcriptome reconstruction from high-expression profiles across sex- and sex-steroid-defined conditions
Authors: Nishio, Y.; Yamashita, T.; Baba, T.
Abstract: Transcriptome-wide profiling at single-cell resolution is limited by sparse detection of gene expression, raising the question of how much transcriptomic information can be recovered from a small set of highly expressed genes. We developed Top2All, a Mouse-Geneformer-based framework for reconstructing transcriptome-wide expression from sample-specific sparse inputs. Using 24 cell-number-normalized RNA-seq profiles of mouse adrenal zona fasciculata cells across eight experimental conditions defined by sex and sex-steroid milieu, we evaluated condition-aware and no-condition models under replicate-wise out-of-fold and leave-one-condition-out validation. Top2All achieved near-unity sample-wise correlation with measured expression, but similarly high correlations were obtained using simple reference profiles, whereas gene-wise evaluation revealed substantially greater differences among methods. Explicit condition information did not consistently improve reconstruction, indicating that sex- and sex-steroid-associated condition information was already strongly encoded in the sparse expression profiles. Nearest-neighbor retrieval provided a stronger baseline than learned reconstruction, and input-depth analysis showed that increasing the number of input genes did not monotonically improve performance. These findings show that a relatively small set of highly expressed genes contains substantial information about transcriptomic state, while accurate reconstruction of gene-specific biological variation remains challenging. Sparse-to-transcriptome models should therefore be evaluated using gene-wise metrics, strong reference baselines, and tests of generalization beyond conditions represented during training.

Title: BioTrajX: evaluating biological plausibility in single-cell trajectory inference
Authors: Li, T. Y.; Chang, Y.-M.; Chen, S.-Y.
Abstract: Trajectory inference (TI) methods reconstruct cellular progression from single-cell RNA sequencing data, typically by ordering cells along a pseudotime axis. However, different TI methods and analytical choices can produce divergent trajectories from the same dataset, making it difficult to determine which inferred trajectory best reflects the underlying biological process. Existing evaluation strategies often rely on computational benchmarks or qualitative biological assessment, with limited standardized approaches for incorporating a priori biological knowledge. Here, we present BioTrajX, an R package for biologically informed evaluation of pseudotime trajectories using three complementary metrics: Directionality (D), which measures agreement between pseudotime and expected biological progression; Order Consistency (O), which quantifies the coherence of marker-program changes along the trajectory; and Endpoint Validity (E), which assesses enrichment of expected cell states at trajectory endpoints. Together, the DOE metrics provide an interpretable framework for comparing alternative trajectory inference results and evaluating root-cell choices prior to downstream analyses.

Title: Developing synthetic auxin-based trans-kingdom signaling
Authors: Furnish, M.; Kokarakis, E. J.; Kopycienski, D.; Thune-Larsen, B.; Ducat, D. C.; Khakhar, A.
Abstract: Synthetic trans-kingdom signaling systems with tunable transduction properties provide a unique avenue to explore how communication between organisms coordinate behaviors without the confounding complexity of natural systems. However, existing trans-kingdom signaling systems suffer from either toxic signal molecules, a need for rare precursors for signal generation, or transduction machinery which is either species-specific or cannot be easily tuned. This limits their capacity to be broadly applied across kingdoms and their utility as a model system to study trans-kingdom interactions. In this work we elucidate the design principles for a trans-kingdom signaling system based on the plant phytohormone, Indole 3-Acetic Acid (auxin), that overcomes these challenges. We demonstrate how auxin biosynthesis can be engineered into a model sender organism, the cyanobacteria Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942, and how this signal can be tuned with low leak and high dynamic range. We also show these signals can be connected to gene expression using tunable synthetic auxin-responsive signaling systems across multiple kingdoms. We demonstrate that S. elongatus generated auxin signals can tune gene expression in co-cultured Saccharomyces cerevisiae via auxin-induced degradation. Additionally, we show that when the S. elongatus are associated with the roots of the model plant, Arabidopsis thaliana, the auxin they generate can control gene expression via auxin-responsive synthetic transcription factors expressed from the plants genome. Taken together, our results demonstrate the design principles for a tunable auxin-based trans-kingdom signaling system that can be broadly applied across species.

Title: IL-23 licenses the transition from preclinical autoimmunity to inflammatory arthritis through IL-17A-dependent mechanisms
Authors: Jarlborg, M.; Circiumaru, A.; Lamacchia, C.; Vaillant, L.; Rakotoarijaonina, E.; Venken, K.; Elewaut, D.; Rodriguez, E.; Caruso, A.; Huard, A.; Santuari, L.; Chammartin, N.; Courvoisier, D. S.; Andreatta, M.; Carmona, S. J.; Finckh, A.; Gabay, C.
Abstract: Objectives: The mechanisms driving transition from systemic autoimmunity to clinical rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain poorly understood. We investigated the role of interleukin-23 (IL-23) in disease transition using a murine model of experimental arthritis, complemented by human transcriptomic analyses in individuals at risk of RA and RA synovial tissue. Methods: Collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) was induced in less susceptible C57BL/6 mice and combined with sustained systemic IL-23 overexpression. Disease severity, histopathology, immune responses, and tissue gene expression were evaluated. The contribution of IL-17A was assessed using a neutralizing anti-IL-17A antibody. Expression of IL-23 pathway-related genes was assessed in whole-blood transcriptomic data from a large cohort of first-degree relatives of patients with RA (n=1080) and in an independent synovial RNA-sequencing dataset (n=218). Results: In mice, sustained IL-23 overexpression converted a mild CIA phenotype into a highly penetrant arthritis characterized by increased expression of innate inflammatory mediators, and enhanced antigen-specific production of IL-17A and IFN-{gamma}, despite unchanged collagen-specific antibody responses. Neutralization of IL-17A prevented arthritis development. In human whole blood longitudinal analyses, lower RORC and KLRB1 expression was associated with a higher risk of RA onset. KLRB1 expression was persistently lower in progressors, whereas RORC expression showed a steeper decline before diagnosis, although this difference did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing. In RA synovium, IL23R, IL23A, and CCR2 expression was increased compared with controls, while IL23R expression was higher in early than established RA. Conclusions: IL-23 acts as a critical regulator of the transition from systemic autoimmunity to inflammatory arthritis by promoting IL-17A-dependent cellular and myeloid inflammatory pathways. The change in IL-23 pathway signatures in at-risk individuals and early RA supports the translational relevance of this pathway during disease initiation.

Title: Competence repression by the SPβ prophage in Bacillus subtilis revealed by transcriptomics across culture conditions
Authors: Grosboillot, V.; Gnidovec, L.; Baebler, S.; Ule, J.; Dragos, A.
Abstract: Prophages are near-ubiquitous in bacterial genomes, yet their effects on host physiology are typically assayed under a narrow range of laboratory conditions, mostly involving DNA-damaging agents or physical and chemical stress. This leaves open the question of which ecological and physiological conditions trigger prophage-host interaction, and whether the outcome benefits the host or the prophage. Here, we used publicly available transcriptomic data to investigate conditions promoting prophage-host interaction in Bacillus subtilis. This analysis identified that competence strongly induces prophage gene expression. To further investigate the role of competence, we used two sets of B. subtilis strains: a natural SP{beta} lysogen strain and its cured counterpart, and a natural non-lysogenic strain and the same strain lysogenised with SP{beta}. Under competence-inducing conditions, both lysogen strains showed lower expression of the competence genes compared with their non-lysogenic counterparts. This result was corroborated by transformation assays that showed consistently lower transformation efficiency in the lysogen strains, and by fluorescence microscopy using a transcriptional reporter for the late competence gene. Because competence is a principal route for horizontal gene transfer in B. subtilis, prophage repression of the competence programme constrains host DNA uptake and evolvability. More broadly, these results show that mining public transcriptomes for condition effects can guide experimental effort towards prophage-host phenotypes that conventional laboratory conditions would miss.

Title: V-SWITCH: A single-vector OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter of live RNA virus infections
Authors: Cid-Rosas, M.; Grunberg, M.; Matia, A.; Lee, S.-C.; Woosley, H.; Pradeep, S.; Kanwar, S.; Khadka, S.; Mehta, S. B.; Huttenhain, R.; Turon-Lagot, V.; Arias, C.
Abstract: Fluorescent reporters of viral infection are powerful tools for studying viral pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions. Here, we present V-SWITCH, a highly modular, single-vector, cell-based OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter that enables robust detection of viral infection in living cells. V-SWITCH is based on a split mNeonGreen (mNG) system employing a release-and-capture mechanism. In the "OFF" state, the mNG3A(1-10) fragment is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum via a Sec61 transmembrane domain, while the mNG(11) fragment, fused to BFP, is constitutively expressed in the nucleus. Upon infection, the viral protease cleaves a protease cleavage site (PCS) adjacent to the mNG3A(1-10) fragment, liberating it for translocation into the nucleus. There, it complements mNG(11) to reconstitute fluorescence. The constitutive BFP serves as both an expression control and a nuclear segmentation marker for image analysis. Each module in this dual-cassette design is flanked by unique restriction sites allowing rapid swapping of virus-specific PCS, split fluorophores, membrane anchors, and promoters. We demonstrate the versatility of the V-SWITCH reporter for several viruses (Dengue virus, Zika virus, West Nile virus and Human Coronavirus OC43) in several cell lines (A549, BJ-5 fibroblasts, HEK293T and HeLa). Reporter activation enables clear discrimination of infected and uninfected cells by flow cytometry and reveals time-dependent and heterogeneous infection dynamics by live-cell imaging at single-cell resolution. Importantly, we demonstrate the potential of V-SWITCH to support both rapid functional screening for host factor dependencies, as well as high-throughput compound screening to enable antiviral discovery and comparative evaluation of therapeutic strategies across multiple viruses and cell types.

Title: Disease-Causing Mutations Alter the Interplay Between Loop Dynamics and Catalysis in the Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2
Authors: Brownless, A.-L. R.; Maghsoud, Y.; Robinson, M.; Kamerlin, S. C. L.
Abstract: The protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) SHP-1 and SHP-2 play complex roles in a variety of signaling pathways, including those involved in cancers and other diseases, making them important drug targets. These two PTPs have superimposable active sites, but different biological functions in vivo, including opposing roles in cancer development. Unique to these PTPs is the presence of two tandem Src homology 2 (SH2) domains, which regulate access to the phosphate-binding site in the catalytic domain through an autoinhibition mechanism. Studies of the allosteric regulation and dynamics of these PTPs, as well as associated drug discovery efforts, typically focus on autoinhibition rather than the dynamics of a catalytic loop in the phosphatase domain, the WPD-loop, which is essential for PTPase activity. However, recent deep mutational scanning data has demonstrated that oncogenic mutations also regulate WPD-loop motion in SHP-2. We provide here a detailed computational study of WPD-loop dynamics and catalysis in wild-type and mutant full-length and catalytic domain only SHP-1 and SHP-2, demonstrating that many oncogenic residues lie on the allosteric pathways regulating WPD-loop dynamics. Mutations at these positions alter WPD-loop dynamics, disrupting the active site and negatively impacting catalysis. Further, our simulations provide molecular insight into the link between the presence of the SH2 domains and loop motion in the catalytic domain, and, importantly, how it differs between the two PTPs. Taken together, our work showcases the impact of altered WPD-loop motion in disease-causing SHP-1 and SHP-2 variants, opening new strategies for selectively targeting these important therapeutic enzymes.

Title: SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming): a simulation-informed Nextflow pipeline for cross-study harmonisation of 16S rRNA metabarcoding datasets
Authors: Terrey, D.; Huber, P.; Pereira, E.; Pelayo, M. C.; Ferguson, R. M. W.; Dumbrell, A. J.; Sweet, M.; Bani, A.; Metz, S.
Abstract: Global syntheses of 16S rRNA metabarcoding data rely on combining datasets, yet amplicon sequence variants generated with different primer pairs can rarely be compared directly. Existing approaches correct batch effects statistically or aggregate taxonomically; none first establishes whether the sequences are positionally comparable. We present SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming), a Nextflow pipeline that maps every studys variants onto a 16S rRNA full-length reference alignment, determines the largest window shared across studies, and tests by simulation whether trimming to that window degrades community structure before any data are merged. Applied to thirteen marine studies sequenced with three primer sets, twelve converged on a consensus window with a median trimmed read length of 249 bp (9,582 alignment columns). Degradation tests across twelve studies and six taxonomic ranks (72 study-rank combinations) returned 31 passes, 38 cautions and three confirmed failures. Eleven studies (682 samples after filtering) were harmonised (trimmed to the window and merged), collapsing 20,891 primer-specific variants into 12,667 MetaASVs, trimmed sequences deduplicated across studies. Harmonisation preserved community structure at family level (Mantel r = 1.00; Procrustes m{superscript 2} < 0.001) without adding between-study variance (|{Delta}R{superscript 2}| < 0.001). Alpha diversity, including observed richness, was recovered across all levels (intraclass correlations 0.93-1.00), whereas sequence-level congruence was moderate (Procrustes m{superscript 2} = 0.52), as expected where between-study similarity at sequence level exists only after harmonisation. The harmonised output supports synthesis from aggregated ranks down to exact sequences. By establishing positional comparability before merging, SeCAT opens the archive of primer-fragmented 16S rRNA surveys to sequence-level synthesis.

Title: PLATE: a global atlas of food metaplasmidomes
Authors: Aslan, M. U.; Kayacan, R. A.; Sögütdelen, S. A.; Sagıroglu, O.; Arıkan, M.
Abstract: Plasmids play a central role in the acquisition and spread of genes underlying important traits in food-associated microorganisms. Although shotgun metagenomics has greatly expanded opportunities to study food microbiomes, their plasmid diversity remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the Plasmid Atlas of Food Ecosystems (PLATE), a curated global resource of food metaplasmidomes. Built from 4,690 food metagenomes spanning 55 countries and 17 categories, PLATE comprises a broad catalog (bPLATE) of 3,904,895 putative plasmid contigs (PPCs) and a refined catalog (rPLATE) of 213,474 PPCs, corresponding to 181,871 unique sequences. Both catalogs are complemented by curated sample metadata, host predictions, taxonomic assignments, and functional annotations covering antimicrobial resistance (AMR), protein families and KEGG orthologs, CRISPR-Cas systems, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and bioactive peptides. We demonstrate PLATE's utility through a case study of AMR genes detected on PPCs from food microbiomes. PLATE is freely accessible and enables users to interactively search for and download sequences, annotations, and associated metadata. By organizing plasmid-associated sequence diversity and functional potential across food ecosystems, PLATE provides a foundation for analyses of food metaplasmidomes.

Title: TensorPLS: an R package for exploring molecular and temporal patterns in longitudinal omics data using PLS-DA
Authors: Giordano, A.; Conesa, A.; Balzano Nogueira, L.
Abstract: Longitudinal omics datasets combine high-dimensional repeated measurements with missing observations, complicating supervised modelling and temporal interpretation. We present TensorPLS, an R package integrating missing-data handling, matrix-based partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), structured variable importance, subject-level nested cross-validation and downstream functional enrichment. Data are represented as subjects x features x time tensors. Missing values are handled by Tucker3 reconstruction or feature-time mean imputation, after which tensors are unfolded along the subject mode for PLS-DA. Cumulative variable importance in projection (VIP) scores are mapped to feature-time coordinates and summarised across time and cumulative PLS models. During nested cross-validation, imputation, component tuning, VIP-based feature selection and refitting are performed within training partitions. Full-cohort models are fitted separately for descriptive interpretation. We evaluated TensorPLS on two public longitudinal transcriptomic datasets using five-by-five nested cross-validation. In GSE68310 (109 subjects), Tucker3 reconstruction yielded Q2Y = 0.670, AUROC 0.971 and balanced accuracy 0.931. In GSE182616 (66 subjects), feature-time mean imputation yielded Q2Y = 0.294, AUROC 0.827 and balanced accuracy 0.756. Predictive metrics were calculated from pooled outer held-out predictions. TensorPLS supports predictive assessment, functional enrichment of selected genes and temporal interpretation of model-assigned feature importance.

Title: Uncovering cross-signal interactions in single-cell and spatial omics
Authors: Sasson, J.; Niasoff, B.; Karin, J.; Ezraty, Y.; Nitzan, M.
Abstract: Individual cells simultaneously encode multiple biological signals in their gene expression profiles, including spatial position, circadian phase, and disease state. These signals can be entangled in complex ways, including circadian patterns that vary along disease progression and cell cycle dynamics that shift along developmental trajectories. While methods to disentangle such signals have been recently developed, characterizing the interaction itself between multicellular signals along with its effects on tissue function, localizing cellular subpopulations which exhibit signal interactions, and identifying potential candidate genes which drive such interactions, all remain major challenges. We present CRISP which characterizes signal interactions in single-cell gene expression data based on the correspondence between the multiple, probabilistic signal-specific projections of the data. Across simulations with tunable couplings and four single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets, CRISP recovers diverse biological signal interactions and localizes them to informative cellular subpopulations and groups of associated genes; CRISP distinguishes healthy from fibrotic liver samples and localizes the loss of zonation-position coupling to individual fibrotic hepatocytes, resolves the asymmetric coupling of TGF-{beta} response, EMT, and cell-cycle phase to specific cell subpopulations, and flags transcriptionally delayed hepatocytes in Plasmodium liver infection. Beyond quantifying and localizing signal interactions, CRISP can refine existing labels, uncover continuous cellular transitions and reveal condition-associated genes.

Title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
Authors: Li, A. W.; Qiu, W.; Arian, C.; Young, J. E.; Lee, S.-I.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

Title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
Authors: Zhang, J.; Cheng, X.; Wang, J.; Chen, W.; Chen, H.
Abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. Existing segmentation methods focus on delineating cell boundaries, yet transcripts that diffuse beyond their cell of origin, fall where cells overlap, or lie in bins that cells only partially cover are still misassigned. Here we present Tracel, a two-stage optimal transport framework that assigns spatial observations to cells under the guidance of a matched single-cell RNA-sequencing reference. Tracel first aligns reference cells to spatial cells to estimate the expected expression profile at each cell location, and then maps transcripts to cells against these profiles. The same formulation assigns transcripts from imaging-based platforms (e.g., Xenium, CosMx) and bin counts from sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Visium HD). Across five human datasets spanning three platforms and three tissues, Tracel improves the separation of cell types over existing methods, assigning cell-type markers to their correct cells, retaining more cell-intrinsic transcripts and reducing contamination from neighboring cells. Tracel also preserves variation within cell types, yielding more accurate differential expression across spatial locations, and its expression profiles attribute ligand-receptor interactions to the correct cell-type pairs in cell-cell communication analysis. Tracel can enter the segmentation workflow at different stages, either refining an existing segmentation or segmenting cells starting from nucleus segmentation.

Title: Long read sequencing reveals changes in measured isoform structure and abundance due to RNA processing
Authors: Aharon, R.; Oshlack, A.
Abstract: Oxford Nanopore Technology enables direct RNA sequencing without reverse transcription (RT) and cDNA sequencing without PCR amplification, allowing investigation of how RNA preparation protocols bias sequencing data. PCR amplification is known to introduce biases related to expression levels, transcript lengths, and GC content. However, biases introduced by RT have been described more recently and their quantification remains more elusive. Using seven cell line datasets from SG-NEx, we compared nanopore sequencing of direct RNA, direct cDNA, and PCR-amplified cDNA. We identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and isoforms between protocols, indicating significant changes in observed expression. Differentially expressed isoforms displayed expected amplification biases, and further we observed decreased PCR counts associated with higher m6A methylation levels on native RNA. We also found differential transcript usage in hundreds of genes across cell lines, showing substantial changes in measured isoform proportions between protocols. Analysis of structural differences between isoforms that switch dominance revealed that while some events involve simple RNA fragmentation, most involve complex structural differences including novel junctions (e.g. exon skipping, intron retention). Compared to non-DTU genes, inserted introns (exitrons) were significantly more common after RT and amplification. Furthermore, visualisation of raw coverage data proved crucial for qualitative validation of experimental findings.

Title: STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY ALLOWS DOUBLECORTIN AND DRUG-STABILIZED MICROTUBULES TO ACCOMMODATE EACH OTHER
Authors: Ramaswamy, V.; Manka, S. W.; Sharma, D. D.; Akhmanova, A.; Rai, A.; Moores, C.
Abstract: Microtubule architecture and dynamics are modulated by small molecules, but how these compounds alter lattice properties and interactions with cellular regulators remains incompletely understood. We used the neuronal microtubule-associated protein doublecortin (DCX), previously reported to preferentially recognize 13-protofilament microtubules, to probe lattices stabilized by different taxanes, including the fluorescent taxane Fchitax-3. We show that DCX binds 15-protofilament Fchitax-3-stabilized microtubules, demonstrating that DCX is not a specific marker of 13-protofilament architecture. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed that the fluorescent moiety of Fchitax-3 inserts into inter-protofilament lateral contacts, explaining its effects on microtubule architecture and dynamics. DCX binds Fchitax-3 microtubules through its N-terminal DC domain, which accommodates the narrower inter-protofilament binding site in the 15-protofilament lattice. Remarkably, although Fchitax-3 induces the longitudinal lattice expansion characteristic of taxanes, DCX remodels its binding site towards its preferred compacted configuration. Thus, taxanes can modify microtubule structure in distinct ways while preserving lattice plasticity and the capacity to undergo conformational remodelling by microtubule-associated proteins. This contrasts with the comparatively rigid lattice of GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules. Consequently, interpretations of microtubule lattice states based on comparisons between taxane- and GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules may conflate structural differences with different degrees of lattice plasticity. Our findings establish the microtubule lattice as a malleable structural substrate whose drug-induced conformations can be further remodelled by cellular binding partners.

Title: Photographic age gap is associated with frailty and predicts survival in laboratory mice
Authors: Perez, K.; Molina, C.; Tagliafico, L.; Ruiqi, F.; Pabis, K.; Sarill, M.; Bigossi, G.; Marcozzi, S.; Monajemi, A.; Alimonti, A.; d'Adda di Fagagna, F.; Bulavin, D.; Malavolta, M.
Abstract: Ageing studies in mice need biomarkers that are cheap, non-invasive and repeatable. We asked how much of a mouse's age can be read from an ordinary photograph, and whether the part that cannot be explained by age carries biological information. We assembled 2,846 photographs of 1,292 mice (four strains, 1 to 34 months old) from seven facilities and predicted age with a frozen self-supervised vision model (DINOv2) and a ridge regression, always tested on facilities the model had never seen. Absolute age transferred poorly between facilities (median absolute error 138 days), because each facility's photographs carried an offset. Relative age transferred well: among mice photographed in the same session, the older mouse was predicted older in 65% of pairs, rising above 95% for age differences over 500 days, and the later photograph of the same mouse was predicted older in 63% of repeat pairs. Sex, in comparison, was inferred more reliably (87%). Mice predicted older than their age were frailer (+0.12 SD per 100 days) and had shorter survival (hazard ratio 1.14 per 100 days), and fourth generation (G4) telomerase-deficient mice looked 151 days older than their wild-type controls. Routine photographs therefore carry a real biological age signal that can be read at no extra cost, best used to compare mice photographed together.

Title: Intestinal molecular siphoning by engineered bacterial spores for non-systemic treatment of nicotine addiction
Authors: Xiong, X.; Zhu, R.; Han, Y.; Yu, M.; Xiang, X.; Shao, Y.; Chen, Y.
Abstract: Eradicating toxic small molecules from the body typically requires the administrations of therapeutic agents for systemic circulation and tissue distribution, resulting in inevitable adverse events from off-target effects. Here, we propose a intestinal molecular siphoning approach for treating diseases caused by toxic substances, in which enzymatic degradation of a toxic substance in the intestinal lumen serves as a driving force for the diffusion of the toxic substance from blood to gut, and continuous elimination of the toxic substance in the gut could effectively ease substance dependence. Using nicotine as a model substance, a live bacterial system was constructed by displaying a trypsin-resistant nicotine oxidase on the surface of Bacillus subtilis spores, and encapsulating in enteric-coated microspheres for gastric protection and targeted intestinal release. After oral treatments with the live bacterial system in mice, peak concentrations of nicotine in blood and brain were remarkably reduced compared to controls. Moreover, the live bacterial system could effectively attenuate nicotine addiction by suppressing dopamine reward surges to reverse withdrawal hyperalgesia, preventing the upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and alleviating anxiety-like behaviors. These findings show the potential of intestinal molecular siphoning as a target-independent therapeutic strategy for lowering circulating toxic substances through non-systemic enzyme reprogramming.

Title: High-fat diet promotes exhaustion-associated T-cell remodeling across vascular and lymphoid tissues in atherosclerosis-prone mice
Authors: Yarahmadi, P.; Xie, Y.; Huynh, D. T. N.; Lai, J.; Ling, Q.; Huang, X.; Nguyen, P. K.
Abstract: Background: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by lipid accumulation and immune dysregulation. How chronic dietary lipid exposure reshapes T-cell states across vascular and lymphoid tissues, and whether these changes resolve after dietary normalization, remains incompletely defined. This study examined diet-associated T-cell remodeling and the contribution of macrophage-mediated stimulation. Methods: ApoE-deficient mice received a vegetarian diet (VD) or high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 or 24 weeks; a dietary reversal group received HFD for 12 weeks followed by VD for 12 weeks. CD45-positive cells from aorta, blood, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow underwent single-cell RNA sequencing with matched T-cell receptor sequencing. T cell states were annotated using canonical markers, and exhaustion- and naive-associated programs were quantified using UCell scores. Analysis assessed T-cell composition, clonal expansion, and predicted macrophage-T cell communication, with splenic flow-cytometric validation. Results: HFD was associated with enrichment of exhaustion-associated states, with the highest exhaustion scores in the aorta. At 24 weeks, the pooled exhausted-cell proportion was 15.7% under HFD versus 10.6% under VD. Dietary reversal restored this proportion to 10.6%, while residual transcriptional changes persisted in a tissue-dependent manner. Flow cytometry corroborated increased inhibitory receptor expression and co-expression. Aortic macrophages exhibited inflammatory and antigen-presentation programs alongside increased predicted communication with T cells. Aortic T-cell activation and clonal expansion accompanied these changes, and clonotype size correlated with exhaustion score (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.57, p = 0.029). Conclusion: Chronic HFD is associated with multicompartment T-cell remodeling, with prominent vascular exhaustion-associated programs and tissue-dependent recovery after dietary normalization. These findings suggest that dietary lipid exposure may leave a durable adaptive immune imprint across organs during atherosclerosis.

Title: A fibroblast-CD8+ T cell circuit drives a Type 1 shift in allergic inflammatory memory
Authors: Kwong, A. C.; Oliver, I.; Yang, L.; Lotfy, P.; Ordovas-Montanes, J.
Abstract: Inflammatory memory in barrier tissues often manifests as exaggerated recall responses to previously encountered stimuli. While recall is generally thought to reinforce the Type of inflammation (e.g., Type 1 (T1), Type 2 (T2), or Type 17 (T17)) induced in the primary encounter, whether and how memory responses engage programs beyond the initiating Type is unclear. Here, we adapted well-characterized murine models of T2 atopic dermatitis (AD)-like and T17 psoriasis-like inflammation into repeated challenge paradigms to compare how inflammatory memory is stored and recalled through longitudinal single-cell RNA-sequencing. In T17 inflammation, a network of IL-17-producing {gamma}{delta}T cells, IL-17-responsive keratinocytes and myeloid cells established in primary challenge re-emerged in recall with increased abundance and accelerated kinetics. By contrast, allergic T2 memory drove a particularly exacerbated and durable recall response in which hallmark features of T1 immunity, including interferon (IFN) signaling and cytotoxic lymphocyte recruitment, were unexpectedly layered onto amplified T2 responses. This T2-to-T1 shift was initiated by CD8+ tissue-resident memory T (Trm) cells that expanded with repeated challenge, produced IFN{gamma}, TNF- and IL-13, and closely resembled treatment-refractory Trm cells in AD. Tissue rewiring was supported by Trm-derived T1 cytokines and the IL-4-rich T2 milieu whose synergy on fibroblasts amplified allergic recall via IL-15 and CCL19. By tuning fibroblast IFN responsiveness in vivo, we mechanistically dissect how this fibroblast-CD8+ T cell circuit supports cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses. In human AD, both arms of allergic recall amplification by this two-cell circuit featuring T1 and T2 effector responses were conserved. Our findings reveal how a stromal-immune circuit drives a clinically relevant T1 immune axis to support allergic inflammatory memory.

Title: Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov. sp. nov., a new gut genus isolated from the stool of a healthy donor
Authors: Semmar, R.; Beye, M.; Orain, N.; Robinne, S.; Alibar, S.; Bakour, S.; Lagier, J.-C.; Dubourg, G.; Tidjani Alou, M.; Valles, C.
Abstract: Strain Marseille-QA0792 (=CSUR QA0792, CECT 31199) was isolated from the feces of a healthy person using the culturomics method. The fecal sample originated from leftover material collected for a fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) procedure, obtained during a routine screening in accordance with the guidelines of the French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM). This strain is Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped, non-motile, and non-spore-forming. It is strictly anaerobic, with optimal growth at 37{degrees}C. Strain Marseille-QA0792 presented its highest 16S rRNA identity, 96.2%, with ''Merdibacter massiliensis'' strain Marseille-P3254 (not validly published) (accession number LT598590) and ANI similarity of 75.0% with the same species. Among validly published species, strain Marseille-QA0792 showed its highest 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (91.5%) with Faecalicoccus acidiformans strain 37-2a (accession number HQ452864), whereas all computed average nucleotide identity (ANI) values were below 75%. Genome sequencing revealed a genome size of 2.67 Mb and a G+C content of 50.01%. This species is classified within the Erysipelotrichaceae family in the Bacillota phylum. Thus, we isolated for the first time a novel genus named Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov., sp. nov., strain Marseille-QA0792. This discovery highlights the importance of continuing culturomics efforts to explore the human microbiome.

Title: Lung Epithelial TLR7 is a Factor in Viral Replication and Pathogenesis
Authors: Granoski, M. J.; McClelland, R. D.; Bilawchuk, L. M.; Hindle, S.; Lopez-Orozco, J.; Kieser, Q.; Jensen, L. D.; Griffiths, C. D.; Elawar, F.; Julien, O. J.; Santer, D. M.; Vinuesa, C. G.; Hobman, T. C.; Jenne, C. N.; Marchant, D. J.
Abstract: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.

Title: The YjfJ protein is the effector of a second PspA/VIPP1 system that is widespread in the Gammaproteobacteria
Authors: Game, D. R.; Livesy, H. C.; Van der Woude, M. W.; Thomas, G. H.
Abstract: Maintaining the integrity of the cytoplasmic membrane is essential for bacterial cell survival. Unsurprisingly, prokaryotes have evolved conserved mechanisms by which they sense, maintain, and repair membrane integrity in response to stress. The phage shock protein (Psp) is one such system, understood primarily through work undertaken in the Gammaproteobacterial species Escherichia coli and Yersinia enterocolitica. The system utilises an effector, PspA, alongside accessory proteins that sense stress and recruit PspA to damaged membranes. Homologues of PspA - part of the PspA/VIPP1 family - are found in a variety of bacterial phyla. Although most work in the Gammaproteobacteria has concerned the canonical Psp response, there have been descriptions of non-canonical PspA/VIPP1-containing systems that warrant further genomic analysis. By analysing the PspA/VIPP1 content of a diverse selection of Gammaproteobacterial genomes, we reveal the existence of two phylogenetically distinct subtypes of PspA/VIPP1 proteins, PspA- and YjfJ-like, which are found at similar frequencies. The YjfJ-like proteins are not only a novel subtype of PspA/VIPP1, having their own unique set of accessory proteins, but in some species, such as the ESKAPE pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, comprise the only PspA/VIPP1-containing system. Our study positions the YjfJ-like containing systems on equal footing with the PspA system in terms of their conservation and distribution in the Gammaproteobacteria. This suggests that studies into the biological functions of YjfJ-like proteins would be well-justified from their unique presence in some important human pathogens.

Title: A genome-resolved atlas reveals lineage-specific activity patterns of prophages in cultured human gut bacteria
Authors: Huang, Y.; Liu, Z.; Li, J.; Hu, J.; Tan, X.; Dai, L.; Ma, Y.
Abstract: Prophages dominate the gut virome, yet their basal activity landscapes remain elusive. Here, we developed ACTIVE (Activity Comparison Test for Induced Viral Elements), a robust coverage-based framework to accurately profile prophage replication activity based on sequencing data of individual bacteria. Applying ACTIVE across 31,150 gut bacterial isolates (875 species), we compiled these data into GPAC (Gut Prophage Activity Catalog) and found that 5.4% of prophages are detectably active under standard culture, with pronounced enrichment in Bacillota. Moreover, we uncovered distinct active viral lineages with broad host distributions. Comparative analyses identified 46 viral families significantly enriched for activity (SA-vFAMs). Notably, SA-vFAM7 represents a hyper-prevalent Candidatus Heliusvirales lineage whose host distribution expands into Bacteroidota (Tannerellaceae). Furthermore, we propose Candidatus Mubacviridae (SA-vFAM1), an active, hankyphage-inclusive transposable phage family associated with Bacteroidales, characterized by conserved MuA/B operons, diversity-generating retroelements, and multi-genus host distribution. Together, these findings establish GPAC as a resource linking prophage activity to host taxonomy and viral evolutionary lineages, providing a foundation for investigating prophage induction, host-phage interactions, and ecological dynamics of the human gut microbiome.

Title: Platelet-endothelial crosstalk drives distinct endothelial dysfunction in bicuspid aortic valve disease
Authors: Weiss, L.; Chelvanambi, S.; Harrison, A.; Kasai, T.; Nakamura, Y.; Turner, M. E.; Blaser, M. C.; Billaud, M.; Aikawa, M.; Singh, S. A.; Aikawa, E.
Abstract: Background: Bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) predispose individuals to premature development of aortic stenosis (AS). The abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV affects both platelets and valvular endothelial cells (VECs), but whether platelet-derived signals contribute to valve morphology-specific endothelial dysfunction remains unknown. Methods: Platelets and VECs were obtained from patients with BAVs or tricuspid aortic valves (TAVs) undergoing valve replacement for AS. Platelets were activated to generate platelet releasate (PR). PR composition and its effects on VECs were investigated using complementary molecular, multi-omic, functional, and computational approaches. Results: BAV and TAV patients exhibited markedly distinct PR profiles, which translated into differential endothelial responses. Strikingly, BAV-derived PR elicited a substantially more pronounced endothelial dysfunction phenotype, characterized by widespread molecular reprogramming and functional alterations. Integrated multi-omics uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction as a central feature of BAV PR-induced endothelial injury, accompanied by activation of pathways spanning endothelial remodeling, migration, and immune-cell recruitment. These molecular signatures translated into mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced VEC migration, and increased neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis. Finally, computational ligand-receptor and ligand-target analyses identified candidate signaling axes linking platelet-derived mediators to endothelial reprogramming, highlighting potential therapeutic targets. Conclusions: We provide the first direct evidence that platelet activation contributes to AS initiation through the induction of endothelial dysfunction and that these effects are amplified in BAV. These findings identify platelet-VEC crosstalk as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking abnormal valve hemodynamics to disease onset. Targeting platelet-derived mediators may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for AS, specifically in BAV.

Title: Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces
Authors: Liang, J.; Bradburd, G.; Terhorst, J.
Abstract: The isolation-by-distance (IBD) principle describes the tendency for genetic relatedness to decline with geographic distance. Although the existence IBD has long been documented in natural populations, recent analyses of spatially referenced genotype data have shown that the strength of this relationship can vary across a landscape due to geographic barriers, habitat compatibility, or other factors. Effective migration surfaces (EMS) have emerged as a popular exploratory tool for visualizing spatial patterns in IBD. However, fitting likelihood-based EMS models is often computationally demanding, requiring repeated large-scale matrix calculations. Here, we introduce Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces (dreems), a graph neural network for amortized inference of effective migration surfaces. dreems maps genetic covariance and sampling locations directly to an effective migration surface, while simultaneously providing predictive uncertainty estimates. Once trained, the network accommodates different graph sizes and sampling designs without needing to re-train. Across independent coalescent simulations that were not seen during training, dreems has roughly 10-30% lower estimation error compared to a state-of-the-art likelihood-based method, with the largest gains observed under sparse sampling designs that are commonly encountered in practice. Reanalysis of several published datasets recovers spatial patterns that are broadly consistent with earlier likelihood-based estimates, while reducing computation time by orders of magnitude.

Title: A Bias Correction Method for Substructure Estimation with Small Reference Sample Sizes
Authors: Tifour, S.; Price, A.; Marker, K.; Hendricks, A.
Abstract: Reference data are important for accurate estimation of population substructure, yet sufficiently large reference samples are often unavailable for some populations. This limitation is especially important for methods that estimate population substructure from genetic summary data using reference allele frequencies derived from reference samples, such as Summix2. Here, we systematically evaluated how reference sample size for five continental reference groups [African (AFR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Indigenous American (IAM), and South Asian (SAS)] affects Summix2 substructure estimates in simulated Latino-like, African American-like, and Peruvian-like populations, as well as real African American genetic data. We show that small reference sample sizes introduce systematic bias in substructure proportion estimates. We identified a sample size threshold of 150 individuals per reference group for accurate estimates with a mean estimation error below 0.05. We also developed two bias corrections: a simple inverse sample size correction and a flexible power-law correction. The power-law correction provided the greatest reduction in mean estimation error when all reference groups had small reference sample sizes, whereas the simple inverse sample size correction performed better when a single reference group had a small reference sample size. These findings provide practical guidance and bias adjustments for reliable population substructure estimation from genetic summary data, particularly when reference populations have small sample sizes.

Title: A Distinct Mode of Chromosome-End Genome Instability Revealed by Circulome Characterization and Analyses
Authors: Roy, G.; Lei, Z.; McCoy, M.; Al Sardar, A.; Shay, J.; Scacheri, P.; Lotan, Y.; Levene, S. D.; Fire, A.; Shoura, M.
Abstract: Genome instability is a central hallmark of cancer and it is characterized largely from sequence: mutation, copy-number change and rearrangement scored against a linear reference. The genome has additional degrees of freedom, such as the physical form (topology) of the DNA itself. A specific mode of localized genome dynamics changes both dimensions (sequence and topology) at once: defined chromosomal regions are also represented as extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA). The biogenesis of eccDNA is a feature of many cancers, supplying the tumor with genetic elements that can participate in phenotypic selection, and supplying the observer with a window into the genomic instability landscape. Genome-wide maps of where these circles arise have not been available at scale or at high resolution. Building such maps requires physical selection of circular species, because most sequenced reads from unselected DNA derive from unrearranged sequence, conflating the signal from dynamic rearrangements with that from bulk chromosomal DNA. Here we combine biophysical and biochemical isolation of circular DNA with next-generation sequencing, applying it to a panel of cancer cell lines and to patient tumors, with non-cancerous cells and adjacent normal tissues as controls. The resulting genome-wide maps of the circular-element repertoire, the Circulome, reveal a consistent and previously unreported enrichment of these elements at particular chromosome ends. The circles map to regions extending well past the telomeres, reaching varying distances up to tens of megabases inward. This activity is accompanied by corroborating rearrangements within the linear genome, consistent with regions of chromosomal instability. Together these features define a spatially localized mode of instability in cancer, which we term Erosion at Distal Genomic Ends (EDGE). We formulate a classification problem to discriminate bladder tumor from matched normal tissue, finding that the EDGE signal outperforms the mean of all interior chromosomal regions, for each chromosome. These findings define a distinct spatial signature of cancer chromosome instability detectable through Circulome analysis, and connect early models of region-specific instability to the human cancer genome.

Title: Rapid Electro-optic Two-photon Bessel Light Sheet Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging for Tissue Volume Interrogation
Authors: Kumar, P.; Knight, V. R.; Lysko, D. E.; Kim, J.-G.; Talbot, W. S.; Bowman, A.; Mudgett, M. B.; Wakatsuki, S.; Kasevich, M.
