Abstract: We report a two-photon light sheet electro-optic fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (TPLS-EO-FLIM) technique based on an electro-optic (EO) modulation detection module. Scanning two-photon Bessel light sheet excitation was used to achieve in-depth volumetric imaging. The low cross-section of multiphoton excitation requires high detection efficiency, and electro-optic detection enables fast wide-field FLIM with a scientific complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (sCMOS) detector. Phototoxicity is minimized by utilizing signal from the entire illuminated sample area in a wide field camera exposure, and time-resolved volume acquisitions are feasible in minutes, with cross-sectional field of view and light sheet length over 300 microns. The method has sub-nanosecond lifetime resolution and is capable of accurate FLIM images in 10 ms exposures with as low as a few hundred photons per pixel. The technique was demonstrated through volumetric FLIM of a green fluorescent protein (GFP) labeled zebrafish embryo heart, of multi-fluorescent protein (multi-FP) labeled plant root structures and of dynamic cardiac cycles in live zebrafish embryos. For the latter, we recorded the cardiac cycle dynamics of a zebrafish embryo at 50 frames per second and measured biomechanical parameters such as heart rate, ventricle/atrium areas, atrioventricular valve dynamics, and fractional area change. Taken together, these studies show the capability of the system for rapid, high resolution, and functional imaging in diverse biological contexts.

Title: NORMA 3.0: aesthetic and group-aware visualization and analysis of annotated biological networks
Authors: Baltoumas, F.; Karatzas, E.; Koutrouli, M.; Galaras, A.; Aplakidou, E.; Chasapi, I. N.; Chasapi, M. N.; Lazanas, P.; Lamari, E.; Przulj, N.; Georgakopoulos-Soares, I.; Pavlopoulos, G. A.
Abstract: Summary: Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation: NORMA 3.0 is freely available at https://normaviz.org. The source code is available at https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA.

Title: CloneVI: A deep generative model for deciphering the relationships between cell state and mitochondrial genotype
Authors: Hibi, T.; Kojima, Y.; Hayashi, S.; Hisose, H.; Mizukoshi, C.; Shimamura, T.
Abstract: Cellular diversity arises from both genetic lineages and non-genetic regulation of cell states, and knowing which cell states are tied to lineages is central to understanding how clones shape disease. Single-cell multi-omics technologies measure mitochondrial DNA mutations together with gene expression or chromatin accessibility in the same cells, but clones are usually inferred from mutations alone, making such clones difficult to identify. We developed CloneVI, a deep generative model that infers clonal structure from a latent cell state derived from gene expression or chromatin accessibility. It estimates the clonal probability of each cell from this cell state, together with the allele frequency of each clone by reconstructing the observed mutation counts. In simulated data, CloneVI recovered the ground-truth clonal structure in both single-clone and mixed-clone cell populations. In clonal hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data with enriched mitochondrial transcripts, the inferred clones were associated with specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, and some of them showed high expression of a T-cell receptor variable-region gene. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia mitochondrial single-cell ATAC-seq data, CloneVI separated populations with different heteroplasmy levels and identified increased PAX9 accessibility. In a multi-donor ovarian tumor cohort, CloneVI captured mutant-cell populations enriched in particular cell states, and a differential test weighted by the clonal probability revealed the transcription factor activity of the cell state in which the mutant cells concentrated. CloneVI thus identifies populations defined by mitochondrial DNA mutations and associated with cell states in single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. CloneVI is available at https://github.com/TaichiHIBI/cloneVI.

Title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
Authors: Zhou, X.; Guan, X.; Zhou, Y.; Wang, J.; Peng, Z.; Ren, W.; Wang, W.; Xie, R.; Li, W.
Abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

Title: XRN1 couples RNA granule remodelling to global mRNA decay triggered by the activity of a viral endoribonuclease
Authors: Tweedie, A.; Möller-Levet, C. S.; Towler, B.; Elliott, G.
Abstract: Cytoplasmic mRNA turnover is a fundamental determinant of gene expression, yet the spatial organisation of RNA decay remains unresolved. Although decay factors are enriched in processing (P)-bodies, whether these condensates actively mediate mRNA degradation or serve primarily as storage compartments remains controversial. Here, we exploit the alphaherpesvirus endoribonuclease, virion host shutoff (vhs), to synchronously trigger rapid, global cytoplasmic mRNA accompanied by nuclear relocalisation of the poly(A)-binding protein PABPC1. Expression of vhs caused the dispersal of P-bodies, but when the 5' to 3' exonuclease XRN1 was depleted, PABPC1 remained in the cytoplasm, and P-bodies stayed intact, associating with previously undetected G3BP1-dependent RNA granules. Similarly, catalytically inactive vhs failed to disperse P-bodies but instead induced RNA granules that also contained vhs itself and recruited decay factors in an XRN1-dependent manner. Translational shutoff by this endoribonuclease did not require RNA cleavage, G3BP1 condensation or XRN1 activity supporting a sequential model in which translational arrest precedes endonucleolytic cleavage, promoting transient RNA granules that engage P-bodies and XRN1-dependent machinery for rapid mRNA degradation within the granules, thereby precluding the biogenesis of deleterious RNA condensates.

Title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
Authors: Shao, J.; Chen, M.; Liu, Y.; Sun, J.; Zhang, G.; Yan, Z.-Y.; Lin, H.; Ren, M.; Pei, S.; Peng, J.; Gong, Y.; Wang, S.-W.
Abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.

Title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
Authors: Oeller, M.; Vasconez Grunauer, S.; Sitron, C. S.; Mahul Mellier, A.-L.; Diedrich, L.; Schuele, A.; Ruf, V.; Oliinyk, D.; Kuttler, F.; Dransfeld, U.; Prassler, J.; Ben-Moshe, S.; Rodriguez, E.; Heymann, T.; Ugur, E.; Madden, K.; Sun, Y.; Ulrich, C.; Jasiqi, Y.; Lashuel, H. A.; Hartl, F. U.; Mann, M.
Abstract: -Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson's disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell's proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic. Inclusions took up whole assemblies, with subunits moving together in 421 of 438 complexes, and the V-ATPase alone was enriched in all three systems. Degradation cargo stayed with the receptors that route it, consistent with sequestration and failed degradation acting together. Neuritic and somatic inclusions differed, the former rich in UBQLN2 and the latter in intermediate filaments. In the cell line, phosphorylated -synuclein was tenfold higher in the inclusion than in the rest of the cell, with about one third of the rise already present before an inclusion was visible. Measured against its host, the composition of an inclusion becomes a readout of how it formed and a source of candidate markers and therapeutic targets.

Title: Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning: A Stability-Constrained Framework for Molecularly Enhanced Survival Prediction in Lung Adenocarcinoma
Authors: Shringarpure, P.; Divakar, S.; Khobragade, S.
Abstract: Accurate survival prediction in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains challenging because high-dimensional molecular data can introduce overfitting and unstable feature selection. We developed Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning (CAISL), a framework that integrates a sparse molecular risk correction with a clinical baseline to improve prognostic discrimination while constraining model complexity and prediction variability. CAISL was evaluated using The Cancer Genome Atlas LUAD cohort comprising 470 patients and 119 observed deaths. Performance was compared with clinical Cox, molecular-only, and unanchored multimodal models using five independently seeded, event-stratified five-fold cross-validation runs. CAISL achieved a mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.7246, compared with 0.6970 for clinical Cox, yielding an absolute improvement of 0.0276 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 0.005 to 0.050). Time-dependent discrimination was higher at three years (AUC, 0.742 vs. 0.712) and five years (AUC, 0.721 vs. 0.691), while the integrated Brier score was lower for CAISL than for clinical Cox (0.164 vs. 0.181). Ablation analysis identified clinical anchoring as the component associated with the largest reduction in discrimination when removed. Stability analysis showed a mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 0.46 between selected feature sets and a mean Spearman correlation of 0.86 between molecular correction scores. These findings support the potential of clinically anchored, stability-constrained molecular learning to improve internal survival-risk prediction in LUAD. Independent-cohort validation is needed to establish generalizability.

Title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
Authors: Ota, K.; Chen, T.-H.; Yamaguchi, T.; Otsubo, T.; Murakami, Y.; Masaki, M.; Leproux, P.; Suzuki, R.; Node, K.; Kano, H.
Abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In two participants, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in adjacent stained sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73). Across 15 fields from nine participants, including one of these two, kurtosis values did not overlap between severe-deposition and amyloid-negative tissue. Among the descriptors examined, kurtosis showed the largest standardized participant-level separation. Exploratory multivariate curve resolution yielded a deposit-associated component with aromatic-residue features shared with reagent transthyretin. Second harmonic generation (SHG), acquired simultaneously with CARS, showed a broadly inverse spatial pattern relative to kurtosis, providing complementary architectural contrast. These findings support a label-free approach to detecting cardiac amyloid deposits that combines broadband CARS-derived amide I kurtosis with SHG.

Title: Gene regulatory architecture in antibiotic resistance is optimized for specific dynamic regimens
Authors: Geng, H.; Schultz, D.
Abstract: Cellular responses to antibiotics face a fundamental trade-off: resistance must be deployed quickly enough to prevent the accumulation of drug inside the cell, but expression of resistance genes is costly in the absence of the drug. Therefore, antibiotic responses are typically regulated, controlling not only whether resistance is expressed, but also when, how strongly, and for how long. These regulatory strategies are implemented through the strength and arrangement of promoters and operators. However, it is still not clear how the dynamics of drug exposure select for specific regulatory strategies. Here, we develop a dynamical model of a typical antibiotic response, where a transcriptional repressor senses the drug and regulates expression of a resistance protein, coupled to the effects of the drug on cell growth and gene expression. We define a cost function that weighs the different burdens imposed on the cell over the course of the response, and perform in silico optimization of the regulatory parameters under different selective pressures for three architectures of increasing complexity: constitutive expression of resistance, repression by a constitutively expressed repressor, and repression by a self-regulated repressor. We find that strong drug exposures favor constitutive expression of resistance, high costs of basal expression favor repression by a constitutive repressor, and self-regulation of the repressor is favored only when the response must provide protection while also restraining overexpression of resistance. Stochastic simulations further show that self-regulation of the repressor protects cells against fluctuations in repressor levels, which cause unnecessary induction of resistance before exposure and failed induction after exposure. This framework links the dynamics of the environment to the evolution of gene regulation, providing a basis to predict which regulatory strategies are expected to arise under specific selective pressures.

Title: Identification of T-Cell specific signature miRNAs and target pathways in Psoriasis
Authors: Madaan, P.; Tyagi, N.; Tyagi, S.; Kushwaha, H. R.; Tandon, R.; Sangma, D. A.; Jain, M.
Abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation, involving T cells as the major players in the manifestation of lesional and systemic inflammation. With the extensive exploration of keratinocyte dysfunctionality, T cell centric deregulation has gained much focus with limited molecular understanding in the context of disease etiology. miRNAs, the molecular switches known to drive disease manifestation via altering keratinocyte biology, have not been much studied in the context of T cell alterations. This study aims to explore T cell-associated miRNAs and their target signaling networks to understand their role in modulating psoriasis specific T cell changes. miRNAs with altered expression in psoriatic T cells were identified through a comprehensive analysis of the available literature and datasets. The relevant miRNAs were used for prediction and enrichment of cognate targets and mapping of associated pathways involved in different modalities of T cell functionality. The study identified 14 miRNAs dysregulated in psoriatic T cells along with 256 downstream targets involved in 15 distinct T cell associated signaling pathways. 5/14 miRNAs identified were further validated with a significant increase in their expression in enriched CD3+T cells from blood of psoriatic patients versus healthy subjects. The psoriatic T cell specific miRNA driven signaling cascades identified were modelled to propose yet unexplored molecular basis of dysregulated T cell activation, proliferation, survival, and subset differentiation associated with the disease. The new findings delineate candidate miRNA target signaling components that need to be validated in T cell disease etiology. Importantly, the key miRNAs/targets can be employed towards psoriasis-specific diagnostics and therapeutic interventions.

Title: Clonally Convergent Tph/Tfh-like CD4+ T Cells are Shared Across Recovery and Recurrence in Experimental Periodontitis
Authors: Sharma, A.; Olmedo, V.; Rojas, L.; Suliman, S.; Mohammadi, S.; Lauwens, K.; Nguyen, G.; Cruz-Dwyer, K.; Aguilar Angulo, A.; Khan, Y.; Dang, J.; Bluff, C.; Yakar, N.; Tornaas, S.; Costea, D.-E.; Dongre, H.; Guney, Z.; Oner, F.; Bor, B.; Ali, S.; Hasturk, H.; Hajishengallis, G.; Kirkwood, K. L.; Kantarci, A.; Alvarez Rivas, C.
Abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting structures (periodontium) that requires life-long maintenance to prevent progression. Using a sensitized model of recurrent periodontitis in mice (SeRPD), in which regulatory breakdown was induced by temporary Treg depletion concurrent with disease, we mapped the gingival T cell imprint across each disease phase. Transient regulatory breakdown left a durable mucosal imprint after clinical recovery, characterized by enrichment of local and regional CD4 T cells. Paired single-cell RNA and TCR sequencing of gingival immune cells identified a convergent clonotype expanded from recovery into recurrence that carried a Tfh/Tph-like transcriptional identity. An analogous CD4 T cell population was detected in human periodontitis lesions by single-cell transcriptomics. Together, these findings support a paradigm in which clinical recovery does not ensure a local T cell repertoire reset; instead, a reservoir of antigen-experienced, tissue-adapted CD4 T cells persist in the mucosa and participate in recurrence.

Title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
Authors: Gallichotte, E. N.; King, D. C.; Marsico, B.; Fitzmeyer, E. A.; Ogg, H. A.; Kimball, K. X.; Ebel, N.; Campbell, C. L.; Ebel, G. D.
Abstract: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection. Thus, temperature impacts bottlenecks in the Culex-WNV system independent of known antiviral pathways, possibly by altering virus replication dynamics. While temperature had a dramatic impact on bottleneck stringency, this is likely independent of antiviral pathways and instead some other change to mosquito biology. Together, these results shed light on the relationships between temperature, virus evolutionary dynamics and antiviral immunity.

Title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
Authors: Hernandez Viera, A. J.; Gross, N. R.; Tran, P. Q.; Shahin, O.; Kosmopoulos, J. C.; Anantharaman, K.; Mo, C. Y.
Abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro, type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo, suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.

Title: Phage lysates are reservoirs of biologically active quorum sensing signals
Authors: Eichler, A. H.; Mauritzen, J. J.; Koonce, K. C.; Kaur, G.; Hoyland-Kroghsbo, N. M.
Abstract: Bacteriophage lysates are widely used to study phage-bacterial interactions and are typically applied after filtration without further purification. As a result, host-derived metabolites produced during phage propagation are transferred alongside phage particles, yet the biological consequences of this carryover remain largely unexplored. Here, we show that the Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum sensing signal PQS persists in a bioactive state in phage lysates for at least one year. In contrast, the quorum sensing molecules 3OC12-HSL and C4-HSL are rapidly degraded. We demonstrate that PQS stability is caused by its association with outer membrane vesicles, which protect the signal from degradation. PQS from phage lysates induces production of the virulence factor pyocyanin and increases mortality in a Galleria mellonella model of P. aeruginosa infection. Importantly, PQS carryover does not explain previous reports of phage mediated activation of the PQS system, as this response also occurs in PQS free phage lysates, establishing phage lysate-mediated signal transfer and phage-induced signaling as distinct mechanisms. Because hydrophobic signaling molecules are associated with outer membrane vesicles in diverse Gram-negative bacteria, including Vibrio harveyi (CAI-1) and Paracoccus (C16-HSL), our findings suggest that phage lysates may serve as reservoirs and overlooked vectors of host-derived communication signals in a broad range of phage-host systems. Our results reveal a previously overlooked layer of phage-host interactions in which biologically active bacterial signals persist beyond phage lysate preparation and influence recipient-cell behavior independently of phage infection.

Title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
Authors: Kottom, T.; McLean, J. L.; Limper, A. H.
Abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2{Delta} complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, {beta}-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced {beta}-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2{Delta} mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with {beta}-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function. Given the importance of {beta}-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target.

Title: Optimal compositions of potent sliced-siRNA with DNA bases substitution and insights of Ago2 slicing actions
Authors: Sun, G.; Lizhar, E. M.; Shi, Y.; Riggs, A. D.
Abstract: We have previously characterized the nucleotide compositions of single-stranded ago2-sliced small interfering RNAs (sliced-siRNA, sliRNA), a novel type of potent RNAi trigger designed based on the biogenesis mechanism of miRNA-451. sliRNAs have on par antisense mediated silencing activity but about 1000-fold reduced passenger strand activity compared to siRNA. In the current study, to further characterize sliRNAs to facilitate their in vivo application, we have investigated the effects of substituting RNA nucleotides (nts) in sliRNA with DNA nts (sliDRNAs), which will allow us to study the potential effects on their processing, maturation, and silencing activity from individual or multiple nts at different positions. Our results showed sliDRNAs have distinguished composition from siRNA with DNA nts (siDRNA), indicated that, in addition to their different biogenesis mechanisms, these two types of RNAi triggers may also have adopted additional different silencing mechanisms. Our results also revealed some mechanism related to how Ago2 executes its slicer activity and the effects on sliRNA potency by trimming and tailing during sliRNA maturation. These results have paved the way for using other chemically modified nts in sliRNAs that may enhance their in vivo stability and transportability to facilitate their in vivo applications.

Title: Insulin stimulation induces dynamic interaction between 14-3-3 and the C-terminal tail domain of Kinesin-2 subunit KIF3B in vitro
Authors: Kumari, D.; Tangri, A.; Girotra, M.; Ray, K.
Abstract: Heterotrimeric kinesin[ndash]2 mediates diverse intracellular transport processes, yet the mechanisms governing its cargo specificity and regulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we report the regulation of interaction between the kinesin[ndash]2 subunit KIF3B and a candidate adaptor protein, 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon];. Using splitAPEX2 proximity labelling and fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) assays in HEK293T cells, we demonstrate that 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon]; interacts with KIF3B within discrete subcellular compartments. This interaction is significantly enhanced upon insulin stimulation, indicating regulation by signalling pathways. Time resolved FLIM analysis further reveals that the site of interaction is dynamic, suggesting spatial and temporal control of motora[ndash]daptor association. Finally, the interactions are mapped to two serine residues in the C[ndash]terminal tail region of KIF3B that are highly conserved across species. Together, these findings uncover a conditional and reversible interaction between KIF3B and 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon], providing insight into how kinesin[ndash]2 may achieve context specific cargo engagement and transport within cells.

Title: N-terminal cysteine independent effects of oxidative stress on the stability of RGS4 and 5
Authors: Kim, H.; Shang, N.; Tian, Y.-M.; Ratcliffe, P.; Keeley, T. P.
Abstract: Oxidative post-translational modifications on the sulfhydryl group of cysteines can occur spontaneously or enzymatically. The enzymatic dioxygenation of N-terminal cysteines has emerged as a new oxygen sensing paradigm, catalysed by 2-aminoethanethiol dioxygenase (ADO) in mammals. Conflicting evidence has been reported in recent years on whether this reaction can occur spontaneously in the absence of ADO. Here we sought to address whether cellular oxidative stress can interfere with ADO-catalysed N-terminal cysteine dioxygenation. Using a system to produce titratable intracellular levels of H2O2, we demonstrate that the stability of RGS4 and 5 is not affected by physiological levels of oxidative stress, whether ADO is present or not. However, cytotoxic levels of oxidative stress induced by tert-butyl hydroperoxide did induce a substantial increase in RGS4/5 protein stability that occurred independently of the Cys N-degron pathway. This effect of tBHP was abolished by Fe2+ chelation, lysosomal pH perturbation, and lipid peroxide scavenging. We conclude that N-terminal cysteine dependent proteolysis of RGS4/5 is not sensitive to physiological oxidative stress, but these proteins can be stabilised during the process of oxidative stress-induced cell death through an N-terminal cysteine independent mechanism.

Title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling
Authors: Nguyen, T. C.; King, H. D.; Amgalan, D.; Pushkarev, O.; Mo, Y. A.; Munger, C. J.; McCreery, C.; Gupta, R.; Zeng, T.; Zhou, R.; Conley, S. D.; Batta, S. P. R.; Sheth, M. U.; Mattei, E.; Masaltseva, A.; Kang, H. Y.; Ma, X. R.; Tran, N.; Gaskell, L.; Shoresh, N.; Orlova, V.; Kundaje, A.; Sumanas, S.; Ang, L. T.; Loh, K. M.; Engreitz, J. M.
Abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2, the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro. Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro. Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.

Title: WheatPanRef: a unified linear pan-reference genome for wheat genomics
Authors: Niu, J.; Zhao, P.; Du, W.; Zhang, X.; He, H.; Appels, R.; Zhao, J.; Ma, S.; Chen, T.; Haberer, G.; Spannagl, M.; Cao, Z.; Zhang, Y.; Miao, L.; Chen, S.; Zhang, B.; Wu, W.; Wang, L.; Li, G.; Wu, J.; Wang, Z.; Chen, Y.; Jiao, C.; Zhang, X.; Pozniak, C. J.; Krattinger, S. G.; Choulet, F.; Ling, H.; Jia, J.; Wang, D.; Yan, W.; Hu, Z.; Xin, M.; Peng, H.; Ni, Z.; Grewal, S.; Alaux, M.; Varshney, R. K.; Guo, W.; Deng, X. W.; Sun, Q.
Abstract: Linear reference genomes provide coordinates for read mapping, variant discovery and multi-omics data integration, yet assembly-specific coordinate systems limit data reuse, particularly in the large, repetitive and polyploid wheat genome. Here, we present WheatPanRef, a scalable linear pan-reference and coordinate framework that integrates wheat sequence diversity within a stable coordinate system. We reconciled independent Chinese Spring assemblies by resolving structural and sequences discrepancies to constructed a 14.50-Gb consensus sequences CS-NP. Using CS-NP as backbone, we incorporated 4.37 Gb of non-redundant non-CS sequences from 37 diverse wheat accessions, generating WheatPanRef (18.87 Gb). WheatPanRef improves read-alignment performance and captures putative wild-relative introgressions and sequences absent or unanchored in conventional references. Bidirectional coordinate-translation system enables accurate projection between WheatPanRef and individual assemblies without remapping, facilitating genomic resource integration and reuse. WheatPanRef provides a common sequence and coordinate foundation for population-scale wheat genomics, with potential utility for genomic resource integration in other complex crops.

Title: A Binuclear  Cluster Supports Functional Asymmetry in Dark-Operative Protochlorophyllide Reductase
Authors: Zhao, K.; Kashyap, R.; Abernathy, M. J.; Antony, E.; Sarangi, R.
Abstract: Many photosynthetic bacteria rely on the nitrogenase-like dark-operative protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase (DPOR) to sustain (bacterio)chlorophyll synthesis in the dark. DPOR couples ATP hydrolysis to electron transfer from a reducing component (L-protein) to a catalytic component (NB-protein) that reduces protochlorophyllide. NB-protein is an 2{beta}2 heterotetramer, and each heterodimeric half contains an active site and a [Fe4S4] cluster. Although the two halves are identical, they react sequentially rather than in parallel. How the two halves communicate has remained unknown. Here we show, using Cu K-edge x-ray absorption spectroscopy and cryo-EM, that the NB-protein tetramer interface holds a binuclear, sulfur-bridged [Cu2S2] cluster. Each Cu is reduced and three-coordinate, with short Cu-S and Cu-Cu distances (2.26 and 2.62 &Aring). Mutagenesis excludes the nearest cysteine as the bridging ligand, supporting inorganic sulfide as the most likely sulfur donor. To our knowledge, this is the first sulfide-bridged dicopper cluster identified in a protein. The cluster is conserved in three purple non-sulfur bacteria and connects the BchB C-terminal helices that contact opposing active sites. Loss of Cu abolishes DPOR activity and asymmetric L-protein binding without disturbing overall fold. We propose that the cluster relays substrate-binding information between active sites, suggesting a metal-mediated mechanism for cooperativity in nitrogenase-like enzymes.

Title: Unlocking Targeted Underwater Delivery of Coral Probiotics
Authors: Facchinelli, M. P.; Contardi, M.; Caldwell, J.; Fiorentini, F.; Ghizzi, I.; Calabretta, V.; Ceseracciu, L.; Pomili, T.; Isa, V.; Corigliano, G.; Rinaldi, C.; Scribano, V.; Bellini, E.; Ravelli, L.; Lavorano, S.; Gandolfi, I.; Galli, P.; Montano, S.; Athanassiou, A.
Abstract: The rapid global decline of coral reefs has intensified the need for innovative conservation strategies, including microbial therapies to enhance coral health and resilience. A major limitation, however, is the lack of effective delivery systems for administering Beneficial Microorganisms for Corals (BMCs). In this study, we present natural, biodegradable systems for the underwater delivery of probiotic bacteria to corals. Three customized alginate-based delivery formats (beads, hydrogels, and filaments) were developed and loaded with the probiotic Pseudoalteromonas peptidolytica. The materials were loaded with the bacterium at an average concentration of 10^(4) CFU/g of dry polymer and engineered to sink underwater while keeping their structural integrity over time. In vitro assays showed controlled release kinetics, with encapsulated probiotics remaining viable and capable of replication. In vivo experiments compared syringe-based inoculation with the application of alginate beads, hydrogels, and filaments to corals. Microbiome analyses performed before and after inoculation confirmed successful probiotic colonization following deployment of the alginate-based delivery systems. Relative abundance of the probiotic genus Pseudoalteromonas increased markedly in treated corals, reaching 11.5 % after 48 h with alginate beads, 12.7 % after 48 h with hydrogels, and 12.6 % after 24 h with filaments. Furthermore, the degradation mechanisms of the three delivery systems were investigated. As the first biomaterial-based underwater delivery systems specifically engineered for coral probiotics, these alginate-based materials provide a promising foundation for advancing microbial therapies in both controlled aquaria and natural reef environments.

Title: MorphoProt: RNA-Conditioned Integration of Multiscale Histology for Spatial Protein Inference
Authors: Xu, L.; Zheng, L.; Zhan, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Zhang, K.
Abstract: Spatially resolved protein abundance reveals cellular states and tissue organization that RNA expression cannot fully capture, yet direct spatial protein profiling remains costly and limited in coverage. Histology images routinely accompany spatial transcriptomics and offer complementary morphological information for protein inference. Here, we introduce MorphoProt, a multimodal framework that jointly predicts spatial protein abundance from RNA expression, multiscale histology and tissue neighborhoods. MorphoProt uses RNA-guided cross-attention over five histological fields of view, so that the morphological context read for each spot is conditioned on its molecular state. The fused representation is refined by gated aggregation of RNA-derived information from physical and transcriptomic neighborhoods before joint protein prediction. On held-out sections of human tonsil, mouse spleen and human liver, MorphoProt achieves mean proteinwise Spearman correlations of 0.652, 0.604 and 0.372, outperforming matched RNA-only and graph-based baselines and the histology-based HIPI and multimodal SPRINT baselines in all three tissues. Combining fields of view, rather than any single one, carries the histology gain: in spleen and liver, the multiscale model outperforms every single-field model, and its learned scale preference separates white-pulp from red-pulp compartments. Predicted proteins preserve protein-defined tissue domains and their marker identity, and recover pathologist-annotated germinal centers as accurately as measured proteins.

Title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
Authors: Wang, Y.; Zhang, F.; Peng, G.; Qiu, L.; Zeng, L.; Liu, Y.; Kinchagawat, J.; Yang, X.; Liu, C.; Johnson, C.; Su, Q.; Wang, C.; Shen, X.
Abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.

Title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
Authors: Baril, T. J.; Feurtey, A.; Croll, D.
Abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda. The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

Title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
Authors: Liu, Y.; Zheng, S.
Abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

Title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
Authors: Wang, P.; Ahsan, M. U.; Chen, T.; Wang, K.
Abstract: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.

Title: TIGRdisco: a tool for the discovery of TIGR arrays and TIGR-associated Tas proteins from nucleotide sequences
Authors: Gu, S.; Gong, Z.; Mortimer, J.
Abstract: Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR)-TIGR-associated protein (Tas) systems mediate DNA targeting through a hypercompact Tas effector, guided by dual spacers within a tigRNA that is processed from TIGR arrays. TIGR-Tas loci are composed of a Tas coding sequence associated with TIGR arrays of short units in either dual-repeat or stem-loop architecture. Unlike CRISPR (Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) arrays that comprise units of direct repeats interspersed with unique spacers, units within the two distinct TIGR architectures only conform through extremely short box motifs, complicating detection. Here, we present TIGRdisco, an integrated tool capable of discovering both the Tas protein and its associated TIGR arrays directly from unannotated nucleotide sequences. TIGRdisco implements independent engines to detect the two array architectures through a motif-agnostic approach. We benchmarked TIGRdisco against a reference dataset of TIGR-Tas loci, recovering more than 80% of array units within its search window. Furthermore, TIGRdisco recovered arrays for loci within entire clades of Tas where associated arrays were unannotated in the reference. We found that these arrays largely contain non-canonical box motifs or unit lengths. Lastly, as a case study, we utilized TIGRdisco and successfully uncovered TIGR-Tas loci across metagenomic and genomic datasets.

Title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
Authors: Yan, D.; Duan, S.; He, H.; Sheng, J.; Zhang, Y.; Li, Y.; Du, S.; Tang, S.; Fu, Y.; Yang, X.
Abstract: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.

Title: T cell transcriptomes in simulated microgravity in vivo
Authors: Kuznetsov, N.
Abstract: Spaceflight exposes astronauts to a combination of stressors, among which microgravity remains the least well characterized at the level of human immune cell function. We examined the in vivo effect of long-term simulated microgravity (SMG) on T cell transcriptomes in ten healthy male volunteers who completed a three-week dry immersion protocol without countermeasures. Peripheral blood was collected at five time points covering a pre-immersion baseline (day -7), three intra-exposure time points (days 7, 14 and 21) and a recovery time point one week after the end of exposure (day 28). CD3+ T cells were isolated and analysed by RNA-seq, with differential expression assessed per volunteer and KEGG pathway enrichment used to identify the most affected gene networks. SMG was associated with transcript-level changes in genes mapping to key molecular pathways, including those involved in cell proliferation, cell-cycle regulation, maintenance of genome integrity, and oncogenic and tumour-suppressor networks. Hub genes shared across the most significant pathways were differentially expressed in the majority of volunteers. A notable finding was pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity: samples clustered primarily by volunteer identity, yet a coordinated temporal shift during exposure and a partial return toward baseline by day 28 were detectable across donors, and these changes occurred in the absence of detectable systemic inflammation. These results indicate that SMG is associated with altered T cell transcriptional programs in vivo and that the response is sufficiently variable between individuals to favor personalized rather than uniform countermeasure strategies.

Title: Genome evolution and glycosyltransferase diversification shape asperosaponin biosynthesis in Dipsacus asperoides
Authors: Yang, R.; Fu, C.; Zhao, X.; Zhao, Y.; Huang, W.; Li, M.; Xiang, G.; Xiong, J.; Wang, Y.; Chen, G.; Liu, Q.; Yang, S.; Zhang, G.; He, S.; Liang, Y.
Abstract: Deciphering the genomic and enzymatic features associated with high-abundance specialized metabolism is important for understanding and engineering bioactive natural product biosynthesis. Asperosaponin , a hederagenin-based saponin, accumulates at exceptionally high levels in Dipsacus asperoides roots and is by far the predominant triterpenoid saponin. Here, by integrating a chromosome-level genome assembly with comparative genomics, transcriptomics, metabolite profiling, and biochemical characterization, we reconstructed a major biosynthetic route to asperosaponin and identified diversification of triterpenoid-associated gene families. Functional analyses revealed an ordered glycosylation sequence in which DaUGT73GZ2 preferentially accepts C-3-glycosylated substrates retaining a free C-28 carboxyl group, thereby establishing a C-3-before-C-28 glycosylation order during asperosaponin biosynthesis. Phylogenetic and biochemical analyses further uncovered functional differentiation among UGT85CA enzymes involved in C-3 arabinosylation, while genomic and expression analyses revealed lineage-specific patterns of pathway gene duplication and transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify genomic, enzymatic, and transcriptional features associated with the distinctive, high-abundance triterpenoid saponin profile of D. asperoides roots and provide a framework for understanding and engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis.

Title: Salinity adaptation in date palm (Phoenix dactylifera): evidence for selective sweeps at Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) genes
Authors: Muchina, P.; Younuskunju, S.; Ahmed, A. A.; Mohamoud, Y. A.; Malek, J. A.
Abstract: The date palm is a high salinity tolerant fruit tree grown mainly in the region spanning from North Africa to parts of South Asia. Climate change models of this region indicate the possibility of increasing salinity in the future. The Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway is crucial for salinity tolerance in plants, serving as a primary defense mechanism by facilitating sodium exclusion. To better understand date palms' salt tolerance, we analyzed variation in SOS pathway genes in a set of 197 date palm genomes collected from across the range of cultivation. Here, we show evidence for selective sweeps in multiple SOS pathway genes. A single major pdSOS1 haplotype is at very high frequency in Eastern and Western subpopulations, with a minor, likely ancestral haplotype still present in both geographical locations. Allele-specific gene expression analysis showed differences in salt-treated roots between swept and ancestral haplotypes. Interestingly, sequence-based analysis of the pdSOS1 haplotype suggested a second, much earlier introgression event between P. theophrasti and date palm, though direction is unclear. This event happened before both the selective sweep and the previously reported recent introgression to date palm. We identified a MITE transposable element inserted into a pdSOS1 intron on the swept haplotype, and a similar insertion was found in an intron of the SOS2 paralog pdCIPK8. Both insertions are unique to date palm among Phoenix species. The pdCIPK8 haplotype containing the MITE is also at high frequency in both populations. Further analysis showed evidence for a selective sweep spanning the pdSOS3 region in the western population that shares similarity to an Eastern haplotype spanning the promoter region only. Slower extended haplotype homozygosity decay surrounding the genes in the western population suggests that the swept haplotype originated in the East and spread to the West in all cases. Altogether, our data provide evidence of selective sweeps in the date palm SOS pathway and may go to explaining how this species has developed such high salinity tolerance.

Title: TRPP Ion Channels Function in the π-Conformation Rather Than the α-Conformation
Authors: Zhang, C.; Kopec, W.; Michel, J.
Abstract: PKD2 (TRPP1) is a TRPP ion channel whose dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Understanding its conformational states and gating mechanism is important for elucidating its function and for structure-based drug discovery. Cryo-EM structures of WT-PKD2 contain a local {pi}-helical turn in the S6 pore-lining helix ({pi}-conformation). In contrast, a fully -helical S6 (-conformation) was observed in the gain-of-function mutant F604P-PKD2 and interpreted as the open state, leading to the proposed {pi}-to- activation mechanism. However, whether the -conformation can support function has never been directly established. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the functional properties of the -and {pi}-conformations of PKD2. The -conformation remains dewetted unless the lower gate is widened beyond the conformational range observed in mammalian TRP channels. By contrast, the {pi}-conformation supports pore hydration and ion conduction following a small opening of the L677 gate, with simulated conductance comparable to experimental measurements. The closely related PKD2L1 (TRPP2) channel shows a similar dependence on conformation, with a hydrated {pi}-conformation and a dewetted -conformation. Together, these findings challenge the assignment of the -conformation as the conductive state and support a model in which the {pi}-conformation represents the functionally relevant state of TRPP channels. This model suggests that activation may involve an -to-{pi} transition rather than the previously proposed {pi}-to- transition, providing a new framework for understanding TRPP channel gating. This work sheds light on the molecular basis of polycystin channel dysfunction and could facilitate the development of PKD2-targeted therapeutic strategies for ADPKD.

Title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
Authors: Freidlin, P. J.; Rubinstein, M.; Fass, E.; Kutikov, I.; Zizelski Valenci, G.; Losev, Y.; Dveyrin, Z.; Rorman, E.; Nissan, I.
Abstract: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of the tuberculosis burden of a country, while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports.

Title: Genome-wide chromatin accessibility during early embryogenesis in a generalist cichlid fish
Authors: Midhukrishna,  ; Smith, A. M.; Joyce, D.; Di-Palma, F.; Haerty, W.; Mehta, T. K.
Abstract: Background Lake Malawi's haplochromine cichlids are one of the most rapid and species-rich vertebrate adaptive radiations known, generating hundreds of species within < 1 million years, yet how regulatory regions shape their embryonic development remains poorly understood. Astatotilapia calliptera, a generalist riverine lineage and proxy for the ancestral stock that seeded this radiation, offers a developmental chromatin baseline against which regulatory divergence in specialised lineages can be compared. Results We generated genome-wide ATAC-seq profiles of A. calliptera embryos across three developmental stages (3, 7 and 12 days post-fertilisation, dpf), identifying 550,876-701,889 accessible chromatin peaks per stage. Accessible chromatin was enriched at gene promoters and at both highly conserved and accelerated conserved noncoding elements at every stage. The functional repertoire of accessible-promoter genes shifted across development, from early patterning at 3 dpf to the broadest regulatory repertoire at 7 dpf, and an increasingly neural- and locomotory-behaviour-enriched repertoire by 12 dpf, coinciding with post-hatching motor maturation. Differential accessibility showed that chromatin opening, rather than closing, dominates the earliest transitions (3 vs 7 and 3 vs 12 dpf), driven mostly by general metabolic genes, whereas the smaller, later 7 vs 12 dpf transition combined targeted gains at tissue-remodelling and apoptosis genes with losses at genes governing early neural and retinal patterning; almost all of these losses (96%) were at promoters that had opened between 3 and 7 dpf, indicating transient rather than sustained opening. Transcription factor (TF) footprinting identified stage-specific regulatory activity among developmentally important TFs, while the broader TF-promoter network remained topologically stable across all three stages, built around conserved hub regulators of core neural and sensory patterning genes e.g., SOX2, FOXG1, PTF1A, SOX10. This suggests that wiring is established early and largely maintained, following the hourglass model, with developmental progression driven by changes in activity of this conserved programme. Conclusions Together, these findings establish the first embryonic epigenomic resource for A. calliptera, revealing a developmental chromatin landscape of broad early opening and progressive functional specialisation, and providing a comparative framework for understanding how regulatory evolution has shaped Lake Malawi cichlid diversification.

Title: Prokaryotic homologs of the major vault protein form engineerable vault nanocapsules
Authors: Athukoralage, J. S.; Yoon, P. H.; Shanehsazzadeh, A.; Kauderer-Abrams, E.; Perry, N.; Durrant, M. G.
Abstract: Vaults are the largest ribonucleoprotein particles in eukaryotic cells, built from 78 copies of the major vault protein (MVP), yet their function remains unknown four decades after their discovery. MVP homologs occur in prokaryotes and bacteriophages, but whether they form vaults is unknown. Here, we show that prokaryotic and bacteriophage MVP homologs assemble into vault particles. We surveyed approximately 15 billion proteins, found MVP homologs in 29 bacterial and 4 archaeal phyla, and used size-exclusion chromatography to rapidly screen and isolate vault particles of eight homologs expressed in Escherichia coli. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of the phage homolog L05 at high resolution reveal a shell of 96 MVP chains enclosing a volume ~25% larger than human vaults, among the largest protein shells of defined size outside virus capsids. Prokaryotic MVPs typically carry seven wall repeats and eukaryotic MVPs nine, and adding wall repeats to L05 yields larger vaults. Prokaryotic vaults expand the known diversity of vault architecture and offer a tractable system for studying vault assembly and a size-tunable scaffold for cargo encapsulation.

Title: Classifying tumors from broad category to hierarchical molecular subtype: an interpretable hierarchical framework for precision oncology
Authors: Song, Q.; Liu, F.; Lai, X.
Abstract: Precise tumor subtype classification is important for guiding personalized treatment, characterizing tumor heterogeneity, and investigating molecular mechanisms. However, most existing multi-label classification models use flat architectures and do not fully exploit the inherent hierarchical relationships and biological constraints among tumor types, which limits their performance and interpretability in complex, fine-grained pan-cancer classification. Here, we present the cancer Hallmark-based Hierarchical Recursive Model (HHRM) for pan-cancer hierarchical multi-label classification. HHRM integrates hierarchical label structures with recursive neural networks, enabling simultaneous modeling of multi-level dependencies from broad cancer categories to specific subtypes. We trained the model on a comprehensive pan-cancer cohort of 11,476 samples spanning 26 primary cancer types and 405 subtypes across up to eight hierarchical levels. HHRM achieved an accuracy of 0.7924 for predicting hierarchical tumor subtypes and was further evaluated on a validation dataset of 887 samples. Compared with other hierarchical modeling frameworks, HHRM achieved higher accuracy in all three output modes. Ablation experiments showed that replacing the hallmark-based graph convolutional network reduced model performance. On an independent dataset of 1,608 breast cancer samples, HHRM also achieved an accuracy greater than 0.86. Finally, we combined SHAP with a network-based method to rank and analyze predictive genes at different levels of the tumor hierarchy, which identified both known and potentially novel biomarkers for cancer diagnosis. In conclusion, to our knowledge, HHRM is the first hierarchical model for multi-level tumor subtype classification. Its competitive performance, combined with post hoc biological interpretation, suggests potential value for precision cancer diagnosis.

Title: Provenance-aware handling of identical dengue genome records alters inferred envelope-protein variation in Bangladesh DENV-3
Authors: Begum, K. T.; Rafea, K. A. G.
Abstract: The reliability of interpreting dengue virus (DENV) envelope (E) protein variations depends on whether identical public sequence records are kept as representatives or eliminated based on provenance reviews. We evaluated three record-handling strategies using a frozen Bangladesh-associated dataset of 426 E sequences: exact-sequence deduplication, a prespecified provenance-sensitive exclusion method, and an independently curated Nextstrain accession list. Within the 2021 DENV3 subset (96 accessions), 18 records dated August 2021 were identical across 10,707 nucleotides to the older Sri Lankan genome AY099336.1. There were 21 variable E positions within the original 96-accession DENV3 cohort. Whole-cohort deduplication (47 retained) and retaining one representative of the 18-record group (79 retained) preserved all 21 positions. Excluding the group (78 retained) resulted in eight variable positions: 13 of 21 (61.9%) were lost due to differences in state at those positions between the excluded group and retained cohort. Nextstrain reference-specific exclusions selected the same 18 records; applying its full saved list produced 77 accessions and the same eight variable positions. E270 and E383, which had pre-2021 antibody-related evidence, did not meet the sequence-variation criteria for follow-up; however, E223 and E224 remained variable. Antibody-position enrichment was not statistically significant. These results indicate that cohort eligibility decisions may impact dengue E-protein variant prioritization despite representative-retaining deduplication. Genome identity does not indicate specimen identity or an antigenic phenotype.

Title: SPECHTacle: An Efficient Detection and Visualization of Cell Specific Regulation in Single Cell-Based Experiments Using a Novel Combinatorial Computational Tool
Authors: Specht, K. M.; Schwierling, H. C.; Robson, M. J.
Abstract: Herein, we describe SPECHTacle, a novel computational tool affording the ability to efficiently visualize and delineate the specific cellular population(s) impacted by an experimental paradigm utilizing heterogeneous cell-based samples. SPECHTacle can be employed to efficiently determine, in a cell specific manner, the populations preferentially impacted by treatments, drugs, injuries, disease states, and/or development within datasets continuously being generated across nearly countless subfields in molecular biology. SPECHTacle accomplishes this task by harnessing the power of Waddington optimal transport analysis and Shannon entropy in a combinatorial fashion to distinguish cell populations preferentially altered due to nearly any experimental paradigm and generates a visual representation of cellular entropy (i.e. change) across entire datasets. Ultimately, this allows for efficient determination of specific populations preferentially impacted by an experimental paradigm and identifies populations to target for downstream analyses employing quantitative measurements. We propose that SPECHTacle represents an immediately useful computational tool with the potential to be integrated into single cell-based workflows and greatly enhance the efficiency of both manual and machine-based learning workflows.

Title: Dated public evidence and known genes for retrospective evaluation of gene prioritization
Authors: Huang, C.-H.; Wang, Y.
Abstract: Retrospective evaluation of gene prioritization needs evidence that was public before the evaluated genes became known. Public resources are open and reproducible, but are distributed as current releases that also contain evidence produced after the genes became known. This Data Descriptor presents per-gene evidence tables for four areas (oncology, inflammatory bowel disease, metabolism and psoriasis) from public resources. Every feature carries a time axis, the date of its release in a calendar of 183 archived releases of 20 sources, and a leakage axis, a provenance class (A to E) with two risk grades that define five feature sets. Nineteen lists of known genes are dated by the first trial, study, release or classification that supports each gene. They cover targets of a kind of drug, targets of drugs tested in a disease, and genes associated with a disease. The oncology lists also carry the first day the trial registry showed the trial.

Title: A three-factor model can explain symmetry breaking and the n-1 rule during X-chromosome inactivation
Authors: Guan, K.; Liu, J. M.; Calabrese, J. M.; Elston, T. C.
Abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is a mammalian gene regulatory process that via chromosome-scale transcriptional silencing, leaves active a single X chromosome per diploid genome complement. The mechanisms that enable cells to select the appropriate number of X chromosomes to inactivate while leaving others active remain unclear. We demonstrate that all known chromosomal counting scenarios during XCI can be accounted for by a three-factor mathematical model that includes (1) Xist, the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) responsible for gene silencing during XCI in eutherians, (2) an X-linked transcriptional activator of Xist, and (3) the autosomally-encoded SPEN, an Xist RNA-binding protein that is essential for gene silencing during XCI. In our model, symmetry between active X chromosomes is broken by stochastic differences in the number of Xist molecules that associate with the X chromosomes at the onset of XCI. Subsequently, integrated positive and negative feedback loops amplify then propagate superstoichiometric assemblies of SPEN complexed with Xist on the inactive chromosome(s), and select for levels of X-linked activator that enable only one X chromosome per diploid genome complement to remain active. Thus, asymmetric propagation of the SPEN-Xist ribonucleoprotein complex may play an essential role in symmetry breaking and chromosomal counting during XCI, independently of or in concert with cis-acting networks of DNA regulatory elements. Our results also have conceptual implications for gene regulatory circuits on autosomes.

Title: γδ T cell-derived IL-17A aggravates experimental epidermolysis bullosa acquisita in response to IL-1β
Authors: Deng, F.; Jukic, S.; Wannick, M.; Holscher, A.; Prinz, I.; Ludwig, R. J.; Schmidt, E.; Yu, X.; Petersen, F.; Holscher, C.
Abstract: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is a mucocutaneous autoimmune blistering disorder mediated by autoantibodies against type VII collagen and subsequent splitting of the dermal-epidermal junction. Interleukin (IL)-17A promotes the production of chemokines and cytokines involved in neutrophil recruitment and activation, suggesting that IL-17A may contribute to EBA pathogenesis. We aimed to clarify the role of IL-17A in experimental EBA. Using an antibody transfer-induced EBA mouse model, we demonstrate that IL-17A promotes disease development, as pharmacological blockade of IL-17A with a neutralizing antibody ameliorated skin lesions. Gamma-delta ({gamma}{delta}) T cells were identified as the predominant cellular source of IL-17A, supported by the attenuated disease phenotype observed in {gamma}{delta}TCR-deficient mice. In addition, CD4+ T cells and neutrophils contributed to IL-17A production in experimental EBA. Mechanistically, IL-1-beta, rather than IL-23, was identified as a critical mediator of IL-17A production by {gamma}{delta} T cells in vitro, consistent with our in vivo findings. Whereas EBA severity was not reduced in IL-23p19-deficient mice, disease was markedly attenuated in IL-1R-deficient animals. Together, our study provides the first evidence that {gamma}{delta} T cell-derived IL-17A plays a pivotal role in experimental EBA and identifies a previously unrecognized IL-1{beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell/IL-17A axis that expands current understanding of EBA immunopathogenesis.

Title: A noncanonical function of Dicer fuels self-dsRNA-driven inflammation
Authors: ter Haar, L. R.; de Lange, S.; Gravekamp, D.; Kooij, A. R.; de Wolf, J. W.; Asschert, Y.; Oosenbrug, T.; Paul, M. W.; van Veelen, P. A.; van Roon-Mom, W. M. C.; Mei, H.; Van der Veen, A. G.
Abstract: Self-derived double-stranded RNA (self-dsRNA) acts as potent triggers of autoinflammation and damage-associated molecular patterns in cancer and infection. However, the upstream processes controlling self-dsRNA homeostasis remain unclear. We uncover a non-canonical role for human Dicer in driving cell-intrinsic immunity to self-dsRNAs that arise from editing or splicing defects, epigenetic deregulation or mitochondrial stress. Dicer loss abolishes type-I interferon induction, PKR activation, and OAS-RNase L activation in response to self - but not exogenous - dsRNA in multiple cell types, including a clinically-relevant hiPSC model of neuroinflammation. Dicer interacts with G3BP1 and LGP2 to regulate self-dsRNA availability and recognition, respectively, independently of miRNAs. As immunostimulatory self-dsRNAs fail to accumulate and activate dsRNA sensors in absence of Dicer, these findings position Dicer as a central regulator of self-dsRNA sensing.

Title: Cell-scale confinement reorders bacterial speed rankings
Authors: Shimada, Y. Y.; Uemura, N. A.; Yoshioka, A.; Nakane, D.; Kan, T.
Abstract: Which bacterium swims fastest depends on where the race is run. Speeds are usually measured in open liquid, yet many bacteria live in pores, mucus and host passages no wider than a cell. Using a microfluidic device with eight channel widths (0.80-3.00 m) in one field of view, we tracked unlabeled cells of eight species spanning five motility systems. Chamber height, a polymer additive and channel width each reordered the ranking. Vibrio alginolyticus, the fastest in open liquid, slowed to ~4 m/s in 1.25-m channels, whereas Campylobacter jejuni and Bacillus subtilis kept 33-46 m/s. Open liquid speed did not predict robustness to confinement. In two unrelated lineages, host symbionts that pass through narrow passages during colonization, Caballeronia insecticola and Vibrio fischeri, outran their non-symbiotic relatives in the channels, and crossed them with flagella wrapped around the cell body at nearly the speed of unwrapped cells. Where space is tight, the ability to keep moving, not top speed, sets the ranking.
