Title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Authors: Du, Y.; Lin, A.; Brown, J. A. R.; Howe, L.; Xao, W.
Abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

Title: ER stress-associated IRE1α signalling links impaired QPRT-dependent NAD⁺ biosynthesis to reduced oocyte competence
Authors: Athar, M.; E, A. K.; Birajdar, P.; M, R.; Kumar, A.; Kumari, A.; Sabnam, S.; Verma, A.; L, P.; Nial, P. S.; G, T. S.; Prasada Rao, H.
Abstract: Oocyte quality is closely linked to metabolic and organelle homeostasis, but the mechanisms underlying naturally occurring differences in oocyte quality remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a link between endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired NAD biosynthesis and poor oocyte quality. Poor-grade goat oocytes exhibited profound NAD depletion, accompanied by quinolinic acid accumulation and reduced expression of quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT), suggesting a bottleneck in de novo NAD biosynthesis. Restoring QPRT expression or bypassing this metabolic step improved meiotic maturation. Further analyses revealed altered ER stress signalling, increased IRE1-associated activity and reduced QPRT RNA stability. Recombinant IRE1 processed QPRT RNA in vitro, suggesting a possible link between IRE1 activity and QPRT transcript regulation. Supplementation with nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) restored NAD levels and improved several features of poor-quality oocytes, including calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial membrane potential. NMN treatment also improved early embryonic development, with its beneficial effects involving SIRT6 activity and changes in DNA methylation-associated fluorescence. Importantly, NMN supplementation improved meiotic maturation in poor-grade bovine and porcine oocytes, indicating that this metabolic intervention may have broader relevance across mammals. Analysis of published human oocyte proteomic data further revealed age-associated changes in ER proteostasis and NAD-related proteins. Together, our findings identify ER stress-associated disruption of QPRT-dependent NAD biosynthesis as a potential contributor to poor oocyte quality and suggest that restoring NAD metabolism may offer a strategy to improve the functional properties of compromised oocytes.

Title: A Dynamic Stem Cell State Links Environmental Cues to Skeletal and Regenerative Fates
Authors: Wang, Y.; Zhao, L.; Chen, K.; Xiang, J.; Hunt, E. J.; Sokol, J.; Ding, K.; Steininger, H. M.; Martinez, N. R.; Weldon, K. C.; Chan, E.; Morales, D. A.; Martinez, C.; Wang, S.; Marquez-Arreguin, G.; Chen, H.; Hoover, M. Y.; Lu, W.-J.; Xiao, J.; Guo, F.; Longaker, M. T.; Weissman, I. L.; Chan, C. K. F.; Ambrosi, T. H.
Abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.

Title: Proteome-wide profiling reveals compartment-specific RNA buffering of protein aggregation during stress
Authors: Seidler, J. F.; Thelen, F.; Wäber, N. B.; Weber, J.; Lohle, L.; Timm, T.; Lochnit, G.; Blom, J.; Goesmann, A.; Strässer, K.; Kilchert, C.
Abstract: Cellular adaptation to stress requires extensive remodeling of RNA metabolism. The rewiring of the RNA-protein interaction landscape and the assembly of biomolecular condensates are central to this response, yet the global stress-induced reorganization of macromolecular RNA-protein assemblies remains incompletely characterized. Here, we apply R-DeeP, a density gradient approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry, to profile the RNA-dependent sedimentation behaviour of the Saccha-romyces cerevisiae proteome during heat and salt stress. We demonstrate that stress triggers a profound, stress-specific reorganization of the RNA interactome. Many proteins undergo pronounced, selective shifts into high-molecular weight fractions, indicative of aggregation. RNase treatment markedly exacerbates this aggregation, consistent with the model that RNA acts as a general chaperone that keeps proteins with intrinsically disordered regions soluble. Strikingly, our data demonstrate that this protection is compartmentalised. Nuclear proteins are partially shielded from stress-induced aggregation. This protection coincides with the nuclear accumulation of RNA caused by a block of RNA export during stress, and RNase treatment abolishes this protection. Nuclear RNA retention may therefore act as a buffer that actively increases the local chaperoning capacity of the nucleus. In contrast, cytoplasmic proteins, including translation factors and ribonucleoprotein granule components, exhibit increased aggregation under stress. Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that increased biochemical aggregation in density gradients reflects changes in assembly state in vivo. For many stress-induced aggregators, these changes are visible as spatial reorganisation in stressed cells, such as the formation of foci. Our findings suggest that cells use subcellular RNA distribution to tune the condensation and/or aggregation threshold of proteins in a compartment-specific manner.

Title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
Authors: Ortigas-Vasquez, A.; Guarracino, A.
Abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. In response, we developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Analyses reveal centromere-length differences between related lineages, extend observations of short non-centromeric arrays across a lineage, and show unequal component variability and composition changes with heterochromatin length within lineages. Yruler brings satellite variation into population-scale phenotype studies.

Title: Epigenome-informed Polymer Modeling Reveals Chromosome Folding Landscapes across Distinct Genetic and Epigenetic Contexts
Authors: Bazmi, S.; Turco, A.; Kumar, S.
Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is critical for gene regulation, enabling long-range interactions between genes and distal regulatory elements. Genomic structural variations and epigenetic differences can perturb this organization, contributing to phenotypic variation and tissue-specific gene regulation. Prior studies have assessed the impact of these genetic and epigenetic changes on 3D genome folding, primarily using population-averaged features such as topologically associating domains and loops. However, growing evidence from single-cell and live-imaging studies indicates that chromosomes are highly dynamic and exist as heterogeneous ensembles of conformations. Here, we applied an epigenetic-state-informed polymer modeling framework to generate chromosomal conformational ensembles directly from cell- and tissue-specific epigenomic data. The resulting ensembles reproduced experimental Hi-C maps across cell lines and tissue types. Comparison of these conformational ensembles revealed that, although polymer dynamics were conserved across cell lines, their folding landscapes diverged. These differences arose primarily from cell-line-specific chromatin-state interaction networks and were concentrated in rare, long-lived contacts. Furthermore, modeling a TAD-boundary-disrupting deletion without re-optimizing the model parameters indicated a shift in the chromatin conformational ensemble from predominantly insulated to predominantly fused states. The modeled deletion also selectively strengthened active chromatin contacts and differentially disrupted enhancer contacts involving neighboring genes. Finally, comparison of two tissue types from the same donor revealed epigenetically driven rewiring of chromatin-state interaction networks. These findings establish chromosomal conformational ensembles as a sensitive readout of genome reorganization across distinct genetic and epigenetic contexts.

Title: Sexing carnivores from faecal metagenomes: calibrating Rx for stone marten and red fox
Authors: Vujic, V.; Mayer, C.; Helyes, G.; Maroti-Agots, A.; Maroti, G.; Csabai, I.; Solymosi, N.
Abstract: Knowing the sex of the animal that deposited a scat adds value to non-invasive monitoring, but read-ratio sexing methods were developed for human ancient DNA. We examined their use in shotgun metagenomes of seven stone marten (Martes foina) and red fox (Vulpes vulpes) scats. Human DNA, present in every library, was removed by competitive mapping against the host assembly and the human reference. Applying the Skoglund Ry metric to the marten samples yielded 0 to 25 Y-mapping reads per sample and failed to identify either of the two animals that Rx places firmly in the male range, so we adopted the X-to-autosome ratio Rx of Mittnik et al. instead, reimplemented as an open-source, species-agnostic Python tool. To test whether its human-derived thresholds transfer, we simulated female and male genomes of both species and drew 200 replicate subsamples at each of fourteen depths from 1,000 to 100,000 mapped reads. Nine of 11,200 replicates were assigned to the wrong sex, all of them below 2,000 mapped reads; above that depth the only failure was non-assignment, in under 5% of replicates above 7,500 reads and under 1% above 15,000. Applied to the scats, Rx identified four females and two males; one sample with 596 host-assigned reads was left unassigned. With competitive removal of human reads, Rx and its original thresholds are usable in these carnivores.

Title: A Minimal Synthetic Cleavage Module Enables Selective Degradation of Pathogenic r(CUG) Repeats in Cells
Authors: Shan, J.; Kovachka, S.; Sung, K.; Disney, M. D.
Abstract: Although direct RNA degradation offers an alternative to occupancy-driven activity, it has relied on complex natural product-derived cleavage modules such as bleomycin. Here, we show that a compact synthetic Fe(II)-coordinating warhead can be programmed for selective RNA degradation in cells. Coupling this cleavage module to a small molecule that recognizes expanded r(CUG) repeats that cause myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) afforded selective degradation of the pathogenic RNA while sparing wild type and transcripts harboring short r(CUG) repeats. In DM1 patient-derived myoblasts, degradation of mutant repeat RNA reduced DM1-associated pathology including formation of nuclear foci, sequestration of MBNL1, and alternative pre-mRNA splicing defects, without inducing DNA damage. These studies establish that minimal synthetic cleavage modules can replace complex natural product warheads to enable selective degradation of disease-causing RNAs in cells.

Title: The structures of two intermediates en route to DNA repair within a (6-4) photolyase
Authors: Yang, C.; Yu, Q.; Cao, X.; Falke, S.; Nan, J.; Beale, E. V.; Chapman, H. N.; Zhong, D.; Lane, T. J.
Abstract: Pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts (6-4PPs) are mutagenic DNA lesions produced when UV light crosslinks two adjacent pyrimidine bases. These lesions must be repaired to maintain genome integrity, a function executed by the (6-4) photolyase enzymes. This repair chemistry is complex, involving the transfer of a hydroxyl group from one base to another, accompanied or followed by cleavage of an interbase bond. It remains unclear how the enzyme orchestrates this reaction. Typically, models invoke a stepwise process in which an oxetane intermediate is transiently populated, but despite over thirty years of investigation, such an intermediate has never been definitively observed. Conducting dose-controlled X-ray crystallography on the (6-4) photolyase from Vibrio cholerae, we observed the transformation of 6-4PP into an oxetane species. Furthermore, we identified a previously unanticipated hemi-cleaved intermediate. The progressive transformation of 6-4PP into oxetane, hemi-cleaved, and fully repaired species requires a reexamination of the existing models of DNA repair by (6-4) photolyases.

Title: RNA-targeted aminopyridine compounds provide a new antifungal strategy
Authors: Hwang, J.; Sisto, L. J.; Shi, T.; Van Zandt, M. C.; Pyle, A. M.
Abstract: While RNA is an emerging therapeutic target class, progress is limited by a shortage of well-defined targets in which ligand binding is coupled to measurable function. The group I intron, a self-splicing ribozyme essential in fungal mitochondria but absent from humans, offers both a tractable platform for exploring first principles of small molecule-RNA targeting and a selective antifungal target. We recalibrated an intron-splicing assay to approximate cellular conditions and performed an extensive, cryo-EM-guided structure-activity relationship campaign against the Candida albicans mtLSU intron. Ligands containing a flexible diamine outperformed conformationally constrained analogues, suggesting a general principle for engaging dynamic RNA surfaces and yielding lead aminopyridine 56 (IC 21.6 nM). Compound 56 synergizes with amphotericin B against C. albicans, suggesting a path for combination therapies. RT-qPCR confirmed direct target engagement in cells. This work establishes the fungal group I intron as a viable, mechanistically distinct antifungal target and a model platform for RNA-targeted discovery.

Title: Active site electrostatic effects modulate DBO inhibitor potency against OXA-48 variants
Authors: Wang, D.; Chahal, R.; Hirvonen, V. H. A.; Spencer, J.; van der Kamp, M. W.
Abstract: The OXA-48 class D {beta}-lactamase and its variants are clinically concerning through their carbapenemase and cephalosporinase activity. Effective inhibitors are therefore urgently needed. Diazabicyclooctanes (DBOs) are newly introduced non {beta}-lactam based inhibitors, but their potency is affected by mutations, with the more recently developed nacubactam consistently less potent than avibactam, the first DBO, towards OXA-48 variants. This difference is most pronounced for OXA-48 compared to its variants OXA-163 and -405, which contain mutations in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop and preferentially hydrolyse cephalosporins over carbapenems. Here we use multiscale simulations to uncover the origin of these differences after determining that the second step of DBO acylation is rate-limiting. Using QM/MM MD simulations we show that nacubactam exhibits a consistently higher energy barrier than avibactam for covalent inhibition of OXA-48-like enzymes, a difference attributable to DBO-specific changes in the active site electric field. Simulations of non-covalent complexes further indicate that weaker binding, due to electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nacubactam tail and Arg214 in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop, partially explains the lower potency of nacubactam towards OXA-48, compared to OXA-163 and -405. Combining computational predictions of covalent reaction rates and non-covalent binding affinities accurately reproduces the relative order of experimental IC50 values, and predicts potency towards OXA-517, a recently discovered OXA-48 variant capable of hydrolysing many antibiotics. This work provides mechanistic insight into the inhibition of class D {beta}-lactamases and reveals the origins of differential DBO potency towards OXA-48 variants, highlighting how subtle differences between enzymes modulate inhibitory effects.

Title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya virus
Authors: Park, Y.-J.; Song, J.; Gen, R.; Stewart, C.; Lee, S.; Veesler, D.
Abstract: Langya virus (LayV) was recently discovered in infected individuals with febrile illness and classified as a Parahenipavirus, a group of poorly understood pathogens. LayV is distantly related to Nipah henipavirus which causes recurring outbreaks with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. No vaccines or therapeutics are approved for use in humans for any parahenipavirus or henipavirus despite their broad geographic distribution and pandemic potential. Here, we discovered that human endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is an entry receptor for LayV and that the tetrameric LayV attachment glycoprotein (G) binds EPCR avidly. We reveal the molecular basis of LayV G recognition of the EPCR receptor and provide a blueprint of the determinants of receptor ortholog usage. We found that human and shrew EPCR orthologs promote cell entry of LayV and of the closely related Mojiang pseudoviruses. These results along with the detection of several Parahenipaviruses in shrews set these pathogens apart from Henipaviruses, which use Pteropid fruit bats as reservoir hosts. Our data support future surveillance efforts, by enabling prediction of EPCR utilization among newly discovered Parahenipaviruses, and the development and evaluation of countermeasures targeting this emerging group of human pathogens.

Title: Material context and TGF-β blockade timing determine retained matrix in patient-derived bioprinted keratoconus stroma
Authors: Jiang, H.; Zhou, C.; Gao, F.; Pang, Y.; Li, Y.; Jie, Y.; Yang, H.; Jiang, Y.
Abstract: Stromal repair requires newly formed matrix to persist while the contractile response to TGF-{beta} is controlled. We developed patient-derived bioprinted gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) stroma to connect material-dependent cell responses with matrix retention after timed receptor blockade. In constructs from six keratoconus (KC) and six normal donors, KC cells retained disease-associated transcription while secreting procollagen I and lumican at normal-donor levels per unit DNA. Comparisons with two-dimensional culture and matched cast GelMA showed that the three-dimensional environment increased matrix induction and lowered resting contractile expression. Printing added a stromal identity response that persisted as retained lumican. Delayed blockade after a TGF-{beta}1 pulse preserved matrix transcription and late secretion. Eleven days after withdrawal, this finite course left more native collagen and lower contractile-gene expression than vehicle in 9/12 donors. Across the tested blockade regimens, at least one regimen achieved both outcomes at the final endpoint in 11/12 donors, including every KC donor. Culture format changed the preferred regimen. Choosing finite blockade by retained collagen instead of secretion changed the schedule in half the donors; the selected arms contained 22.2% more collagen. Retained collagen and contractile expression therefore provide joint endpoints for designing when TGF-{beta}-pathway courses, including losartan and TGF-{beta}3 treatment for keratoconic and scarred corneas, should start and stop.

Title: MitoDecode: quantitative phenotypic decoding of mitochondrial stress states from fluorescence images
Authors: Jia, Y.; Ward, E.; Kaminski, C. F.
Abstract: The quantitative measurement of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence images of cells remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. Here, we present MitoDecode, a deep learning network that automatically assesses type and severity of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence microscopy images. MitoDecode eliminates the need for mitochondrial segmentation, is parameter-free, and operates across both diffraction-limited and super-resolution optical imaging modalities. It assigns a phenotypic probability profile for each individual cell, indicating both type and severity of phenotypic stress. The readout thus enables comparisons between different stressors and provides clues for underlying mechanisms. Furthermore, the method captures phenotypic shifts continuously across treatment doses, revealing subtle variations that would otherwise be missed. We demonstrate MitoDecode's adaptability across diverse cell types, imaging modalities, and stress conditions, and show that it can reliably detect mitochondrial phenotypes, even when stressors target non-mitochondrial pathways. We validate the reliability of the model with biochemical assays, showcase its utility for phenotypic stress profiling of drug treatments, and envisage its application for early-stage disease detection, drug discovery, and mechanistic lead generation.

Title: Extensional Flow Microfluidics Reveal Size-Dependent Core-Shell Mechanical Heterogeneity in Pancreatic Tumor Spheroids
Authors: Ghanbarpour Mamaghani, S.; Costa, T. M.; Wagner, E. C.; Kargar, S.; Celli, J. P.; Dahl, J. B.
Abstract: Understanding the mechanical behavior of cancer cell aggregates is important for investigating metastatic potential and developing effective therapeutics. Tumor cell clusters are major contributors to metastasis and can undergo extreme deformation to migrate through capillaries smaller than the cluster size, suggesting complex multicellular mechanics. Despite their clinical significance, the mechanics of multicellular spheroids remain underexplored. In this study, the mechanical behavior of spheroids formed from the pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1 was investigated using a cross-slot microfluidic device. Suspended spheroids from two size ranges were stretched in non-contact extensional flow (small spheroids mostly 40 < D0 < 75 m, large spheroids mostly 90 < D0 < 145 m). Digital image correlation analyses of intra-spheroid strains revealed strong deformation differences for small and large spheroids while analyses based on 2D projected contours of the spheroid shape did not show trends. Smaller spheroids deformed relatively homogeneously and exhibited significant overall stretching. In contrast, larger spheroids displayed heterogeneous deformation characterized by a stiff central core and a deformable outer shell. To investigate the origin of these mechanical differences, cellular morphology and the expression of stiffness-associated proteins, including vimentin and E-cadherin, were assessed from confocal microscopy. Larger spheroids display significantly lower nuclear sphericity than small spheroids, indicating more cellular packing with increasing spheroid size. Additionally, vimentin expression was concentrated in the outer shell of large spheroids, whereas small spheroids exhibit vimentin expression throughout the aggregate. Thus individual cell morphology and cytoskeletal networks seemed to contribute to the core-shell biomechanical behavior of the large spheroids and lack thereof for small spheroids. Taken together, this study suggests that as spheroids grow, they transition from an irregular and disorganized cluster at low cell numbers to a coordinated and hierarchical structure at sufficient cell numbers that corresponds to diameters {gtrsim} 100 m.

Title: Multicellular Perturb-seq Reveals Lineage-Specific Transcriptional Control During Human Cardiac Organoid Development
Authors: Klosa, P.; Cai, K.; Nansubuga, C.; Sun, Y.; Lin, X.; Liu, C.
Abstract: Heart development requires the coordinated differentiation of multiple cell lineages, including cardiomyocytes (CMs) and endothelial cells (ECs). Transcription factors (TFs) orchestrate lineage specification, morphogenesis, and maturation, yet how cardiac and vascular TFs shape multicellular organization and their interactions remain poorly understood. Many TFs exhibit pleiotropic and stage-dependent effects across cardiac lineages, particularly in cardiac progenitor cells, suggesting the presence of shared regulatory networks that synchronize cardiac and vascular programs during development and in response to stress. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) differentiated cardiac organoid provides a physiologically relevant 3D model to study these multicellular interactions, enabling simultaneous differentiation of ECs and CMs within a human genetic context. When combined with CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) based Perturb-seq, this system allows systematic, high-throughput dissection of TF-driven regulatory programs at single-cell resolution. In this study, we investigated how cardiac and vascular TFs coordinate lineage commitment and the cross-lineage signaling in human cardiovascular differentiation.

Title: A multipotent mouse distal airway secretory cell population that contributes to both airway and alveolar regeneration
Authors: Valiya Chembazhi, U.; Li, S.; Ying, Y.; Miller, Z. A.; Shen, C.; Kim, M.; Basu, S.; Zhou, S.; Morley, M. P.; Schaefer, S. E.; Morrisey, E. E.
Abstract: The distal airway is a spatially distinct compartment whose contribution to lung repair remains poorly defined. We have identified an epithelial cell population enriched in the most distal airways of the mouse lung, that is not present in the alveolar epithelium. Using lineage tracing tools based on Cldn10 expression which marks these cells, we show that the Cldn10+ lineage in homeostatic conditions marks distal airway secretory cells in a highly specific manner, with only a small contribution to multi-ciliated cells and no contribution towards the basal stem cell lineage. Remarkably, these Cldn10+ distal secretory cells proliferate and display a high degree of multi-potency across the lung epithelial axis after injury, generating basal cells, multi-ciliated cells, and alveolar epithelium. In severely remodeled regions after injury, we show that Cldn10 lineage-labeled cells migrate from the airways and differentiate into alveolar epithelial cells. These findings establish the Cldn10 lineage that defines a distal airway secretory facultative progenitor with both intrapulmonary airway and alveolar potential, providing a genetic system for studying distal lung repair.

Title: Deep transcriptomic analysis of molecular mediators of complex traits in heterogeneous stock (HS) rats
Authors: Munro, D. B.; Nguyen, K.-M. H.; St. Pierre, C. L.; Bimschleger, H.; Cohen, K. A.; Wang, Y.; Ward, R.; Holl, K.; Chen, D.; Johnson, B. B.; Ang, G.; Mortazavi, M.; Keung, E.; King, C.; Tripi, J. A.; Kuhn, B. N.; Thompson, B. M.; Lionikas, A.; Daniels, D.; Vulpe, C.; Kalivas, P. W.; George, O.; Adams, D. J.; Dietz, D. M.; Flagel, S.; Hitzemann, R.; Gusev, A.; Saba, L. M.; Jablonski, M. M.; Jhou, T. C.; Telese, F.; Meyer, P. J.; Mitchell, S. H.; Solberg Woods, L. C.; Chen, H.; Polesskaya, O.; Mohammadi, P.; Palmer, A. A.
Abstract: Rats are a powerful model organism for genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of physiological and behavioral traits. Heterogeneous Stock (HS) rats, which were created by intercrossing 8 inbred rat strains, are heavily used for this purpose because of their genetic diversity and accumulated recombinations due to over 100 generations of outbreeding, which improves mapping precision. However, functional genomics resources for post-GWAS interpretation of genomic findings have been limited. We processed 3,160 RNA-seq samples, 1,932 of which were previously unpublished, from 13 tissues as part of RatGTEx. We used Pantry to quantify six modalities of transcriptome regulation (expression, isoform ratio, intron excision ratio, alternative transcription start site (TSS), alternative poly(A), and RNA stability) in each sample, which allowed us to identify 144,876 independent quantitative trait loci (QTL) for 22,599 genes. We performed a transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) with 19,796 unique genes across tissues and transcriptional modalities and 308 traits collected from 14 studies using FUSION, which identified 7,473 significant gene-trait associations. This work presents a significant expansion of the RatGTEx resource in terms of samples, modes of transcriptome regulation, and genetic analyses. Our findings provide molecular evidence for the involvement of specific genes in mediating GWAS signals through a range of transcriptome regulatory mechanisms. These gene-to-phenotype relationships can be easily applied to genetic analyses in humans and other species. Further experiments can use this evidence to confirm these molecular mediators and target them for the treatment of behavioral and physiological traits and disorders. To facilitate use of these results, we have updated results on RatGTEx.org and provided a new interactive TWAS web portal (twas.ratgtex.org).

Title: Genomic and Epigenomic Relationships Capture Different Patterns of Genotype-by-Environment Interaction in Grapevine Clones
Authors: Robinson, H.; Schmidt, M.; Callipo, P.; Robles-Zazueta, C. A.; Brunner, S.; Hintzsche, J.; Vafadarshamasbi, U.; Frotscher, J.; Strack, T.; Crisp, P. A.; Piepho, H.-P.; Voss-Fels, K. P.
Abstract: Genotype-by-environment interaction (GEI) challenges selection in clonally propagated perennial crops by reducing the consistency of clone performance across years. In perennial crops, both genetic and epigenetic variation are likely to contribute to complex trait variation among clones. However, the extent to which each molecular source contribute to GEI remains poorly understood. Here, we used UMR-seq, an assay that recovers SNPs and unmethylated-region (UMR; DNA methylation) profiles from a single library, to generate paired genomic and epigenomic profiles for 206 Riesling (Vitis vinifera L.) clones phenotyped for yield and juice quality traits across nine growing seasons. We then partitioned the contribution of each omic layer to clonal variation and GEI, and examined the genomic distribution of their effects. In models without explicit GEI, environmental and residual effects were the largest source of phenotypic variance and the clonal main effect was modest. Genomic relationships accounted for most of the clonal variance in four of five traits, and adding an epigenomic relationship matrix (ERM) to the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) had little effect. In contrast, when GEI effects were modelled using factor-analytic covariance structures, the epigenomic layer captured a substantial proportion of GEI variance and exceeded the genomic contribution in four of five traits. The two omic layers differed not only in the amount of GEI captured, but also in the pattern of clone re-ranking across years. When back-solved effects were aggregated into genomic windows, the largest genomic and epigenomic effects tended to fall in different regions, with overlap no greater than expected by chance. Together, these results show that genomic and epigenomic relationships capture complementary components of year-to-year variation in clone performance, with the epigenomic contribution expressed primarily through GEI. These findings provide a basis for investigating the molecular drivers of GEI and for testing whether genomic and epigenomic information can inform selection for stable clonal performance across variable environments.

Title: Long-read DNA sequencing reveals global hypomethylation and focal hypermethylation in SDHx-deficient pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
Authors: Xu, Z.; Prajapati, H. K.; Coey, C. T.; Eriksson, P. R.; Hartmann, I.; Alkaissi, H.; Pacak, K.; Clark, D. J.
Abstract: Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGL) are highly heritable neuroendocrine tumors of the autonomic ganglia. Genomic DNA in most cancer cells is hypomethylated. However, DNA in PPGLs secondary to mutations in succinate dehydrogenase complex (SDHx) genes is reportedly hypermethylated due to succinate-mediated inhibition of DNA demethylases. We used nanopore long-read sequencing to characterize the methylome of tumor and white blood cell DNA from SDHx and non-SDHx PPGL patients, alongside normal adrenal medulla. We find that both SDHx and non-SDHx PPGLs are globally hypomethylated, particularly at centromeres. In normal adrenal medulla, CpG islands marked by H3K4 methylation are hypomethylated, whereas CpG islands lacking H3K4 methylation are hypermethylated. In SDHx-related PPGL, some H3K4me-marked CpG islands are hypermethylated, but most are not. We propose that DNA methylation in SDHx-related PPGL reflects the global hypomethylation generally observed in tumors, partly offset by succinate-mediated inhibition of TET DNA demethylases. Opposing effects of succinate may alter the balance between DNA methylation (indirect inhibition of the DNMT3A/B DNA methylases via inhibition of H3K4me demethylases) and DNA demethylation (inhibition of TET DNA demethylases) at active CpG islands.

Title: Genomic characterization and evolutionary path of human satellite 1B in primates highlight a dynamic relationship with transposable elements
Authors: Vila-Verde, C.; Daponte, A.; Eleuterio, D.; Chaves, R. S.; Catacchio, C. R.; Louzada Gomes Pereira, S.
Abstract: Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ~2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive comparative genomic, phylogenetic and transcriptional characterization of HSat1B across 10 primate species using Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) and chromosome-scale long-read assemblies, combined with DNA-FISH, RNA-FISH and long-read transcriptomic analyses. We demonstrate that while canonical tandem HSat1B arrays are restricted to Homininae (human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla), the core H1B unit and its structural variants (H1Bsv1 and H1Bsv2) occur across all 10 primate genomes, including strepsirrhines (lemur). This indicates that the H1B sequence predates the assembly of the composite HSat1B monomer by at least 60 million years. H1B variants consistently map within TE-rich genomic contexts, supporting a stepwise, TE-mediated model of satellite diversification and mobilization. Within Homininae, humans exhibit a dramatic lineage-specific expansion driven by Yq12 amplification (~14.2 Mb; 92% of total genomic content), whereas non-human great apes carry smaller, highly polymorphic autosomal and Y-linked arrays. Finally, we show that H1B-containing sequences are transcriptionally active in human and gorilla nuclei via RNA-FISH and characterize heterogeneous H1B/Alu chimeric non-coding transcripts in the human male germline. Collectively, our findings uncover the birth and Homininae-specific expansion of a composite satellite DNA seeded by an ancient primate sequence module and sculpted by transposable elements.

Title: Transcriptome reallocation during infection reshapes synonymous codon demand in Botrytis cinerea
Authors: Dowell, J.; Pradhan, L.; Madrigal, M.
Abstract: While genomic codon usage is fixed within an individual isolate, the synonymous codons represented in its RNA pool can change when transcription shifts among genes. We tested whether this transcript-level phenotype accompanies infection by reanalyzing 39 libraries from three public Botrytis cinerea RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) time series in S. lycopersicum, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Physcomitrium patens. Gene counts were corrected for coding length, combined with fixed gene-specific codon inventories, and analyzed as centered log ratios within synonymous amino-acid families. Sampling time accounted for 95-98% of fungal codon-demand variation in each series. The association persisted after effective-length correction, unique-only competitive mapping, host-homology exclusion, depth equalization, protein-family weighting, and removal of translation-associated genes. Change vectors over the interpolated, time-aligned 16-24-h interval were positively aligned among studies, whereas later trajectories diverged. Matched reassignments of complete expression trajectories showed more full-series organization than expected in S. lycopersicum and Arabidopsis, but not in P. patens. Codon-preference-weighted abundance and expression breadth also changed through infection, although their directions were not universal. Across systems, large non-translation contributors repeatedly carried ATP-synthase/respiratory and extracellular annotations, although their timing and companion functions differed. Infection-associated transcriptional reallocation therefore repeatedly restructures the synonymous composition of the inferred fungal transcript pool. This establishes a dynamic allocation phenotype and a basis for testing consequences for RNA stability and translation during host-pathogen interactions.

Title: Global Data Fitting Enables Kinetic Dissection of Cullin-RING Ligase-Catalyzed Ubiquitylation: From Substrate Priming to Poly-ubiquitin Chain Formation
Authors: Purser, N.; Li, J.; Scott, D.; Schulman, B. A.; Dangerfield, T.; Kleiger, G.
Abstract: The discovery and characterization of the ubiquitin system was founded on classical enzymology approaches that established fundamental principles of protein ubiquitylation. Cullin-RING ligases (CRLs) represent the largest class of human ubiquitin ligases, yet detailed enzymology of these multi-subunit assemblies has lagged behind other systems such as nucleic acid polymerases. Here, we employed pre-steady state kinetics and global data fitting using KinTek Explorer to systematically investigate the kinetic parameters controlling CRL-dependent ubiquitin transfer. Using a well-characterized in vitro reconstituted system exploring CUL2-dependent CRLs, we modeled substrate priming, showing that the system is highly amenable to global fitting of kinetic data. The results show that product dissociation from the CRL is significantly slower than substrate dissociation, explaining previously reported slow steady-state ubiquitylation rates. Extending this framework to poly-ubiquitin chain formation revealed catalytic efficiencies 15-42-fold greater than substrate priming. Comparative analysis of CUL1-dependent and CUL2-dependent systems showed remarkably similar kinetic parameters, including the Km of ubiquitin-carrying enzyme for CRLs, despite differences in substrate receptor and enzyme architecture. We further examined drug-induced neo-substrate ubiquitylation using the pomalidomide-CRBN-SALL4 system, revealing atypical kinetics characterized by rapid ubiquitin transfer paired with an elevated Km, ultimately yielding catalytic efficiencies comparable to natural substrates. The findings establish pre-steady state kinetics and global data fitting as powerful enzymological tools for dissecting CRL-dependent ubiquitylation across different CRL families and substrate contexts, with important implications for understanding both physiological ubiquitylation and therapeutic targeted protein degradation strategies.

Title: Commensal Engineered Living Materials for Sustained Secretome Delivery and Wound Healing
Authors: Lois, C. O.; Grice, E. A.; Kloxin, A. M.; Sullivan, M. O.
Abstract: Using living cells as dynamic biological factories offers immense potential for the continuous, localized production of therapeutic proteins within compromised tissues. This strategy is particularly compelling for treating chronic non-healing wounds, which lack therapeutics that are able to function effectively in the inflammatory microenvironment. Commensal bacteria have been shown to promote healing in these hostile microenvironments, yet applying live microbes directly onto compromised tissue is clinically unfeasible due off-target safety risks and engraftment challenges. Herein, we establish a well-defined commensal Engineered Living Material (cELM) that allows encapsulation, retention, function, and delivery of native beneficial bacteria for localized production and release of a pro-healing secretome over weeks. We specifically encapsulated a pro-healing human wound bacterial isolate, Alcaligenes faecalis, using biocompatible, click-reactive hydrogel building blocks (thiol- or vinyl-sulfone-functionalized multi-arm poly(ethylene glycol)) and systematically varied the density of the polymer network and of the encapsulated bacteria to establish design rules for creating pro-healing cELMs. Physical confinement in the hydrogel network ensured bacterial biocontainment, while the hydrogel mesh size still permitted diffusion of the therapeutic secretome. Notably, controlling encapsulation density revealed an inverse relationship wherein lower cell densities yielded significantly enhanced per-cell metabolic activity and provided sustained production of pro-healing secreted factors. In a murine diabetic wound model, these A. faecalis cELMs shielded the encapsulated bacteria from host clearance, maintained biocontainment, accelerated re-epithelialization, and improved wound bed maturity. Together, these findings establish design principles for cELMs that couple bacterial biocontainment with sustained secretome delivery, providing a promising platform for localized treatment of chronic wounds.

Title: From Fill to Freeze: Redesigning homeRNA to Enable Robust Sampling and Scalable Downstream Processing Workflows for Remote Blood Transcriptomics
Authors: Eakman, M.; Robertson, I. H.; Wei, X.; Stefanovic, F.; Caira, T.; Guckenberger, D. J.; Adams, K. N.; Berthier, E.; Brown, L. G.; Thongpang, S.; Theberge, A. B.
Abstract: In-person research can introduce barriers to participation, including proximity to a study site and scheduling constraints. Our lab developed the homeRNA platform to address these barriers, enabling remote blood collection and RNA stabilization for transcriptomic research. To increase the applicability of homeRNA for large-scale studies, a redesigned version was developed with modifications to 1) improve usability for both participants and downstream processing laboratories, 2) allow for high-throughput manufacturing, and 3) extend the shelf life of the stabilizer tube. In this work, we systematically tested this design against anticipated stresses that can occur throughout a remote study (e.g., high temperature exposure during shipment) to identify and characterize its limitations. We found that the homeRNA device can be prepared and stored at room temperature at least three months in advance of sampling with continued shelf life analysis underway. We also found that the homeRNA platform produces RNA of sufficient quality for downstream transcriptomic analysis under standard shipping durations (i.e., 2 days in transit) and ambient-to-high temperature conditions (i.e., 25-40 {degrees}C) and that RNA quality is unaffected by variable blood volumes collected by participants (mean RIN=7.8 in blood volumes 0.25-1 mL). Lastly, we also found that samples can be stored in typical cold storage temperatures and even up to standard room temperature for at least 4 weeks (mean RIN=8.1 after 4 weeks of storage at -80 to 20 {degrees}C). This work validates that the new homeRNA platform is robust to many of the expected stresses that samples can experience during remote studies.

Title: scCont: Interpretable Contrastive Learning for Functional Characterization of Cellular State Transitions
Authors: Kewalramani, N.; Wuchty, S.; Crovella, M.; Paul, I.; Emili, A.
Abstract: Timecourse single-cell RNA (scRNA) datasets have become indispensable biological tools for studying and uncovering the underlying regulatory processes driving continuous cell-state transitions such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, these highly fluid, non-linear gene program dynamics remain difficult to disentangle. While deep neural network models can effectively map complex topologies, they are biological black boxes, lacking the gene-level interpretability required by experimental practitioners. Here, we introduce scCont, a fully unsupervised contrastive learning framework for extracting interpretable functional transition units from scRNA-seq data. Rather than relying on explicit temporal labels or clustering priors, scCont uses an unsupervised k-nearest neighbors approach to project local transcriptomic neighborhoods into a low-dimensional embedding. During post-training analysis, scCont employs Shapley network attribution to determine gene-latent relationships, mapping latent dimensions directly into functional gene programs. We quantitatively and qualitatively validate this representation by demonstrating that scCont captures biologically interpretable dynamics more effectively than baseline methods such as LDVAE. Evaluated across 13 diverse EMT timecourse datasets and four simulated datasets, scCont exposes interpretable functional dynamics and effectively maps context-dependent functional groups, helping to bridge the gap between deep learning representation and translational biological utility. scCont is an open source software available on GitHub (https://github.com/nramani611/scCont).

Title: QUANTA: A quantum annealing framework for species tree estimation using weighted quartet amalgamation
Authors: Kumar Mondal, N.; Bayzid, M. S.
Abstract: Reconstructing species trees from genome-scale data is challenging due to pervasive gene tree discordance. Maximizing quartet consistency is a widely used approach for species tree inference from multi-locus data. Quartet amalgamation approaches, such as Quartet Fiduccia-Mattheyse (QFM) and Quartet MaxCut (QMC) families, have emerged as highly accurate quartet-based species tree inference techniques, but their reliance on computationally expensive classical bipartitioning heuristics, such as Fiduccia-Mattheyses (FM) and MaxCut, limits their scalability. Here, we introduce QUANTA, a quantum annealing-based quartet amalgamation method that, to our knowledge, represents the first quantum formulation of quartet-based approaches and the first species tree estimation method for multi-locus data that runs on real quantum hardware. At the core of QUANTA is a novel, general formulation of weighted quartet bipartitioning as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem that enables quantum annealing to replace the classical bipartitioning strategies underlying the QFM and QMC families of methods. We prove that our formulation uses the minimum possible number of qubits to represent bipartitions and that its energy function correctly orders satisfied, deferred, and violated quartets for any positive penalty weights. We implemented QUANTA on real D-Wave quantum annealing hardware, and evaluated it on a wide range of simulated and biological datasets. QUANTA achieves accuracy comparable to the state-of-the-art methods, including ASTRAL and wQFM, under challenging evolutionary conditions. We also reanalyzed several biological datasets, including the avian phylogenomic dataset comprising 14,446 genes across 48 genomes, on which QUANTA reconstructed a species tree with a higher quartet score than wQFM. Remarkably, despite running on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, QUANTA's bipartition technique achieved 4100x speedup over the FM bipartitioning technique in wQFM on bipartition containing 90-200 taxa, while maintaining comparable tree accuracy. By establishing a theoretically grounded, hardware-independent quantum optimization framework for weighted quartet amalgamation, QUANTA opens a new direction for quantum-assisted phylogenomics and provides a foundation for increasingly scalable and accurate species tree estimation as quantum computing hardware advances. QUANTA is publicly available at https://github.com/QuitttCat/QUANTA-Phylogenomics.

Title: Theoretical prediction of assembly contiguity
Authors: Abrar, M. H.; Medvedev, P.; Novikov, A.; Sahlin, K.
Abstract: Theoretical methods for predicting the performance of assembly algorithms have the potential to guide experimental design on a scale that simulations cannot. A fundamental question of experimental design is how deep to sequence in order to obtain an assembly with long-enough contigs. More precisely, given a certain read length and coverage, what is the expected contig length that an assembler would produce on a given genome? The foundational work of Lander and Waterman tackled this question, but their method is not applicable to modern high-throughput sequencing. In this paper, we derive what we call a Z-value, which is a formula that takes as input the read length, coverage, and basic properties of the genome, and returns a prediction of the mean contig length produced by a simple single-k assembler on error-free data. We show on a benchmark of 14 genomes that the Z-value is highly accurate, with a mean absolute prediction error of less than 2 percent. We further show how this formula can be used to determine the best choice of k for the assembler and how to choose a coverage level that gives contig lengths within a desired fraction of the optimal. Finally, we show how the Z-value can also predict the performance of a more complicated assembler like Velvet and how it can be used to guide the choice between instruments when there is a tradeoff between coverage and read length and the budget is limited.

Title: Virtual dynamics of spatiotemporal single-cell interactions
Authors: Zhang, Z.; Wang, Z.; Tian, Q.; Hou, H.; Han, J.; Shen, J.; Sun, Y.; Zhou, X.; Peng, Q.; Nie, Q.; Li, T.; Zhou, P.
Abstract: Building virtual cells and tissues requires reconstructing how interacting cell populations evolve in space and time, yet spatial omics experiments provide only sparse snapshots of this process. Here, we introduce CytoBridge, a computational method that reconstructs continuous virtual cell dynamics from discrete spatial transcriptomic data. Starting from a joint transcriptomic-spatial space, CytoBridge learns stochastic trajectories of cell states, positions, and population sizes through an unbalanced mean-field Schrodinger bridge formulation that explicitly incorporates cell-cell interaction as a dynamical driver. A time-varying interaction graph built from spatial proximity and ligand-receptor priors allows the velocity to be decomposed into an interaction component estimated from observed neighborhoods and ligand-receptor features, and an intrinsic-context component that captures intrinsic regulatory processes and unmeasured contextual influences. Applied to five datasets across three spatial transcriptomics platforms and spanning development, regeneration, and neurodegeneration, CytoBridge accurately generates tissue dynamics at unmeasured time points, follows ligand-receptor signaling through measured and unmeasured stages, and supports hypothesis-generating in silico perturbation. CytoBridge provides a general method for turning heterogeneous spatiotemporal transcriptomic measurements into continuously evolving virtual tissues.

Title: Contrastive Learning Improves Generalization on M2OR Olfactory Binding Dataset
Authors: Snider, L.; Nakano-Baker, O.; Mackenzie, J. D.
Abstract: Olfaction-based biosensors stand to have profound impacts in fields such as medical diagnostics, national security, and drug discovery. A promising mode of vapor phase biodetection mimics volatile organic compound-olfactory receptor (VOC-OR) interactions with target-specific protein or peptide probes; however, lack of experimental coverage remains a core bottleneck. Current computational approaches aim to improve prediction of VOC-OR binding to reduce experimental burden, and current machine learning approaches fail to demonstrate a level of generalization that addresses current engineering challenges. Here, using the Molecular to Olfactory Dataset (M2OR) and Insect Olfactory Binding Protein Database (iOBPdb) datasets, data partitioning methods and their performance are evaluated on a neural network and contrastive learning framework on such VOC-OR binding datasets, varying: model training, architecture, and structure of the input data distribution. It was found that holding out certain chemical or proteomic motifs from the training data diminished model performance with a two layer neural network model. The model was able to generalize to state of the art performance (0.88 AUCROC) on every data split by applying a contrastive learning objective defined by shared molecular constituents and a stochastic sampler. This suggests the contrastive objective provides a strong inductive bias for neural networks to predict novel VOC-OR pairs. These findings highlight that model performance on pairwise biological interaction datasets can be inflated through identity leakage from constituent overlap, and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we show contrastive regularization mitigates dataset degeneracy through enforcement of compatibility in the models latent geometry that may extend to other binder target-datasets where identity leakage confounds evaluation.

Title: QRAFT: Scaling coalescent-based species tree inference to one million taxa
Authors: Rahman, A.; Saha, A.; Bayzid, M. S.
Abstract: Species tree inference from multi-locus data under the multispecies coalescent has not kept pace with phylogenomic datasets that now span hundreds of thousands of species. We present QRAFT, a statistically consistent method for estimating species trees by maximizing quartet support on phylogenomic datasets at unprecedented scales. For n taxa and k gene trees, QRAFT achieves near-linear running time of O(kn log^2 n) when its recursion is balanced, which is within a polylogarithmic factor of the O(kn) time required simply to read the input. It also achieves asymptotically optimal O(kn) memory, so its memory requirements grow only linearly with the input size. QRAFT infers a million-taxon species tree from 1,000 genes in just three hours using only 298 GB of RAM, 64 CPU threads, and no GPUs. We estimate that the same analysis with ASTRAL-MP, a scalable parallel implementation of the widely used method ASTRAL, would take about 36 years (>100,000 times longer) and require prohibitive amounts of memory, far beyond practical computational limits. QRAFT maintains accuracy comparable to, and in many cases better than, leading species tree estimation methods. Notably, QRAFT reconstructed a microbial tree of life comprising 199,330 genomes in just a few hours using modest CPU resources. Thus, QRAFT brings highly accurate statistically consistent coalescent-based species tree inference to the unprecedented million-taxon regime and enables phylogenomic analyses towards the scale of the tree of life. QRAFT is publicly available at https://github.com/risenfromashes/qraft.

Title: Towards a foundation model for raw nanopore signal through discrete tokenization
Authors: Cheng, G.; Pitkänen, E.
Abstract: Nanopore sequencing reads nucleic acids as changes in ionic current that carry information beyond the base sequence. Self-supervised pretrained models have advanced genomic sequence modeling and single-cell analysis, but remain underexplored for raw nanopore signals, which are continuous and lack a native token vocabulary. Here we present Brieno, an approach combining reconstruction-based tokenization through residual vector quantization with a Transformer for contextual representation learning. We pretrain the Transformer using masked-token prediction on raw nanopore signals from 118 million reads. With frozen or fine-tuned features, the model identifies species without requiring reference genomes. It complements Dorado by accurately classifying reads left unclassified in native-barcode demultiplexing, approaches Dorado's basecalling performance across six genomes, and exceeds Dorado's specialized 5-methylcytosine model as well as a dedicated 6-methyladenine caller. Brieno also supports accurate CpG methylation detection with limited labeled data. Across tasks, pretrained contextual representations improve downstream performance over non-pretrained baselines and generalize across sequencing runs. Together, these findings support self-supervised pretraining as a basis for transferable representations of raw nanopore signals.

Title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
Authors: Tolstoganov, I.; Sahlin, K.
Abstract: One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.

Title: DisCell: Separating Spillover from Niche Response in Spatial Transcriptomics
Authors: Molen, R.; Toosi, H.; Ferreira, P. F.; Lagergren, J.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution measures every cell in its place in the tissue, but diffusion and segmentation errors also add transcripts of neighboring cells to a cell's counts. This spillover makes a cell resemble its neighbors, and a response to the niche makes cells in the same niche resemble each other. Both tie a cell's expression to its surroundings. The count data alone cannot tell the two apart. Findings from single-cell transcriptomes, such as a gene program that is higher in one niche than in another or signaling genes that change depending on the neighborhood, may therefore be artifacts of spillover. Current models describe a cell by its intrinsic state together with either its niche response or spillover, but none models all three. We present DisCell, the first method that models all three components jointly and measures how robust each finding is to spillover. DisCell is a generative model that describes single-cell gene expression profiles in terms of two latent variables, an intrinsic state and a response to the niche, and adds spillover from its neighbors as a separate term. DisCell fits the model at increasing levels of spillover and recomputes each finding on the spillover-free expression to see how much spillover it withstands. DisCell also estimates the most spillover a section can contain, and a finding that holds even at that amount is not explained by spillover. In simulated tissue, DisCell recovers each cell's intrinsic state and response and tells findings created by spillover apart from genuine responses. On five sections of ovarian and lung tissue, the intrinsic state keeps more of each cell's own properties, measured by its cell-cycle phase, than any competing method that holds as little of its neighborhood. Within each cell type, the model partitions the variation of each gene into intrinsic state, niche response and spillover. Using DisCell, we rank findings about niches by their robustness to spillover and confirm that a previously reported finding withstands spillover, that esophageal cancer cells in niches infiltrated by immune or stromal cells express more of an epithelial-mesenchymal transition program. DisCell also predicts what the gene expression of a cell type would be in another niche, with its spillover part separated, at lower error on most tasks than the competing method built for this purpose. Training the model takes under ten minutes on one consumer GPU for sections of up to 400,000 cells.

Title: Growing a Root from Its Genome : Emergent Tissue Layers and Zones in a GPU-Native Simulation of the Arabidopsis Root Tip
Authors: Auger, E.; Gandecki, M.; Heng, F.-X.
Abstract: Models of the Arabidopsis root tip usually take its cell identities as given. Here we grow a root tip from a single genome. In a two-dimensional median section, every cell reads the same network of 62 genes (26 core genes from an earlier, unpublished model of callus and 36 added for the root) and starts with the same expression; the only spatial cues are the polarity of auxin transport, auxin from the shoot and the free surface. Identities and zones are never given to the simulation; they are read from gene expression. Cells are polygons of a shared mesh, relaxed towards mechanical equilibrium under turgor at every step. In 48 simulated hours, a tip-shaped template grows into a root of 3 000-4 500 cells with epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and stele in order along most of its length, SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW in the endodermis, an auxin maximum, a quiescent centre and a cap at its tip, and meristem, elongation and mature zones. A WOX5 gate built from published interactions and one hypothesis keeps a quiescent centre to 48 h in 17 of 20 simulated roots that were not used for tuning (85%; Wilson 95% interval 64-95%; criteria fixed before the run), against 9 of 20 roots used for tuning, before the gate. The niche is not maintained beyond 48 h: grown on to 73 h, only 6 of these 20 roots still have a quiescent centre (30%; 15-52%). All pre-registered criteria hold in only 1 of 20 roots, because the quiescent centre is too wide at 0 h; without that count, 12 of 20. The meristem is too long, and cortical cells made after the start of growth elongate only three- to four-fold instead of eightto thirty-fold, a limit set in large part by the numerical growth scheme. Mutants are a major weakness: several look like their published phenotype, but an exploratory re-run of a mutant benchmark fixed in advance for our first model passes one of nine predictions. Nor does the root regenerate: cut near its tip, it re-forms an auxin maximum and a columella but no quiescent centre. On a first, simpler model and without any polarity cue, a mass of identical cells still sorts into concentric layers and, when PIN carriers follow the auxin flux, concentrates auxin into a few foci, but forms no stem-cell niche: the genome lacks a lateral inhibition between foci. We state the limitations and the next stages.

Title: Predicting Transcriptional Responses to Unseen Compounds through Context Modeling and Multi-View Transfer
Authors: Lei, Y.; Liang, H.; Peng, K.; Wen, J.
Abstract: Predicting drug-induced transcriptional responses could support in silico screening of new compounds, yet existing models barely use the compound: on a drug-blind L1000 benchmark, removing the drug input from seven published models changes accuracy by at most 0.012 Pearson correlation. They capture shared cellular and experimental variation while overlooking the compound-specific signals that distinguish drug effects. We present UnDetect, a framework that separates contextual variation from compound effects to predict responses to transcriptionally unprofiled compounds. UnDetect integrates chemical structure, annotated targets, mechanisms of action and Cell Painting morphology into a normalized multi-view kernel that accommodates incomplete compound information, and transfers residual responses within and across profiled cell lines, so that pharmacological and phenotypic relationships inform predictions beyond chemical similarity. On a drug-blind benchmark, where the paired control reveals the assay plate, UnDetect is the only model to beat a network that ignores the compound, in every fold; on a within-plate score that is zero for any compound-blind prediction, it reaches 0.117 against 0.092 for the strongest published model. On DeepCE's benchmark it reaches 0.602 Pearson correlation against the reported 0.491. Transfer across cell lines improves 28 of 28 LINCS L1000 and, at the two higher doses, 47 and 49 of 50 Tahoe-100M cell-line evaluations. These results show that separating context from compound effects and integrating complementary compound information improves transcriptional prediction and extends the utility of perturbation atlases for virtual screening.

Title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
Authors: Dinse, T.; Englaender, V. R.; Metz, S.; Schrezenmeier, H.; Messerer, D. A. C.
Abstract: Background Residual barcode-like sequences after preprocessing are a quality-control concern in multiplexed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing data, particularly in low-biomass, host-dominated samples such as blood. Using blood datasets spiked with a microbial mock community and prepared with the Native Barcoding Kit 96 V14 (SQK-NBD114.96), we compared Dorado 1.1.1, Dorado 2.0.0, and Barbell 0.3.2. Results Dorado demultiplexing reduced barcode-positive reads to approximately 2% of reads, with internal barcode-like matches in 0.17-0.19% of reads. Barbell 0.3.2 applied to untrimmed Dorado basecalls yielded an approximately 50-fold lower detector-defined internal-match rate (0.0035-0.0037%) while retaining 91.2-91.8% of input reads. In the NCBI core_nt release of 12 September 2026, the focused screen identified complete, ungapped 24 nt identity for 64 of the 96 barcodes (66.7%), comprising 505 distinct barcode-accession pairs across 482 accessions and 195 exported TaxID groups of mixed taxonomic ranks. Records annotated as rRNA genes, chromosomes/genomes, and plasmids accounted for 35.6%, 23.2%, and 22.4% of the pairs, respectively. The barcode was located within its native ligation flanks in 224 pairs (44.4%), including 170 (33.7%) with the complete Dorado barcode search window and 3 (0.6%) with the full adapter construct. Conclusion Barbell combined 91-92% read retention with lower detected internal barcode signals. After demultiplexing, barcode-like sequences remained in sample data. Moreover, kit barcode sequences, often within their native ligation flanks, were detected in reference records. Both findings call for careful preprocessing, reference inspection, and downstream validation. Further research should determine whether barcode-associated artifacts in reads and reference records affect taxonomic classification in clinical metagenomic workflows.

Title: siRNA/mRNA payload of lipid nanoparticles quantified using fluorescence microscopy and correlation spectroscopy
Authors: Kirchmair, B. R.; Stoyanov, N.; Maksutova, D.; Peulen, T.-O.; Hagemeier, J. A.; Kellerer, T.; Cordes, T.; Faendrich, M.; Raedler, J. O.
Abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most promising vectors to deliver nucleic acids to mammalian cells. Advanced delivery strategies involving multiple nucleic acid species require a reliable determination of RNA payload and LNP size. Here, we use total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) to determine mRNA payload and siRNA/mRNA codelivered payload. Particularly, FCS proves to be a reliable method for payload determination, independently of fluorophore properties that can be altered during encapsulation. By varying the PEG-lipid fraction relative to the reference ONPATTRO formulation, we find that mRNA payload of enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) coding mRNA increases from [~]10 with LNP size according to a power law with an exponent 1.3. Cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) reveals that in this case blebs occur more frequently in small LNPs. For siRNA/mRNA coencapsulation the siRNA fraction within LNPs exceeds that in the initial RNA mixture, suggesting that coencapsulation is competitive and constrained by nucleic acid diffusion. Together, our findings highlight the importance of particle size and encapsulation kinetics in controlling the loading and composition of RNA payloads in LNPs.

Title: Maximum Likelihood Localization Maps
Authors: Zarei Oshtolagh, H.; Foerster, R.; Ries, J.; Heintzmann, R.
Abstract: Single-molecule localization microscopy commonly reconstructs images from estimated emitter coordinates. We calculate maximum-likelihood localization maps (MLLM), a non-iterative approach that evaluates positional likelihood from measured data and a supplied point-spread function. The MLLM of each detected single molecule image is added into a final upsampled image representing the overall molecular probability map, preserving the positional likelihood structure and obviating separate coordinate-based rendering. MLLM calculation is noniterative, fast, supports any calibrated point-spread function, accounts for local background variation, supports two- and three-dimensional reconstruction, and can be calculated in parallel.

Title: Homeostatic fibroblast niche collapse in clinically uninvolved skin marks a pre-fibrotic stage of systemic sclerosis
Authors: Hu, A.; Tung, L. W.; Pulliam, T.; Simpson, C. L.; Lord, S.; Carlin, J. S.; DeBerg, H. A.; Campbell, D. J.; Morawski, P. J.
Abstract: Systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Heterogeneous clinical presentation and polygenic risk complicate our understanding of disease mechanisms and the path to effective therapy. Single-cell analyses have revealed substantial transcriptional diversity in skin, but disease-associated reprogramming remains poorly defined. To address this, we performed high-resolution spatial transcriptomic profiling of paired clinically uninvolved and clinically affected scleroderma donor skin alongside healthy controls. We identified a continuum of cellular, molecular, and spatial changes to the stroma that were already evident in clinically uninvolved tissue yet still distinct from the broader and more advanced changes in paired fibrotic samples. Uninvolved skin was comparable to healthy tissue by clinical and histopathological assessment, but distinguishable by the numerical reduction, transcriptional reprogramming, and spatial isolation of LGR5+SCARA5+PI16+ progenitor fibroblasts. In parallel, the dermal vascular smooth muscle compartment shifted from a contractile to a synthetic, activated state, suggesting reprogramming that begins before overt fibrosis. Cell neighborhood analysis revealed that progenitor fibroblasts occupy dense stromal niches in healthy skin that collapse in clinically uninvolved tissue, replaced by isolated, disease-associated cellular networks. These data indicate that clinically uninvolved skin occupies an intermediate stage along the pathologic continuum of scleroderma, establishing a framework for strategies to preserve homeostatic fibroblast niches before tissue remodeling and fibrotic commitment.

Title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells
Authors: Feldman, H. A.; VonHandorf, A.; Alianiello, K. E.; English, K. L.; Reighard, S. D.; Brunner, H. I.; Kottyan, L. C.; Weirauch, M. T.; Kaufman, K. M.; Waggoner, S. N.
Abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate therapeutics regimens of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2, encoded by EPAS1) but not HIF-1 in NK cells. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2 was not dependent on limited oxygen availability. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2 protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2 transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2/HIF-1{beta} heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolism. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1{beta} independent, HIF-2 pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2 to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies.

Title: LAP-TLR2 Axis Drives Inflammatory Pathology during Listeria monocytogenes Gastroenteritis
Authors: Liu, D.; Tenguria, S.; Irizarry-Tardi, N.; Franklin, J.; Park, S.; Gallina, N.; Xu, L.; Nathan, V.; Li, X.; Fu, Y.; Drolia, R.; Bai, X.; Gao, Z.; Reddivari, L.; Ristroph, K.; Cox, A. D.; Olson, M. R.; Bhunia, A. K.
Abstract: Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) causes acute gastroenteritis that precedes systemic invasive listeriosis, yet the molecular mechanisms coordinating bacterial virulence with host inflammatory responses during the enteric phase remain poorly understood. We show that Lm-associated gastroenteritis is dose-dependent, and a high infectious dose (~1x10^10 CFU/mouse), reflecting epidemic cases, recapitulates hallmark features of gastroenteritis in a mouse model, including early onset, epithelial erosion, and profound inflammatory cell infiltration. We identify Listeria adhesion protein (LAP), rather than classical virulence factors such as internalin A and listeriolysin O, as the primary mediator of enteric pathology, driving epithelial cell death and neutrophil recruitment. Transcriptomic (mRNA-seq) profiling implicates LAP-driven engagement of the TLR2-MyD88 pathway. Using the HEK-Dual hTLR2 (NF-kB) reporter cell line and TLR2 knockout mice, we show that LAP engages TLR2 to activate TNFalpha; NF-kB signaling and compromises the gut epithelial barrier. Disease severity correlates with myeloid hyperactivation and intestinal ion channel dysregulation, as CD11b-; mice exhibit attenuated diarrhea despite elevated bacterial tissue loads. Finally, studies in MLCK knock-out mice confirm that this myeloid-driven pathology requires MLCK-dependent tight junction opening for paracellular neutrophil migration, which works in concert with LAP-TLR2 signaling during Lm-induced gastroenteritis.

Title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
Authors: Goodman, A. M.; Tolman, E.; Kohli, M.
Abstract: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica, reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ~275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

Title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
Authors: Islam, U. I.; Marsico, F.; Garrison, E.; Boucher, C.
Abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries.
