GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once. On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.

Title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
Authors: Behrens, C.; Chatterjee, M.; Jernigan, C. M.; Reed, R. D.; Toth, A.; Sheehan, M. J.
Abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

Title: Plumage diversity without differential expression of pigmentation genes in a rapid avian radiation
Authors: Recuerda, M.; Repenning, M.; Toomey, M. B.; Kraemer, S.; Rosoni, J. R. R.; Silveira, L. F.; Kopuchian, C.; Campagna, L.
Abstract: Uncovering the molecular basis of reproductive traits is key to understanding species divergence. Capuchino Seedeaters ( Sporophila ), a radiation of genetically similar birds differing mainly in male reproductive plumage color, can be leveraged to study how such traits evolve. Outlier scans identified candidate pigmentation variants primarily in noncoding sequence, implying regulatory changes. However, RNA-seq of growing feather follicles generally did not show differential expression of pigmentation genes among different colors, with only ASIP downregulated in crown feathers. Gene expression patterns instead varied by body region. The largest difference between dimorphic sexes was the upregulation of the carotenoid-degrading gene BCO2 in males, accompanied by lower carotenoid content in male feathers. An improved genome annotation assigned 9.5% of candidate variants into coding and untranslated sequence. This suggests species-diagnostic variants lie within transcribed sequence and could act post-transcriptionally, rather than through transcript abundance, leading to a revised hypothesis for plumage divergence in this radiation.

Title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
Authors: Ueda, H. H.; Tucs, A.; Tsuda, K.; Umetsu, M.; Saito, Y.
Abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

Title: Generative 3D Spatial Reconstruction of Cellular Organization from Single Cell Expression
Authors: Azim, E.; Alif, M. N.; Hwang, T. H.; Zheng, H.; Zhang, W. i.
Abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles cellular states at scale but removes their three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization. Reconstructing this organization requires recovering not only individual cell positions but also the physical size, geometry, and neighborhoods of an entire tissue. Existing methods either map cells onto measured spatial references or reconstruct two-dimensional sections independently, leaving the joint reconstruction of a new 3D specimen unresolved. Moreover, predicting the average plausible position of each cell can reduce per-cell error while compressing tissue geometry. We introduce ORBIS, a generative framework that jointly reconstructs whole 3D specimens from single-cell gene expression without requiring a spatial reference at inference. ORBIS learns spatial organization through flow matching in a shared physical coordinate frame, using training views sampled from sparse serial sections, tissue blocks, and whole specimens. At inference, a shared spatial state is iteratively updated through dynamically regrouped windows, enabling the generation of millions of cell positions without independently reconstructing and stitching tissue regions. We evaluate physical size, cell-population shape, per-cell placement, and neighborhood organization separately to distinguish accurate tissue geometry from low per-cell error. Across eight held-out specimens spanning whole mouse brains, thick brain blocks, and Drosophila embryos, ORBIS achieves lower cell-population shape error than all five evaluated baselines on every test and reconstructs specimens containing up to 3.7 million cells. On a single GPU, ORBIS samples million-cell brains in 0.9-2.8 minutes, approximately 38 times faster than the sampler of LUNA-3D, our 3D extension of the state-of-the-art generative spatial reconstruction method LUNA. On two held-out brain tests, sampling reduces size error by 3.3-fold and shape error by 1.8-fold compared with a single-call variant. On an independent dissociated single-cell brain atlas, ORBIS returns on average 37.9% of each region's cells to their dissection region across 23 regions, compared with 28.5% for LUNA-3D.

Title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
Authors: Libiseller-Egger, J.; Gotsmy, M.; Guillen-Gosalbez, G.; Zanghellini, J.
Abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

Title: FUSION PORE CLOSURE DETERMINES SUBQUANTAL KISS-AND-RUN SEROTONIN RELEASE FROM FULLY LOADED DENSE-CORE VESICLES
Authors: De-Miguel, F. F.
Abstract: During kiss-and-run exocytosis, a transient fusion pore opens, releases part of the vesicular quantum, and closes without full fusion. This report investigates two questions: first, whether dense-core vesicles undergoing kiss-and-run contain the same number of molecules as those undergoing full fusion; second, whether subquantal release results from pore closure or vesicle depletion. We analyzed amperometric recordings of extrasynaptic serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in cultured leech Retzius neurons. Full-fusion events released 91,585{+/-}34,428 molecules (n=14), whereas kiss-and-run events released 58,344{+/-}20,759 molecules, 64% of the quantum. We analyzed the biexponential dynamics of the filtered amperometric current using Ohmic equations for cylindrical and toroidal pores. Hydrated flux packing (HFP) independently estimated the minimum peak pore diameter from the number of hydrated serotonin molecules crossing the pore. Kiss-and-run peak diameters were 2.1 to 3.2 nm, corresponding to the passage of 4 to 10 hydrated molecules. The vesicular serotonin content of individual kiss-and-run events was estimated by a frozen pore extrapolation (FPE), in which pores were kept at the peak HFP diameter. FPE yielded 102,650{+/-}10,989 molecules per vesicle (n=15), similar to the quantum obtained by integrating full-fusion events. Therefore, kiss-and-run subquantal release did not reflect a smaller quantum. We then compared the decay of serotonin flux with that estimated through the frozen pore at its peak diameter. In every event, the flux decayed faster, reaching half its peak in 0.59 (0.23 to 0.95) of the time taken by the frozen pore flux. We conclude that subquantal release during kiss-and-run exocytosis is governed by fusion-pore closure rather than vesicle depletion.

Title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
Authors: Yan, L.; Marschmann, G. L.
Abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.

Title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
Authors: Le Verge-Serandour, M.; Bienau, A.; Simmel, F. C.; Alim, K.
Abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.

Title: Genomic analysis of the Streptococcus anginosus group; taxonomic implications, evolutionary insights and clinical considerations
Authors: Coleman, A.; Liaw, J.; Maresco-Pennisi, D.; Deehan, R.; Harris, P. N. A.; Cervin, A.; Edkins, O.; Zaugg, J.; Bialasiewicz, S.
Abstract: Background: The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) (S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group's diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods: Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results: Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa (S. anginosus, S. hominis, S. whileyi and S. vaginalis). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex-S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ~15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity (S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions: Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.

Title: Microfluidic sieve and detector for rapid ultrasensitive assays with single-molecule sensitivity
Authors: Kim, G.; Shafique, H.; Shen, M. L.; Ng, A.; Juncker, D.
Abstract: The advent of ultrasensitive assays enabled many new research and clinical applications, but the time-to-result is hours and has not significantly improved over time, limiting their potential. We introduce the microfluidic sieve and detector (MFSD) that can sieve 200 microlitres in just one minute, and quantify captured analytes in four minutes, down to zeptomolar (10^-19M) concentration. The MFSD comprises half a million 8-m-diameter pores that bind analytes upon Brownian motion-induced wall collision. Conventional ensemble models and a stochastic Brownian agent dynamics introduced here reveal rapid, predictable and tuneable analyte capture under flow. Digital sandwich assays are completed by sequentially flowing the sample and reagents, partitioning the pores, and digitally revealing single trapped analytes by enzymatic amplification. The MFSD tests are specific and reproducible, exhibit a large dynamic range, and are simple, tuneable and versatile, enabling measurement of different proteins including influenza A nucleoprotein in clinical samples, and even nucleic acids while being both faster and more sensitive than PCR. As such, the MFSD could open a new chapter for analysis and diagnostics.

Title: Scalable high-density tactile arenas for measuring ground-contact forces in freely moving animals
Authors: Lu, W.; Slepyan, A.; Perkins, P.; Ascani Orsini, A.; Quinn, K.; Thakor, N.
Abstract: Understanding how animals physically interact with their environment is fundamental to studying movement, sensorimotor control, and neurological function. Yet most behavioral measurement systems primarily capture movement and posture, while direct measurements of contact forces often require specialized instrumentation or involve trade-offs among spatial coverage, resolution, and acquisition speed. Here, we introduce a scalable tactile sensing platform that transforms the surface beneath freely moving animals into a high-resolution contact-imaging instrument. By combining modular sensor arrays with adaptive compressive tactile sampling, the platform provides 16,384 tactile sensing elements at 2-mm pitch across a 512 x 128-mm runway, with nominal 1 kHz acquisition. Rather than exhaustively scanning the entire array, the system concentrates measurements around active contacts, enabling high-speed sensing across an extended behavioral surface. Synchronized overhead video and a camera-assisted analysis pipeline enable paw-resolved measurements of contact loading, stance dynamics, footprint morphology, interlimb weight redistribution, and center-of-pressure trajectories. In a longitudinal rat model of sciatic nerve injury, the platform detected reduced loading of the injured hindlimb and increased loading of the contralateral limb, including changes that conventional gait timing measures underestimated. The modular architecture, together with openly available hardware designs, software and data, provides an accessible framework for studying the mechanical interactions underlying freely moving behavior, with potential applications across neuroscience, injury, and motor recovery research.

Title: Metastable Dimeric Intermediate Drives Native-like Spidroin Fibrillogenesis, while Dehydration Promotes Cross-β Transition
Authors: Kajimoto, H.; Yonezawa, K.; Chan, K. S.; Hayashi, K.; Okamoto, Y.; Aiba, R.; Nakatani, Y.; Kimura, K.; Bessho, M.; Yamazaki, Y.; Toma-Fukai, S.; Uchihashi, T.; Sato, T. K.; Kamikubo, H.
Abstract: The exceptional mechanical properties of spider dragline silk originate from hierarchical spidroin self-assembly, yet mimicking this process to generate native-like structures remains challenging. Here, we report a metastable dimeric intermediate as an essential molecular factor for fibrillogenesis. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) revealed a compact core stabilized by solvent-excluded "dry interfaces" surrounded by extended random coil regions. Within the core, a subset of the polyalanine blocks is held by side-chain packing rather than by main-chain {beta}-sheets; the majority remain exposed in the surrounding coil regions. Upon lowering the denaturant concentration, these exposed polyalanine segments pair with their counterparts at a fibril end, forming intermolecular {beta}-sheets that act as linkers and drive the stepwise end-to-end polymerization of the dimeric particles. In solution, the resulting fibrils exhibit an ordered {beta}-structure in which the polypeptide chains run parallel to the fibril axis, in contrast to amyloid-like cross-{beta}, in which the strands lie perpendicular to it; this matches key features of native silk nanofibril architecture. However, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis demonstrates that these native-like nanofibrils undergo an effectively irreversible transition toward amyloid-like cross-{beta} structures upon drying. Native-like fibrils are thus achievable by self-assembly, but structural control is lost during the final dehydration step. Accordingly, we propose a general principle for decoupling self-assembly from dehydration: native-like nanofibrils are formed first, then dried under conditions that restrict molecular-chain mobility (for example, mechanical constraint or immobilization on a surface), which we expect to suppress thermodynamic relaxation into cross-{beta} structures.

Title: From exact gradients to exact standard errors: third- and fourth-order sensitivities for the Laplacian population likelihood family
Authors: van de Beek, H.; Beldjenna, M.; Almquist, J.; Fidler, M. L.; Zwep, L. B.; van Hasselt, J. G. C.
Abstract: Asymptotic standard errors for the parameters of a nonlinear mixed effects model fitted by Laplacian estimation, first-order conditional estimation (FOCE), or FOCE with interaction (FOCEI) require the observed (Fisher) information, the negative second derivative of the population objective at the optimum. The gradient of this objective can be computed exactly from sensitivity equations, but the observed information is still formed by finite differencing, which is less accurate, step-size dependent, and requires empirical Bayes reoptimization. These perturbed individual optimization problems can fail even after a successful fit. Our objectives are to (1) extend the exact-gradient sensitivity framework by one differentiation and give the observed information of the Laplacian population likelihood family in closed form and (2) illustrate covariance calculation without further empirical Bayes optimization in a case example. Writing the objective as a data term plus the log-determinant of the inner Hessian, the population Hessian splits so that the data term reuses second-order sensitivities, whereas the log determinant term requires third-order sensitivities for FOCE/FOCEI and fourth-order sensitivities for the full Laplacian method. We illustrate this on a two-compartment oral model with first-order absorption fitted to simulated data. The analytic covariance involves no differencing step and uses the fitted empirical Bayes estimates without reoptimization, avoiding this source of covariance-step failure. Implemented for FOCE/FOCEI in the open-source R package nlmixr2, the construction provides exact, reproducible standard errors for the approximate likelihood, limited by numerical solution accuracy and conditioning. This supports more dependable confidence intervals, identifiability assessment, and uncertainty propagation.

Title: Non-canonical peptidoglycan cross-linking is essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis acid resistance
Authors: Ma, R.; Rea, D.; Ocius, K.; Naick, A.; Healy, C.; Ioerger, T.; Pires, M.; Cava, f.; Ehrt, S.; Gouzy, A.
Abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis withstands acidic conditions to survive and replicate within macrophages. To define the genetic determinants of this adaptation, we performed a transposon screen in a lipid-rich, acidic medium that mimics the host environment and supports robust M. tuberculosis growth. This screen identified ldtB, encoding an L,D transpeptidase, as essential for growth and survival under acid stress. Loss of LdtB decreased 3-3 peptidoglycan cross-linking, disrupted cell wall architecture, and impaired intrabacterial pH homeostasis, resulting in increased susceptibility to cell wall-active antibiotics. Notably, M. tuberculosis lacking LdtB displayed heightened sensitivity to meropenem within macrophages, suggesting that targeting this enzyme could potentiate beta-lactam efficacy during infection. These findings establish LdtB as a key mediator linking peptidoglycan homeostasis to acid stress resistance and underscores the importance of in vitro culture models that recapitulate the host microenvironment for uncovering new in vivo active therapeutic targets.

Title: Do plasmid-dependent phages enable the survival of costly plasmids?
Authors: Yuly, J. L.; Avallone, M.; Abad, L.; Wingreen, N. S.
Abstract: Plasmids store auxiliary genes that address environmental challenges such as antibiotics. In the short term, plasmid loss can be advantageous to hosts if plasmid benefits are temporary but costs are permanent. However, this loss can proceed to plasmid extinction, with access to plasmid-derived benefits permanently lost. We consider a worst-case scenario: a plasmid that yields benefits only infrequently, imposes heavy costs that cannot be alleviated, and whose host population faces a competitor that cannot acquire the costly plasmid. Thus, horizontal transmission of this plasmid is detrimental to the host population when the plasmid does not provide benefits. Using population models, we demonstrate that -- counterintuitively -- plasmid-dependent phages can enable high-cost plasmid survival. Phage predation pins the plasmid at low abundance, effectively neutralizing the plasmid cost at the population level and boosting persistence time. When the costly plasmid becomes beneficial, it spreads and survives by vertical transmission until benefits subside.

Title: FMRP safeguards long mRNA expression by opposing repressive RNP states
Authors: Ma, K.; Hossain, A. R.; Judson, K. L.; Cheng, T. Q.; Greenblatt, E. J.
Abstract: Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) is widely viewed as a translational repressor, yet its loss paradoxically compromises expression of exceptionally long, dosage-sensitive neurodevelopmental mRNAs. First shown in Drosophila oocytes, this selective loss extends to mouse cortex and hippocampus, but its mechanism remains unknown. Here, we uncover a protective function for FMRP: shielding long mRNAs from repression by Me31B/DDX6, a conserved RNA helicase that organizes repressive RNP complexes. In Drosophila oocytes, FMRP loss redirects target mRNAs into Me31B-marked P-bodies. Transcriptome-wide binding maps reveal extensive FMRP-Me31B co-occupancy, preferentially concentrated on long coding sequences whose translation depends on FMRP. Strikingly, disrupting Me31B-dependent repression preferentially enhances translation of FMRP targets in FMRP-deficient oocytes. We identify Rin/G3BP, Caprin, and Lig/UBAP2L as FMRP-associated cofactors supporting expression of distinct targets. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing view of FMRP as a translational repressor, revealing instead a mechanism that safeguards vulnerable neurodevelopmental mRNAs from inappropriate cytoplasmic silencing.

Title: An integrated workflow for dual-guide CRISPR-Cas9 targeting and amplicon-based genotyping of Pla2g6 in primary mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages
Authors: Challa, A. K.; Nair, R.; Gurusamy, A.; Huynh, T. Y. L.; Folmar, J. R.; Ahamed, A.; Chowdarapu, S.; Ramanadham, S.
Abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 editing in primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMD-M{phi}s) requires coordinated assessment of cellular morphology, target modification, and sequence-level editing outcomes. We describe a workflow for dual-guide targeting of murine Pla2g6 that integrates guide design, ribonucleoprotein nucleofection, PCR-heteroduplex mobility analysis (PCR-HMA), and targeted amplicon sequencing. At 24 h after nucleofection, cells receiving ribonucleoproteins assembled with chemically synthesized single-guide RNAs preserved the elongated, adherent morphology, whereas cultures receiving in vitro-transcribed guides contained predominantly poorly adhered, rounded cells and appeared less densely populated; both guide preparations generated indels and deletions, so the difference observed was in cell appearance rather than in target modification. PCR-HMA provided a simple, qualitative screen for sequence heterogeneity and for a putative deletion product, which was subsequently characterized by sequencing. In two independent BMDM samples, one each from C57BL/6 and NOD mice, breakpoint-based analysis identified editing-associated indels in 54.7% and 44.5% of analyzed reads, compared with 0.28% and 0.07% in matched Cas9-only controls. Deletions spanning both target sites represented 33.1% and 26.2% of analyzed reads; none were detected among 4,383 analyzed control reads. The modal spanning deletion was 137 bp, the size predicted from precise joining of the two blunt Cas9 ends. Sequence interpretation depended on verified guide coordinates, deletion-aware analysis settings, and matched controls: scored permissively, the same control reads returned 22-23% apparent editing. Modest-depth Nanopore sequencing recovered the major editing classes, although low-frequency variants and small indels required additional caution. This workflow supports a simple and streamlined screening and sequence-based genotyping of edited BMDM populations, allowing the discernment of the comprehensive mutation spectrum arising from CRISPR-Cas9 gene targeting.

Title: Evolutionary tuning of rhodopsin-mediated light protection
Authors: Dbouk, N. H.; Bagshaw, M.; Bose, A. A.; Arner, A.; Zhao, K.; Praveen, N.; Bautista, I.; Musayeva, N.; Xue, L.; McElhinney, M.; Kasthuri, R.; Bick, A. G.; Lea, A. J.; Castiglione, G. M.
Abstract: Visual sensitivity introduces the inherent risk of blinding photodamage. Rhodopsin directly mediates this vulnerability, as activation drives excessive signaling via the Meta-II (MII) state, which subsequently releases the toxic, desensitizing agonist all-trans retinal (atRAL). In dim-light specialists, slow atRAL release is assumed to reflect extended MII signaling; however, this model ignores that arrestin quenches signaling in milliseconds and that apparent release reflects reversible atRAL rebinding. Here we reveal that extended post-bleach lifetimes, including an atRAL-driven shift toward non-signaling Meta-III (MIII), evolved independently of intrinsic G-protein signaling to dually protect retinal cells against photochemical toxicity and shield neighboring receptors from agonist noise. Dim-light specialists whose rod-dense retinas experience daytime solar flux, such as megabats, possess an extremely cytoprotective rhodopsin that retains nearly 60% of atRAL at equilibrium by partitioning into MIII, validating long-standing predictions that MIII buffers retinoid toxicity while explaining why bat rhodopsin signals more weakly than faster-releasing human or bovine orthologs. To definitively uncouple sequestration from intrinsic signaling, we engineered an active-state-locked, signaling-null rhodopsin that achieves 100% atRAL sequestration and confers extreme cytoprotection in retinal cells. Mimicking partial bleaches with heterogeneous active and inactive receptor populations, co-incubation reveals that this signaling-null sink acts in trans to boost wild-type rhodopsin regeneration and signaling by shielding neighboring dark-state receptors from agonist interference. Lastly, while consensus human rhodopsin is non-protective, alleles restoring cytoprotective sequestration emerged in high-irradiance geographies, conferring a 38% reduced risk of blindness in modern populations. Our findings redefine rhodopsin as a tunable light buffer shaping adaptation and human disease.

Title: Open-source benchmarking of dairy and dairy-free products
Authors: Koosis, A. O.; Cotto, C.; Kuhl, E.
Abstract: Dairy-free products offer opportunities to reduce the environmental impact of food. However, they must reproduce the diverse sensory and functional properties of conventional dairy, from foam stabilization in a latte to acid-gel structure in yogurt and melt--stretch behavior in mozzarella. Yet, large-scale, open-source sensory benchmarks across dairy product categories remain scarce. Here we show that the sensory gap between dairy and dairy-free products varies substantially across ten categories: barista milk, butter, cheddar, cream cheese, creamer, ice cream, fluid milk, mozzarella, sour cream, and Greek-style yogurt. We analyze the NECTAR Taste of the Industry 2026 dataset, which includes 1,437 respondents, 3,220 overall-liking ratings, and 79,027 recorded survey responses, including 35,762 product-linked responses. Leading dairy-free beverages, barista milk ($+0.17$), fluid milk ($+0.02$), and creamer ($-0.06$), closely approach their dairy benchmarks in overall liking on a seven-point scale. In contrast, mozzarella shows the largest deficit ($-1.46$), followed by Greek-style yogurt ($-0.68$) and butter ($-0.54$). All three deficits remain statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Across categories, descriptive penalty analysis identifies off-flavor (1.85 points), stale or cardboard notes (1.81 points), and artificial or chemical notes (1.80 points) as the sensory attributes associated with the largest reductions in overall liking. Together, these results establish the first open sensory benchmark for dairy and dairy-free products, identify beverage categories that approach conventional dairy in overall liking, and reveal the sensory attributes and product categories with the greatest opportunities for future innovation.

Title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
Authors: Pourmirzaei, M.; Alqarghuli, S.; Chen, K.; Pourmirzaei, M.; Xu, D.
Abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

Title: VoroTIDE: Protein domain segmentation through independent hierarchical searches using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
Authors: Le, K. Q.; Postic, G.; Angel, E.; Tahi, F.
Abstract: Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein-protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce VoroTIDE (Voronoi-based Two-way Independent Domain Exploration), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. VoroTIDE applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of elementary structural units until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH-ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, VoroTIDE achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

Title: Fully integrated SNV, fusion, and isoform analysis of cancer drivers with FLAIR3 for improved functional interpretation
Authors: Felton, C. A.; Galvez, A.; Damle, T.; Levine, K. M.; Diekhans, M.; Fuentes, E. L.; Won, T. S.; Vollmers, C.; Sweet-Cordero, A.; Berger, A.; Brooks, A. N.
Abstract: Background: Although the impact of genomic variants and changes in transcriptome regulation are often studied in isolation, their interaction is critical to understanding oncogenesis. We developed FLAIR3, which performs a comprehensive and integrated analysis of single nucleotide variants (SNVs), indels, gene fusions, and alternative splicing using long-read RNA sequencing (lrRNA-seq) and predicts their combined impact on amino acid sequence. Results: By applying FLAIR3 to lrRNA-seq datasets from osteosarcoma and lung adenocarcinoma, we demonstrated that long-read technology captures the full-length molecules required to phase variants with specific isoforms. In the osteosarcoma samples, FLAIR3 identified alternative splicing of gene fusions in known driver genes, including TP53. In the lung adenocarcinoma samples, FLAIR3 revealed isoform-biased expression of oncogenic SNVs, including BRAF, CDKN2A, and TP53. Conclusions: FLAIR3 provides a robust method for resolving the complex interplay between variants and transcript isoforms, offering deeper insights into the molecular drivers of cancer.

Title: RoDPAA: A Robust Dissimilarity-Based Principal Angle Analysis Framework for Multi-View Microbiome Data Integration
Authors: Xu, Y.; Wang, Y.
Abstract: Multiview microbiome studies profile the same participants across body sites or molecular layers, but integration is hampered by sparse, compositional data, modest sample sizes and methods that recognize only exact sharing. We present RoDPAA (Robust Dissimilarity-based Principal Angle Analysis), a framework that represents each view through any data-appropriate dissimilarity, such as Bray--Curtis, without log-ratio transformation or likelihood assumptions. RoDPAA aligns view-specific signal subspaces through principal angles, captures complete and partial sharing, and tests by permutation how many components are shared, using only eigendecomposition and little tuning. In Gaussian simulations, RoDPAA matched JIVE and MOFA given true ranks, ran faster and alone recovered the shared dimension in every replicate. In two inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) cohorts with sparse, zero-inflated data, Bray--Curtis-based RoDPAA recovered shared structure that was stable to prevalence filtering, whereas log-ratio-based alternatives were not. Its leading microbiome--metabolome factors, learned without disease labels, were the only ones associated with IBD.

Title: CryoSHIELDs: tunable amphipathic peptide additives for cryo-EM
Authors: Azumaya, C. M.; Dutka, P.; Johnson, M. C.; Ravala, S. K.; Wu, C.-G.; Delgado, B. D.; Anson, F.; Michaelian, N.; Koo, C. W.; Tom, J. Y. K.; Soong, T. H.; Burt, A.; Ti, S.; Howes, A. C.; Martinez, O. E.; Song, A.; Rohou, A.; Ciferri, C.; Yatskevich, S.
Abstract: While cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has transformed structural biology, sample preparation remains a major determinant of success. Specifically, the air-water interface (AWI) can damage complexes, impose preferred orientation, and reduce particle density. Here, we introduce cryoSHIELDs, a library of peptide additives designed to modulate the AWI and improve cryo-EM grid preparation. Across 24 diverse protein systems, cryoSHIELDs improved particle distribution, angular sampling, complex integrity, and, in selected cases, map quality and resolution. CryoSHIELDs enabled structure determination of the OSMR{beta}-Vixarelimab complex, the multi-subunit CCAN kinetochore complex without chemical cross-linking, and membrane proteins including ABCC6 and the -opioid receptor-Gi complex, the latter resolved at 2.3 A using tenfold lower protein concentration without compromising map quality. CryoSHIELDs provide a simple, tunable, and broadly applicable platform for more reliable cryo-EM in discovery biology and structure-based drug development.

Title: Molecular diffusion and binding kinetics are sufficient to explain condensate-like nuclear clustering
Authors: Kapoor, M.; Mir, M.
Abstract: Many key transcriptional regulators form clusters in cell nuclei that are proposed to promote transcription by concentrating reactants. These clusters exhibit emergent biophysical properties consistent with biomolecular condensates such as high local densities, spherical morphologies, fusion, and rapid molecular exchange kinetics. Whether these properties are specific hallmarks of condensation or can arise from simpler mechanisms is unclear. Here we developed SPARK (Simulation of Protein Accumulation from Reaction Kinetics), a computational framework parameterized by genomic, and molecular diffusion and binding kinetics data, to simulate the spatial distributions of chromatin-binding proteins as they would appear under an optical microscope. These simulations recapitulate key reported features of Brd4, Nanog, Sox2, and Bicoid clusters, without including any higher-order protein-protein interactions or phase separation. We demonstrate that commonly used signatures of condensates instead emerge directly from molecular scale binding and diffusion kinetics. Through systematic variation of nuclear concentrations and enhancer binding-site composition, we show that distinct combinations of molecular kinetics can result in similar spatial distributions of transcription factors. These analyses establish that imaging-based features of protein clusters cannot uniquely define the underlying physical mechanism of their formation. We therefore conclude that condensation is not required to drive transcription factor occupancy and that protein-protein interactions off chromatin are not required to explain cluster formation. Our results instead imply that mechanisms other than clustering are sufficient for target-search acceleration and robust occupancy. SPARK thus provides a quantitative null model for identifying which molecular mechanisms are necessary to explain experimental observations of nuclear protein clustering.

Title: Hierarchical organization in sparse gene regulatory networks shapes structural coherence and emergent regulatory coordination
Authors: Harlapur, P.; Jagadeesan, R.; Ribeiro, A. S.; Kadelka, C.; Jolly, M. K.
Abstract: A fundamental challenge in systems biology is understanding how regulatory coordination is maintained within extremely sparse gene regulatory networks (GRNs). While traditional unsigned network metrics can quantify the overall magnitude of influence a specific node or edge exerts over the network, they cannot predict the functional direction and consistency of these regulatory changes. To address this gap, we introduce the coherence matrix. This topology-based framework for signed, directed GRNs computes a strictly bounded, interpretable measure of directional regulatory coordination between gene pairs. Using synthetic network ensembles, we demonstrate that architectures with low intrinsic structural coherence suffer severe density-driven scaling penalties. Such structures cannot scale without requiring biologically unrealistic edge densities. Applying this framework to six whole-organism GRNs reveals how biological topologies overcome these limitations. Whole-organism GRNs exhibit lower overall coherence and more fragmented structures than expected, avoiding rigid global co-regulation to maximize regulatory degrees of freedom. Furthermore, these systems resolve the scaling penalties of complex, low-coherence architectures by restricting dense regulatory crosstalk to a compact intermediate core. Modeling synthetic hierarchical networks confirms that this architecture, a compact core within a globally feed-forward scaffold, neutralizes scaling penalties by minimizing nodes requiring dense connectivity. This allows GRNs to efficiently route decisions despite extreme sparsity. Finally, validation with transcriptomic data confirms that coherence matrix accurately predicts empirical co-regulation directionality. By moving beyond unsigned connectivity, the structural coherence framework provides a quantitative tool to map how the intrinsic behavior of localized interactions scales into macroscopic, system-wide coordination.

Title: Proteome-wide discovery of novel diagnostic antigens for coccidioidomycosis
Authors: Elko, E.; Ryle, L.; Nelson, G. A.; Sarbo, N. G.; Harms, C. E.; Kelley, E.; Fredericks, M. N.; Keim, P.; Knox, K.; Kala, M.; Fuller, D. H.; Settles, E. W.; Barker, B. M.; Magee, D. M.; Lake, D. F.; Grys, T. E.; Thompson, G. R.; Altin, J.; Ladner, J. T.; Mead, H. L.
Abstract: Coccidioidomycosis, commonly called Valley Fever (VF), caused by Coccidioides spp., is an understudied fungal disease that accounts for a substantial fraction of pneumonias in endemic areas. Diagnosis remains challenging because the mainstay of diagnosis is serology, and current assays have modest sensitivity in early infection. Discovery of new antigens could improve serologic detection early in disease. Here, we use PepSeq, a DNA-programmable serology platform, to represent the complete proteome of Coccidioides within a library of 244,000 DNA-barcoded peptides. By profiling antibody reactivity at the protein and epitope levels in VF patients, naturally infected pigtail macaques, and healthy controls, we identify numerous previously-unrecognized antigens and epitopes, including some shared between humans and macaque responses. When translated into a pooled peptide ELISA, we show that a subset of identified antigens can discriminate VF cases from controls in an independent cohort with high accuracy (AUC = 0.91). These findings establish high-dimensional peptide serology as a scalable approach for fungal antigen discovery and identify new targets for improved VF diagnosis.

Title: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus in summer of 2026 shows antigenic advance of H3N2 subclade K region D mutants and H1N1 D.3.1.1 Sa mutants
Authors: Kikawa, C.; Butler, A.; Huddleston, J.; Turner, S. A.; Peck, H.; Englund, J. A.; Lacombe, K.; Busch, M.; Lanteri, M. C.; Stone, M.; Spencer, B.; Greninger, A. L.; Smith, D. J.; Wallace, S.; Marshall, H. S.; Tosif, S.; Hensley, S. E.; Barr, I. G.; Bloom, J. D.
Abstract: Human seasonal influenza evolves rapidly, necessitating twice yearly decisions about whether to update the strains in the vaccine. To help inform this decision, we have been using high-throughput sequencing-based neutralization assays to make twice yearly measurements of how recent human sera neutralize current human H3N2 and H1N1 strains. Here we provide the third installment in this series of measurements by reporting 52,268 titers representing neutralization of 148 viral strains by 355 human sera collected between April and August of 2026. Our measurements show that new H3N2 subclade K strains with mutations in antigenic region D and new H1N1 subclade D.3.1.1 strains with mutations in antigenic region Sa (such as G155E) have reduced neutralization by human sera, with notable heterogeneity in the impact of some of these mutations across sera from different individuals. This paper is accompanied by an interactive summary (https://jbloomlab.github.io/flu-seqneut-2026/summary.html) that enables detailed exploration of the results, and all titer data are publicly available for further analysis to aid vaccine antigen selection and studies of viral evolution.

Title: Integrated omics analysis reveals reorganization of nitrogen and lipid metabolism in a toluene-degrading bacterium in the gas phase
Authors: Inoue, S.; Naobayashi, T.; Tokiyoshi, K.; Yoshimoto, S.; Tsugawa, H.; Hori, K.
Abstract: Gas-phase bioprocesses, in which microbial cells are immobilized on solid carriers exposed to the gas phase, enable efficient conversion of poorly water-soluble compounds for biodegradation and bioproduction. However, operation without a surrounding bulk aqueous medium can constrain the replenishment of water and nonvolatile nutrients. The metabolic mechanisms that sustain cellular activity in these low-water environments remain largely unknown. Here, we elucidated the metabolic alterations in the highly adhesive bacterium Acinetobacter sp. Tol 5 degrading toluene in the gas and aqueous phases. Polyurethane carriers bearing cells from independent cultures were assigned to the gas phase or to two aqueous media, nitrogen-depleted basal salt medium and phosphate-buffered saline, so that the conditions differed only in phase and nutrient availability. In cells actively degrading toluene, integrated metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics (97 metabolites, 108 lipids, and 3,899 genes) revealed a metabolic state specific to the gas phase. Under gas-phase conditions, amino acid and nucleotide degradation was enhanced while the intracellular glutamate pool was maintained at a high level, and citrulline specifically accumulated. Membrane lipids were remodeled, and the storage lipid triacylglycerol was consumed, suggesting that it serves as an endogenous carbon and energy source and may also contribute to metabolic water production under nutrient- and water-limited gas-phase conditions. These findings highlight nitrogen metabolism and lipid mobilization as features of gas-phase adaptation, providing a rational basis for designing robust gas-phase bioprocesses and selecting suitable microbial chassis.
